papers.title: ASTROLABE: A 3D Particle-Level Surrogate for Cosmology Simulation with Physical Flow Matching
papers.abstract: The microphysics of dark matter (DM) is imprinted on cosmological structure across an enormous dynamic range. Nonlinear cosmological observables are most reliably modeled with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations. However, systematic N-body scans over DM theory space are prohibitively expensive. Machine learning emulators provide a possible solution, but are currently limited by either low resolution or only the ability to emulate specific observables. We introduce Astrolabe, a flow-matching-based generative emulator designed to be free of both constraints. Astrolabe acts directly on the 6N phase-space coordinates of N individual particles. With no voxel grid in the output, there is no voxel-resolution ceiling, and in principle any observable can be measured from inference. Astrolabe is computationally tractable via a field-particle hybrid transformer in which every particle cross-attends to multiscale field tokens, so compute and memory are linear in N. Astrolabe incorporates physical flow matching by taking the prior distribution for the flow to be approximate COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (COLA)-based coordinates rather than unphysical noise, with momentum and mass conservation enforced at all points along flow time. In the Lambda-CDM cases we test, Astrolabe produces realistic fields with accurate power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and halo density profiles. We also observe out-of-distribution generalization, with accurate emulation of dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions. Astrolabe is also capable of being fine-tuned to simulate very large N and we demonstrate this by emulating a TNG50-3-dark simulation at a fraction of the cost. This method represents a first step toward a general and powerful cosmology simulation surrogate, which may eventually permit the inclusion of baryonic physics and a systematic exploration of richer dark sector interactions.
papers.summary: Systematic scans over dark matter (DM) theory space with N-body cosmological simulations are too expensive, and existing machine-learning emulators either work on low-resolution voxel grids or only predict specific observables. `Astrolabe` is a flow-matching generative emulator that acts directly on the phase-space coordinates of individual particles, using a field-particle hybrid transformer in which every particle cross-attends to multiscale field tokens so that compute and memory scale linearly with particle count. The flow starts from approximate COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (`COLA`) coordinates rather than noise, with momentum and mass conservation enforced along the whole flow. **On Lambda-CDM test cases it reproduces power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and halo density profiles**, generalizes to dark-acoustic-oscillation initial conditions it was not trained on, and can be fine-tuned to emulate a `TNG50-3-dark` simulation at a fraction of the cost.

papers.title: scPyviewer: a Python-native interactive viewer from AnnData single-cell data
papers.abstract:
Motivation: Interactive web tools enabling non-programmers to explore single-cell datasets, embeddings, gene expression, metadata, and marker genes are standard laboratory infrastructure. However, actively maintained tools (e.g., ShinyCell, ScRDAVis, sCIRCLE) rely on R Shiny and require Seurat objects. Python/scanpy, the dominant framework for single-cell RNA-seq and spatial analysis, lacks a lightweight, native option pairing a shareable viewer with a scriptable Python API. Sharing scanpy results currently requires converting to Seurat or sharing code notebooks.
  Results: We present scPyviewer, a web viewer that ingests AnnData objects directly and reproduces incumbent interaction patterns within the Python stack. In a feature-parity audit against three R Shiny tools, scPyviewer matches or exceeds baseline capabilities (7/7), uniquely offering native AnnData ingestion without conversion and cross-dataset comparison over shared genes and matched cell types. Benchmark tests across three datasets (22,315 to ~313,000 cells) show scPyviewer renders every core view faster (up to 3.6x speedup) using lower memory (5.2x lower on the smallest dataset). On 313,000 cells, scPyviewer completes all views while Seurat exhausts an 8 GB memory limit and fails. Beyond the app, scPyviewer exposes a Python API returning Matplotlib figures and pandas tables for publication-ready output.
  Availability and implementation: Implemented in Python 3.11 (scanpy 1.11.5, anndata 0.12.19, streamlit 1.59.2, plotly 6.9.0) with a one-command interface to reproduce benchmarks, figures, and launch the app. Source code: https://github.com/xuan13hao/scPyviewer.git
papers.summary: Interactive viewers that let non-programmers explore single-cell datasets are standard lab tooling, but the actively maintained options are built on R Shiny and require `Seurat` objects, leaving the dominant Python `scanpy` ecosystem without a native equivalent. `scPyviewer` is a Streamlit-based web viewer that ingests `AnnData` objects directly, reproduces the interaction patterns of the R tools, adds cross-dataset comparison over shared genes and matched cell types, and exposes a Python API returning Matplotlib figures and pandas tables. In a feature-parity audit against three R Shiny tools it matches or exceeds all seven baseline capabilities, and **on a 313,000-cell dataset it completes every view while `Seurat` exhausts an 8 GB memory limit and fails**, with up to 3.6x faster rendering and 5.2x lower memory on the smaller datasets.

papers.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Algorithmic Resilience and the Non-Linear Governance Premium in Sovereign Capital Flows
papers.abstract: Despite the proliferation of sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics, traditional linear macro-financial models systematically misprice Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) tail risks during systemic shocks. This paper demonstrates that sovereign risk transmission is fundamentally non-linear. Using a forward-chained global panel of 147 sovereign entities (2010-2024), we deploy a gradient boosting architecture that compresses forecast errors by over 39% against L1-regularized baselines precisely during extreme macroeconomic tail events. Moving beyond opaque predictive accuracy, we apply dual interpretability frameworks to mathematically map the discrete threshold effects of institutional quality. We identify a strict, non-linear "Governance Premium": incremental environmental and social improvements yield zero capital advantage until a foundational regulatory threshold is breached. Finally, we establish regime-conditional 95% uncertainty bounds that maintain valid marginal coverage even under severe ESG reporting failures. This framework equips policymakers with a distribution-free tool to quantify sovereign tail-risk, proving that global capital markets price institutional resilience as a discrete boundary rather than a continuous premium.
papers.summary: Linear macro-financial models systematically misprice Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) tail risks during systemic shocks, even when sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics are included. Using a forward-chained panel of 147 sovereign entities from 2010 to 2024, the authors train a gradient boosting model, apply two interpretability frameworks to map threshold effects of institutional quality, and add regime-conditional distribution-free 95% uncertainty bounds. **The model cuts forecast errors by over 39% against L1-regularized baselines during extreme macroeconomic tail events**, and the interpretability analysis finds a non-linear governance premium in which environmental and social improvements yield no capital advantage until a foundational regulatory threshold is crossed. The uncertainty bounds keep valid marginal coverage even under severe ESG reporting failures.

papers.title: Task-Utility IQA: Rethinking Image Quality Assessment in Embodied Tasks
papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.
papers.summary: Image quality assessment (IQA) methods typically regress task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks, which mismatches embodied settings where whether an image is adequate depends on the task goal, context, and the actions an agent must take. The authors argue for reframing IQA as goal-conditioned judgment and propose an agent framework built on a multimodal large language model (MLLM) that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence in the image, and outputs decision-facing assessments. **In a compact evidence study on `VisDrone`, conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream vision-language model (VLM) task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether the input supports the target task.**

papers.title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision-Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation
papers.abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.
papers.summary: Generative vision-language models (VLMs) can have hard-to-anticipate failure modes that disproportionately affect vulnerable communities. The authors probe two widely used VLMs by asking them to transform human face images to reflect a race (Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) or a sexual orientation (gay or straight), then analyze the resulting images and the models' downstream text. **The models often comply, compliance and refusal are non-deterministic and group-sensitive, and the generated images are statistically distinguishable and tend to accentuate stereotypes.** The same representational biases re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks, and the effect extends to criminality, which the authors connect to the possibility of AI-assisted profiling.

papers.title: ReCoPII: A Relation-Grounded Framework for Building Contextual PII Masking Datasets
papers.abstract: Training contextual masking systems for personally identifiable information (PII) requires examples distinguishing maskable from preservable mentions of one entity type, but privacy restrictions limit access to real data. Author-based augmentation (SPY) labels mentions unrelated to the author as non-PII, presuming a single data subject and overlooking others. We propose ReCoPII (Relation-grounded Contextual PII masking), a framework that builds such data without this premise: it plans ontology-constrained entity relations, writes insertion sentences with placeholders, reconstructs annotations with code, checks the result with a separate LLM, and derives MASK/KEEP labels from entity relations. On Korean documents from six domains, it yields ReCoPII-Ko, a corpus with relation, privacy, and MASK/KEEP annotations, which we validate. Across 300 pairs, four annotators agree with 88.42% of its sampled KEEP labels, against 26.27% for SPY-style augmentation of the same sources. Classifiers trained on it over-mask less than under that reference on a matched test. Contextual masking fine-tuned jointly with a PII detector removes most over-masking of detection alone within a fixed leakage budget; on human-verified entity records, the four detectors meeting it over-mask at most 5.04% with at most 4.18% leakage. The detector is comparable to XLM-R-large on KDPII with about a quarter of its parameters.
papers.summary: Training systems that mask personally identifiable information (PII) contextually requires examples that distinguish maskable from preservable mentions of the same entity type, but privacy rules limit access to real data, and author-based augmentation such as `SPY` assumes a single data subject and labels other people's details as non-PII. `ReCoPII` builds such data without that assumption: it plans ontology-constrained relations among entities, writes insertion sentences with placeholders, reconstructs annotations with code, checks the result with a separate large language model (LLM), and derives MASK/KEEP labels from the entity relations. Applied to Korean documents from six domains it yields `ReCoPII-Ko`, and **four annotators agree with 88.42% of its sampled KEEP labels versus 26.27% for `SPY`-style augmentation of the same sources**. A contextual masker fine-tuned jointly with a PII detector removes most of the over-masking of detection alone within a fixed leakage budget, and the detector matches `XLM-R-large` on `KDPII` with about a quarter of the parameters.

papers.title: SCOPE: Source Credibility and Outlet Profiling Engine
papers.abstract: We present SCOPE, a multi-agent system for profiling news media outlets with respect to bias, factuality, and credibility. Given an outlet URL, SCOPE coordinates specialized agents for article acquisition, content analysis, external evidence search, scoring, and report generation. The system follows an MBFC-style methodology while making intermediate evidence and agent outputs inspectable through a structured demonstration interface. On a benchmark of 200 media outlets, SCOPE outperforms LLM-only, article-only, search-only, and media-background-check baselines on most metrics, achieving the lowest bias and factuality MAE, perfect failed-fact-check detection, and the lowest factual error rate. These results suggest that decomposed, evidence-grounded agent workflows can support more transparent and reliable media profiling. Our code is available at https://github.com/mbaisbay/SCOPE, and a live demonstration at https://scope-demo.streamlit.app/.
papers.summary: Profiling news outlets for bias, factuality, and credibility is usually done by hand following methodologies like that of Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC). `SCOPE` is a multi-agent system that, given an outlet URL, coordinates specialized agents for article acquisition, content analysis, external evidence search, scoring, and report generation, and exposes the intermediate evidence and agent outputs through a structured interface. **On a benchmark of 200 outlets it beats LLM-only, article-only, search-only, and media-background-check baselines on most metrics**, with the lowest bias and factuality mean absolute error, perfect detection of failed fact checks, and the lowest factual error rate.

papers.title: Who Convinced Whom? Tracing How LLMs Change Their Minds in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve language-model decisions through the exchange of arguments, yet agreement after debate need not reflect independent corroboration. We investigate how peer communication influences individual decisions and collective outcomes through behavioral and internal interventions. We introduce MAD Bench, a 2,400-question benchmark spanning knowledge and reasoning, values and moral judgment, and safety and refusal, and evaluate three open-weight models using a round-matched independent-reflection control. Among answer-changing responses, a forced-choice readout before rationale generation matches the eventual answer more often in debate than in reflection (65.4% versus 22.3% on Qwen3.5-9B). Message ablations reveal model-dependent effects of peer answers and reasoning, while attributing identical text to the receiver rather than another agent substantially changes its influence. For the tested source descriptions, stated track record affects answer preferences more strongly than professional-status cues across all three models. Attention masking produces different changes in decision margins across the three checkpoints. On fully parsed, reference-labelled non-numeric questions, debate yields small estimated accuracy improvements over initial majority voting, while increasing the rate of unanimous wrong answers by 3.1-7.4 percentage points relative to reflection. Longer debates show persistent consensus and greater correlation between agents' correctness than reflection. These findings show that stronger consensus can coexist with more shared errors, motivating evaluations that assess dependence and unanimous errors alongside accuracy.
papers.summary: Multi-agent debate (MAD) is meant to improve language-model decisions through the exchange of arguments, but agreement after debate may reflect social influence rather than independent corroboration. The authors introduce `MAD Bench`, 2,400 questions spanning knowledge and reasoning, values and moral judgment, and safety and refusal, and compare three open-weight models under debate against a round-matched independent-reflection control, using message ablations, source-attribution swaps, and attention masking to trace where influence comes from. Among answer-changing responses on `Qwen3.5-9B`, a forced-choice readout taken before rationale generation matches the final answer 65.4% of the time in debate versus 22.3% in reflection, and a stated track record sways answers more than professional-status cues across all three models. **Debate yields only small accuracy gains over initial majority voting while raising the rate of unanimous wrong answers by 3.1 to 7.4 percentage points relative to reflection**, so stronger consensus coexists with more shared errors.

papers.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
papers.abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI drafts of the same kind of brief, built from SEC filings made after the models' training data were collected. Told the drafter's true error rate, the reviewer checked more as it rose, but all-or-nothing, switching near where its prompt's costs break even. Told that the drafter erred ten times less often than it did, it checked 7 fewer of 9 figures and let a wrong figure through in 22.5% of briefs instead of none: faster and worse, entirely through reduced effort.
papers.summary: What it means for AI assistance to save time is contested: a stopwatch view counts whatever the clock records, while a ledger view treats time saved as a counterfactual that must be read alongside the errors the work lets through. The author argues for the ledger view, defining time saved, excess escaped defects, and a break-even defect cost, and gives a model of checking in which a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on model quality until the model is good enough not to check, checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate, and over-trust saves clock minutes at a larger total cost. **A replication of the `METR` developer study from its public data shows the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand, with AI helping on anywhere from 3% to 82% of them**, while in the review-every-output workflow of `GDPval` review time alone caps the speedup of `GPT-5` at 3.6x. In a small pre-specified experiment with AI reviewers checking AI-drafted briefs built from SEC filings, telling the reviewer the drafter erred ten times less often than it did made it check 7 fewer of 9 figures and let a wrong figure through in 22.5% of briefs instead of none.

papers.title: Curriculum-Driven Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Far-Range Rocket Landing
papers.abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.
papers.summary: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles involves highly nonlinear dynamics, tight precision requirements, and environmental uncertainty, and prior reinforcement learning (RL) approaches rely on flat training with simplified initial conditions. The proposed framework trains an agent through a three-stage curriculum with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism against catastrophic forgetting, feeds it a full 3x3 rotation matrix in the observation vector, and redesigns the reward so that per-step magnitude is bounded while a progress term accumulates the total distance closed along the trajectory. Starting from horizontal distances of 1,000 to 1,500 units, far beyond earlier benchmarks, **the policy lands successfully in 99.98% of 100,000 evaluation episodes versus 68.31% for the baseline**, retaining 69.1% of initial fuel and reaching a mean final distance of 7.07 units from the pad centre against 13.10 for the baseline.

papers.title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
papers.abstract: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.
papers.summary: Low-bit weight-activation quantization cuts the memory and compute needed to serve large language models, but activation rounding still degrades accuracy after calibration because reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot tell apart activations that fall in the same quantization bin. `ResCom` adds a low-rank correction driven by the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error, with an output-aware calibration that picks residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and solves for the correction in closed form, requiring no gradient training or changes to the calibrated weights. **On `Llama-3-8B` with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce `WikiText-2` perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, lift `MMLU` by 2.89 points, and raise five-shot `GSM8K` accuracy from 23.96% to 36.16%.** Evaluations extend to models from 1B to 70B parameters and held-out `C4`, and the FP32 implementation adds 2.25% to 4K-token prefill time while a compact-storage variant keeps a 27.7% peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.

papers.title: Structured Time-Frequency Representation for Channel Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate CSI forecasting is essential for mitigating channel aging and supporting reliable downlink transmission in high-mobility wireless systems. In FDD systems, forecasting future DL CSI from historical UL observations requires joint temporal extrapolation and cross-band inference. However, defining historical UL as the input and future DL as the target does not specify how elapsed time and UL-to-DL band separation should be represented in a pretrained predictor's positional space. FAR-CSI establishes an FDD-aware representation of channel forecasting within a joint temporal and operating-band positional field. Within this field, historical UL observations and future DL targets occupy segregated regions according to their temporal and operating-band roles, preserving the distinction between observed UL context and unobserved DL prediction targets. This representation is instantiated through a unified structured routing rule that governs encoder positional assignment, decoder-field reconstruction, and future-DL target selection, ensuring the same FDD geometry is preserved from contextual encoding to prediction readout. Under matched backbone, initialization, and training conditions, FDD-aware routing reduces NMSE by 21.44\% relative to generic routing. Across the evaluated FDD baselines, FAR-CSI achieves higher CSI prediction accuracy and MRT-based spectral efficiency, while retaining its predictive advantage across mobility conditions, prediction horizons, reduced training-data regimes, and noisy historical observations.
papers.summary: In frequency-division duplex (FDD) wireless systems, forecasting future downlink channel state information (CSI) from historical uplink observations requires both temporal extrapolation and cross-band inference, and it is unclear how elapsed time and uplink-to-downlink band separation should be represented in a pretrained predictor's positional space. `FAR-CSI` places uplink history and downlink targets in segregated regions of a joint temporal and operating-band positional field and applies a single structured routing rule to encoder positional assignment, decoder-field reconstruction, and target selection, so the same FDD geometry persists from encoding to readout. **Under matched backbone, initialization, and training conditions, FDD-aware routing reduces normalized mean squared error by 21.44% relative to generic routing**, and the method keeps its accuracy and spectral-efficiency advantage over FDD baselines across mobility conditions, prediction horizons, reduced training data, and noisy observations.

papers.title: AgentBaton: Efficient Model Collaboration in Agentic Tasks
papers.abstract: Solving long-horizon agentic tasks requires language agents to interact with their environments over multiple steps, and reliable performance often comes from the expensive capable models available through cloud providers. Meanwhile, alternative efficient models with inferior performance but a much lower cost are emerging, including lower-tier cloud models and smaller open-weights models deployable on local hardware. This raises a natural question that remains less explored than traditional query-level routing: can capable and efficient models collaborate within a single long-horizon agentic task to substantially reduce cost while preserving task accuracy? In this paper, we systematically investigate key design choices for such collaboration through model handoffs, where one model takes over from another, focusing on handoff direction and context transfer. We find that efficient-to-capable handoffs generally underperform capable-only execution with limited or even no cost reduction, whereas capable-to-efficient handoffs at suitable stages of task progress largely preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing cost. These findings suggest that a one-time, simple, well-timed handoff strategy is good enough for cost-effective agent collaboration, motivating AgentBaton, a lightweight detector that learns when to hand off from recurring patterns in task progress. Across 11 model pairs and two representative benchmarks, AgentBaton reduces API costs by 65.9% on average while largely preserving task accuracy, with accuracy gains of up to 8.8 percentage points over capable-only execution. Experiments across various reasoning-effort settings further show that AgentBaton extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agentic tasks are usually run end to end on expensive capable cloud models, while cheaper lower-tier cloud models and small open-weight models that run on local hardware go unused. The authors study model handoffs, where one model takes over from another partway through a task, varying handoff direction and context transfer, and find that efficient-to-capable handoffs underperform capable-only execution with little or no cost saving, whereas capable-to-efficient handoffs at the right stage of task progress preserve or improve accuracy while cutting cost substantially. This motivates `AgentBaton`, a lightweight detector that learns when to hand off from recurring patterns in task progress. **Across 11 model pairs and two benchmarks it reduces API costs by 65.9% on average while largely preserving accuracy, with gains of up to 8.8 percentage points over capable-only execution**, and it extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier across reasoning-effort settings.

papers.title: A Hyper-Logical View on Multi-Agent Path Planning
papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Path Planning (MAPP) requires collision-free paths for multiple agents. MAPP has numerous real-life applications, including the navigation of automated vehicles, and has therefore many variants considering different constraints, requirements, and objectives. For each such variant, a new algorithmic treatment is often developed. This paper takes a complementary, specification-centered view: we show that many MAPP variants can be modeled in HyperLTL, a temporal logic that reasons about multiple paths and their evolution through time, and in its omega-regular extension HyperQPTL. The contribution is not a claim that current hyperproperty model checkers replace specialized MAPP solvers. Rather, the hyper-logical view gives a unified language for comparing MAPP variants, adding cross-agent constraints, expressing optimality, and connecting MAPP to verification, explanation, and causality techniques for hyperproperties.
papers.summary: Multi-Agent Path Planning (MAPP) asks for collision-free paths for several agents, and its many variants, each with different constraints, requirements, and objectives, usually get their own bespoke algorithms. Taking a specification-centered view instead, the authors show that many MAPP variants can be expressed in `HyperLTL`, a temporal logic that reasons about multiple execution paths at once, and in its omega-regular extension `HyperQPTL`. **The claim is not that hyperproperty model checkers replace specialized MAPP solvers, but that the hyper-logical encoding gives a unified language for comparing variants, adding cross-agent constraints, expressing optimality, and connecting MAPP to verification, explanation, and causality techniques for hyperproperties.**

papers.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis
papers.abstract: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
papers.summary: Deploying large language model agents in specialized domains needs task-specific procedures that general models lack, yet parameter training is costly and opaque, hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to experts, and existing multi-agent evolution methods let the backbone model decide where and how much the system changes, so what gets learned follows the backbone's structural preferences rather than observed failures. `EMMA` treats the configuration of a multi-agent system, meaning the controller's routing memory, specialist prompts inherited from a generalist, and per-step procedural skills, as structured episodic memory with explicit ownership and admissibility rules: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope that owns its correction and proposes one edit there, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental, and bounded. **Across `KramaBench`, `AppWorld`, and `BBEH` with five backbones, it achieves the best overall score on every benchmark, up to 32.5% above the strongest of `ACE`, `GEPA`, `EvoMAS`, and `ADAS`**, while using 17 to 38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.

papers.title: Multiple Leak Localization in Water Distribution Networks through Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Leak localization in water distribution networks is challenging when multiple leaks occur simultaneously, particularly under sparse monitoring. Existing data-driven methods often assume a single or predefined number of leaks or require extensive enumeration of leak combinations. This study proposes a graph neural network (GNN) model that localizes a variable number of simultaneous leaks without specifying the leak count in advance or exhaustively generating every possible combination of leak locations for training. The model is evaluated on two benchmark networks of different sizes, the 31-node Hanoi network and the larger 92-node NET3 network, under variable demand, sparse pressure-sensor coverage, variable leak magnitudes, and varying numbers of simultaneous leaks. The GNN outperforms multilayer perceptron, support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, and random forest classifiers by up to 12% and 20% in accuracy respectively in Hanoi and NET3 networks. Consistent performance across both networks supports the scalability of the proposed approach.
papers.summary: Locating leaks in water distribution networks is hard when several occur at once under sparse sensor coverage, and existing data-driven methods either assume a single or fixed number of leaks or require enumerating leak combinations for training. The proposed graph neural network (GNN) localizes a variable number of simultaneous leaks without being told the count and without exhaustively generating every combination of leak locations. **On the 31-node `Hanoi` and 92-node `NET3` benchmark networks, under variable demand, sparse pressure sensors, varying leak magnitudes, and varying leak counts, it beats multilayer perceptron, support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, and random forest classifiers by up to 12% and 20% in accuracy respectively.**

papers.title: UnityBench-Mini3D: Evaluating LLM Agents for 3D Game Development in Unity
papers.abstract: Game development stresses coding agents in ways general software engineering does not: correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact, not on source code alone. Existing benchmarks mainly target platforms such as Godot and heavily rely on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. We present UnityBench-Mini3D, a benchmark of 77 project-level Unity tasks organized around seven expert-defined skill categories rather than tutorials or genres, with three difficulty tiers. Each task pairs a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements and is evaluated using 1,178 held-out, human-authored milestone tests covering scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior. This in-engine evaluation provides deterministic partial credit, localizes failures, and distinguishes partial implementations from complete solutions without relying on subjective judges. Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate reaches 80.9% on easy tasks but falls to 35.2% on hard tasks, with just 57.7% overall. UnityBench-Mini3D provides a reproducible, diagnostic testbed distinguishing systems across difficulty levels.
papers.summary: Game development stresses coding agents differently from general software engineering because correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact rather than on source code alone, and existing benchmarks mostly target Godot and lean on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. `UnityBench-Mini3D` contains 77 project-level Unity tasks across seven expert-defined skill categories and three difficulty tiers, each pairing a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements, and grades them in-engine with 1,178 held-out human-authored milestone tests over scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior, giving deterministic partial credit and localized failures. **Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate is 80.9% on easy tasks but only 35.2% on hard tasks, 57.7% overall.**

papers.title: Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.
papers.summary: Safety-critical automotive software adds two demands that generation-focused coding-agent research neglects: every change must be verified and traced to a requirement against standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR, and the code is written against layered architectures, embedded constraints, and organization-specific conventions that are scarce in general training data. The described assistant for automotive C/C++ exposes generate, edit, and verify tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) so developers can run verification on any code on demand, and customizes the underlying model through prompt engineering and fine-tuning on a dataset built from AUMOVIO production code that pairs each function with its requirement text and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior. **In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers reported verify as the most-used tool and applied it to their own code, not only generated output**, and 75% preferred the faster prompt-engineered configuration. Pattern checkers inspired by MISRA and AUTOSAR show prompt engineering producing fewer violations on C while fine-tuning conforms better to architecture patterns for C++.

papers.title: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
papers.abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. Second, we exploit this generated data in three scenarios: (S1) balancing class distribution in the original dataset, (S2) increasing the number of samples per class, and (S3) expanding the dataset while maintaining balanced classes. Third, we evaluate the impact of these data distributions (S1, S2, S3) on model perfor mance using the EfficientNetV2B0 architecture with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights. The experimental results show a substantial improvement in classifica tion accuracy, emphasizing the critical role of data diversity and class balance. These findings highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed strat egy of data generation and distribution for enhancing dataset quality, offering promising applications in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.
papers.summary: Deep learning classifiers for plant disease diagnosis are held back by small datasets and class imbalance. The authors combine traditional augmentation, `CutMix`, `MixUp`, and synthetic images from Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (`DCGANs`) to generate new samples, then use the generated data in three scenarios: balancing the original class distribution, increasing samples per class, and expanding the dataset while keeping classes balanced. Evaluating each distribution with a pre-trained and fine-tuned `EfficientNetV2B0` on olive tree disease images, **they report a substantial improvement in classification accuracy, which they attribute to data diversity and class balance.**

papers.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
papers.abstract: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random. We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code. GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.
papers.summary: Conditional memory layers such as DeepSeek's `Engram` attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model and carry much of its factual recall: removing them from `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` costs 36.8 `PopQA` points. Low-bit quantization of these tables loses long-tail facts first, and the intuitive fix of giving more bits to frequently accessed rows is worse than refining rows at random, because each lookup's quantization error is weighted by a gate that is small for frequent n-grams and large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities. `GateRQ` exploits the fact that the gate can be computed from a 1-bit code: it stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps the first level in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. **Without retraining, it cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` and raises `vLLM` throughput by 11% to 31% over FP8 tables**, losing about 1 `PopQA` point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

papers.title: PROBE: Frontier Coding Agents Find Different Bugs Than Maintainers Fix
papers.abstract: Proactive bug discovery is an important software-engineering problem. Even though coding agents are already widely deployed in this domain, their capabilities remain understudied. In particular, the challenging task of finding all bugs that human maintainers would repair across an entire repository has not been studied yet. To close this gap, we introduce PROBE, a benchmark consisting of all 2,457 bugs fixed over the course of 18 months across 20 diverse GitHub repositories, together with a method for matching candidate findings to this partial reference set. We evaluate coding agents across frontier models and find they all achieve a recall of below $21\%$ and a precision of less than $9\%$ with respect to the reference set. While stronger models increase recall substantially from $8\%$ to $17\%$, they do not improve precision. Surprisingly, despite the low precision, LLM and human evaluators still judge $85\%$ of findings valid. Crucially, we find that found bug distributions are similar across agents but differ substantially from those of bugs fixed by maintainers. The practical relevance of bug discovery and the low recall of frontier models make this benchmark a valuable resource for both model users and developers.
papers.summary: Proactive bug discovery across whole repositories is a task coding agents are already deployed for but rarely measured on. The authors assemble `PROBE`, a benchmark of all 2,457 bugs that maintainers fixed over 18 months in 20 GitHub repositories, together with a procedure for matching an agent's reported findings against this partial reference set. Agents built on frontier models reach **below 21% recall and under 9% precision** against the reference set, and stronger models raise recall from 8% to 17% without improving precision. Despite the low precision, human and LLM evaluators judge 85% of the agents' findings valid, and the distribution of bugs agents find is similar across agents but differs substantially from the bugs maintainers actually fix.

papers.title: Layerwise Repacking: Variable-Length Hybrid-Attention Training without an Extra Redistribution Pass
papers.abstract:
Variable-length training creates conflicting parallelism requirements across the layers of a hybrid-attention model. The longest samples require wide sequence-parallel (SP) groups of 16 or 32 ranks for full attention, whose cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Sparse-attention layers, dominated by near-linear MoE work, can instead balance most evaluated workloads within node-local SP8 groups. Reusing the wide groups for these layers pushes their all-to-all communication across nodes, where the observed effective rate is 7.0x lower. Yet switching to smaller groups changes which ranks own each sample; a separate redistribution at every full-sparse boundary would introduce another data transfer.
  Layerwise Repacking keeps each SP16/32 parent for full attention and repacks its samples into node-local sparse children at SP{1, 2, 4, 8}, where hidden states persist between full layers. The layout change rides on the two existing full-layer Ulysses sites: at each, one variable-size all-to-all performs both the head exchange and the sample repacking, so no redistribution pass is added. Because the balance the children can reach depends on which samples share a parent, an auxiliary parent solver rebalances parent membership before the children are formed.
  On all 22 steps with SP16/32 parents among the first 200 training steps of a 1F3S hybrid-attention model (one full-attention layer per three sparse-attention layers), repacking alone reduces the mean end-to-end time by 5.95% and raises model FLOPs utilization (MFU) by 3.75 percentage points over the baseline with repacking disabled; with the improved solver, end-to-end time falls by 7.61% and MFU rises by 4.83 percentage points.
papers.summary: Training hybrid-attention models on variable-length sequences creates conflicting parallelism needs: the longest samples require wide sequence-parallel (SP) groups of 16 or 32 ranks for full-attention layers, while sparse-attention layers dominated by near-linear mixture-of-experts (MoE) work could be balanced within node-local groups of 8 ranks, and reusing the wide groups pushes their all-to-all traffic across nodes at a 7x lower effective rate. `Layerwise Repacking` keeps the wide parent group for full-attention layers and repacks its samples into node-local child groups for the sparse layers, folding the layout change into the two existing Ulysses all-to-all exchanges so that no extra redistribution pass is added, with an auxiliary solver rebalancing parent membership before the children are formed. On the 22 wide-parent steps among the first 200 training steps of a hybrid model with one full-attention layer per three sparse layers, repacking with the improved solver **cuts mean end-to-end time by 7.61% and raises model FLOPs utilization (MFU) by 4.83 percentage points** over the baseline without repacking.

papers.title: Pricing Cross-Bank Context in Federated Anti-Money Laundering
papers.abstract: Most graph-based Anti-Money Laundering (AML) methods assume access to a pooled transaction graph containing all accounts and payments, which in reality does not exist. Federated learning offers the necessary privacy guarantees but it remains unclear how money laundering patterns spanning separate graphs can effectively be detected. We exploit transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks to approximate remote account states locally, enabling multi-layer Graph Neural Network (GNN) computation without additional account-specific exchange. Starting from this baseline, we test whether the remaining context is worth sharing, using a disclosure ladder that adds two transaction counts per remote account or the counterparty's own GNN states. On AMLworld HI-Small, across six GNN backbones and up to 32 silos, the observable baseline yields the largest gain and keeps it as fragmentation shrinks the visible slice; counts add a robust correction, while exact remote states help only in specific regimes. In controlled privacy--utility studies, the noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value before it buys meaningful privacy, whereas counts stay useful even under strong privacy protection. These findings support a practical rule for banks: use what they already record, and formally protect the little that must move.
papers.summary: Graph-based anti-money laundering (AML) models usually assume a pooled transaction graph spanning all banks, which does not exist in practice, and it is unclear how laundering patterns that cross separately held graphs can be detected under federated learning. The authors observe that both endpoint banks already record each cross-bank transaction and use those records to approximate remote account states locally, so multi-layer graph neural networks (GNNs) can run without extra per-account exchange; they then test a disclosure ladder that adds two transaction counts per remote account or the counterparty's own GNN states. On `AMLworld HI-Small` across six GNN backbones and up to 32 silos, **the observable baseline delivers the largest gain** and keeps it as fragmentation grows, counts add a robust correction, and exact remote states help only in specific regimes. In privacy-utility studies, the noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value before it buys meaningful privacy, whereas counts stay useful under strong protection.

papers.title: PolicyMediator: Multi-Regional Policy Learning through Mediation Agents with Evolving Skills in OPC Ecosystems
papers.abstract: One-person companies (OPCs) are emerging enterprises operated by individual entrepreneurs through digital platforms and LLM-based AI agents. These highly skilled entrepreneurs are characterized by being digital nomads, with limited reliance on local ecosystems. Governments in China use distinct regional support policies to attract mobile OPCs, turning local support into a cross-regional coordination problem. OPCs compare regions to maximize their own utility, but imperfect policy perceptions may cause them to reject otherwise suitable locations. Existing policy-learning methods optimize resources under fixed perceptions, while consensus-formation methods aggregate views without feeding cognitive changes back into policy learning. This disconnect produces mismatched location choices and inefficient regional policy adjustment. We introduce PolicyMediator, a cognition-constrained leader-multi-follower Stackelberg framework with bilateral mediation. The mediator explains verified policies to OPCs to build awareness and trust, and reports their needs and unresolved concerns to governments for policy learning. Its self-evolving skills retain, revise, or prune strategies using verification, allocation, capacity, and objective trajectories rather than mediation success alone. Across six-region simulations in China with five OPC types, five scenarios, and three OPC-simulator backbones, PolicyMediator ranks first in all 15 OPC-backbone--scenario combinations. Over the eight-baseline mean, it improves the aggregate government objective, combining economic performance, employment benefit, and policy-access equality, by 42.4% and average OPC utility by 40.9%.
papers.summary: One-person companies (OPCs), run by individual entrepreneurs through digital platforms and LLM-based agents, are mobile enough that regional governments in China compete for them with distinct support policies, yet OPCs with imperfect perceptions of those policies may reject locations that would suit them. `PolicyMediator` frames this as a cognition-constrained leader-multi-follower Stackelberg game with a bilateral mediation agent that explains verified policies to OPCs and reports their unresolved needs back to governments for policy learning, retaining, revising, or pruning its own strategies based on verification, allocation, capacity, and objective trajectories rather than mediation success alone. In six-region simulations with five OPC types, five scenarios, and three OPC-simulator backbones, it ranks first in all 15 backbone-scenario combinations, **improving the aggregate government objective by 42.4% and average OPC utility by 40.9%** over the mean of eight baselines.

papers.title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
papers.abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.
papers.summary: System One decision models answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering a fast and cheap form of clinical decision support. The authors evaluate `MedJev`, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, on ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient-level prediction on `MIMIC-IV` and `MIMIC-IV ED`, against zero-shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. It scores 72.5% on `MedQA`, 75.4% on `USMLE`, and 80.1% on `NEJM`, approaching published `GPT-4` results with well-calibrated confidence, and **reaches an AUROC of 0.926 for in-hospital mortality**, above `XGBoost` at 0.902, while trailing supervised models on operational outcomes such as emergency-department triage admission and showing substantial miscalibration on patient-level tasks. A two-parameter recalibration step using 50 to 200 local labeled examples reduces the mortality expected calibration error from 0.286 to 0.007, and the code and evaluation harness are released.

papers.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation
papers.abstract: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
papers.summary: Sparse expert execution in a mixture-of-experts language model does not remove the stored states needed to fine-tune it. `DuplexTune` attaches trainable width bridges that connect two residual streams to the backbone, warms up the bridges before adapting the backbone with router weights frozen, and replays coupled hidden states through the pretrained attention and expert modules, with an analysis of the implicit state-recovery equation giving the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On `Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B` with a single H800, it **peaks at 38.8 GB of memory versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing** at 25.1 versus 19.9 samples per second, scoring 67.2% on `MMLU`, 75.6% on `GSM8K`, and 7.69 on `MT-Bench` but with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline.

papers.title: CIVER: Causal Intervention Verification for Reliable Code Review
papers.abstract: Code review is essential for maintaining software repositories by identifying defects, improving code quality, and supporting reliable software evolution. With the growing adoption of LLM-based coding agents, an increasing number of code contributions and repository changes are generated by these agents. Consequently, LLM-based code review agents are becoming increasingly prevalent to evaluate these contributions and maintain software quality. However, LLM reviewers often generate lengthy reviews containing numerous potential issues, many of which are false positives or lack sufficient evidence. These unreliable reviews can mislead developers and downstream coding agents, motivating the need to distinguish actionable findings from unsupported claims. We propose CIVER, a causal intervention-based framework that identifies the core issues underlying code-review findings and distinguishes genuine defects from false positives. CIVER integrates three modules: a review module assesses findings, an intervention module generates repair-oriented perturbations, and a verifier module scores review reliability. Through joint optimization via expert iteration, the three modules identify genuine defects by responding to targeted repairs while remaining stable under unrelated changes. Extensive experiments on SWE-Review-Bench demonstrate that CIVER correctly identifies 77% of genuine defects through targeted repairs. Cross-project and downstream repair evaluations further demonstrate that CIVER generalizes across repositories and improves coding agents' task success rates, highlighting its effectiveness for reliable automated code review.
papers.summary: LLM-based code review agents tend to produce long lists of potential issues, many of them false positives or unsupported by evidence, which can mislead both developers and downstream coding agents. `CIVER` treats review verification as causal intervention: a review module assesses each finding, an intervention module generates repair-oriented perturbations of the code, and a verifier module scores reliability by checking that genuine defects respond to targeted repairs while remaining stable under unrelated changes, with the three modules jointly optimized through expert iteration. On `SWE-Review-Bench` it **correctly identifies 77% of genuine defects through targeted repairs**, generalizes across projects, and raises the task success rates of coding agents that consume its verified reviews.

papers.title: Do Coding Agents Still Need a Debugger? Frontier-Model-Based Fault Localization at the Accuracy Ceiling
papers.abstract: Background: To localize a fault, a coding agent can reason from source code alone or use debugger assistance by running the program and stepping through it in an interactive debugger. While earlier agents struggled with static execution tracing and debugger operation, frontier LLMs have improved at both. Objective: We evaluate how accurately coding agents localize faults without tools across original and transformed programs, how much debugger assistance improves accuracy and at what cost, and how agents use it when optional. Methods: We seed 610 single-line faults into 144 LeetCodeDataset solutions and rewrite each faulty program with five recipes of behavior-preserving transformations. Agents based on Sol 6.1, Luna 6, and Qwen 3.8 localize each fault with no, optional, or encouraged debugger assistance. Results: Without tools, the agents localized 98.2 to 99.9% of faults in original and 96.7 to 99.9% in transformed programs, losing accuracy mainly where recipes restructured loops and conditions. Encouraged assistance removed 63% and 61% of Luna 6's and Qwen 3.8's remaining transformed errors (+2.1 and +1.3 percentage points) at 14.7 to 27.0 times the token use, while Sol 6.1 stayed at 99.9%. With optional assistance, Luna 6 and Qwen 3.8 still gained +1.5 and +1.3 points, though the agents used the interactive debugger in only 0.2 to 6.2% of runs. Conclusions: On short, precisely specified programs, current coding agents localize nearly all faults from source code alone, and debugger assistance removes most errors that remain. Given the choice, agents executed the program far more often than they stepped through it, yet kept most of the benefit.
papers.summary: Coding agents can localize a fault by reading source code alone or by running the program and stepping through it in an interactive debugger, and this study measures how much the debugger still adds for frontier models. The authors seed 610 single-line faults into 144 `LeetCodeDataset` solutions, rewrite each faulty program with five recipes of behavior-preserving transformations, and have agents based on `Sol 6.1`, `Luna 6`, and `Qwen 3.8` localize the faults with no, optional, or encouraged debugger assistance. **Without any tools the agents localize 98.2 to 99.9% of faults** in original programs and 96.7 to 99.9% in transformed ones, losing accuracy mainly where loops and conditions were restructured. Encouraged debugger use removes about 60% of the remaining errors for `Luna 6` and `Qwen 3.8` at 14.7 to 27 times the token cost, and when assistance is optional the agents step through the debugger in only 0.2 to 6.2% of runs, preferring to simply execute the program while keeping most of the benefit.

papers.title: Rollback: Experience Backtracking in World Models for Policy Improvement
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.
papers.summary: Action-conditioned world models are usually treated as forward-only stand-ins for the physical environment when improving robot policies, which ignores a capability no real environment has: rewinding to an earlier decision point. `Rollback` rolls back to critical decisions inside the world model, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts the outcomes to attribute success to individual actions, producing fine-grained action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. A distributed training system couples world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, and real transitions from the policy being trained continually correct the world model through a lightweight LoRA update the authors call test-time physics grounding. On block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling with real robots, success rates improve over the strongest baseline by 10.67, 11.11, and 11.85 absolute points, and the policy **surpasses the average success rate of human players on ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training** despite starting from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level.

papers.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.
papers.summary: Scaling multimodal agents through interaction is held back by the cost of building heterogeneous, verifiable environments and by manual harness iteration that cannot keep up with growing task diversity. `The Trinity` is a recursive self-improvement loop with three roles: an Evolver reorganizes tasks from surface categories into a hierarchical capability tree based on verified execution trajectories, a Creator abstracts the shared requirements at each node into simplified simulated worlds for capability learning while transfer is measured on the original tasks (a process the authors call `Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real`), and an Explorer evolves reusable capability modules into a harness tree through selective inheritance within a fixed topology. Because the resulting harnesses specialize in different capabilities, a `Capability-Aware Harness Router` uses public task information to pick compatible module configurations, and the evolved harnesses **improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks**, including two real-world embodied tasks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses has so far been text-only and task-specific, which overfits surface task categories and generalizes poorly across heterogeneous multimodal tasks. `The Trinity` instead regroups tasks by the capabilities they share, builds simplified verifiable simulated worlds for each capability node, and evolves a tree of reusable harness modules around a frozen `Claude Opus 5` backbone.

- Three roles cooperate on a shared capability tree: Evolver induces the tree from verified training trajectories as a trie over sorted requirement sets, Creator abstracts each node's common requirements into compact simulated worlds via `Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real`, Explorer evolves node-specific modules with selective parent inheritance, and a Capability-Aware Harness Router picks a compatible branch at deployment from public task information plus retrieved execution experience.
- Over four self-improvement iterations the mean training score climbs from **39.1 to 73.2** across 28 benchmarks, and the final unseen mean reaches **64.1** across 18 benchmarks (a 34- and 26-point gain per the headline), beating Codex (47.5) and DeepSeek (46.2) reference means, though Crafter and DiG-bench stay below both and Eleusis slightly regresses.
- Organization matters: the simulated capability tree scores 56.95/47.26 (train/unseen, modules only) versus 53.04/42.92 for one global harness and 51.17/40.82 for 15 task-specific harnesses, at the lowest inference cost but roughly double the first-iteration training tokens (405.70M vs 211.56M for the real-task tree) because world construction dominates.
- Full agent self-routing reaches 71.27/60.96 against an Oracle's 73.16/63.61 and Random's 52.74/46.23, and controlled interventions show adding one capability-relevant module to the base harness lifts train from 39.06 to 58.45 (**+19.39**) while an irrelevant module adds only 1.02.
- Real-robot success on `SOON` (Unitree G1) and `CaP-X` (AlohaMini2) rises from 0% to 60%, but the authors note these comparisons do not isolate module evolution from skill preparation, and the headline gains likewise bundle evaluation-time skills (skills alone score 58.86/48.67, above modules alone), with the 17 native benchmarks moving only 64.4 to 68.8 after the first iteration.

papers.title: How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient.
