We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.
papers.summary: Financial institutions bound by data-residency rules must use open-weight models small enough to host locally, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning, and the on-policy distillation (OPD) methods that could close the gap require either a strong external teacher or, in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), a full reference solution. `Fin-SD` instead has the student identify the first wrong step in its own failed trajectory and write a short critique, truncates the trajectory just before the error, conditions a frozen copy of the student on that prefix plus the hint, and distills from it under reverse KL over a short rollout, with no external model contributing a gradient. Applied to `GPT-OSS-20B` on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark, it gains 3.03 percentage points over the base model on the `FinanceReasoning` Hard subset, but **a generic-feedback control with no real critique matches the entire gain**, suggesting the benefit comes from where supervision is applied rather than the hint content. Hints written by the roughly 6x larger `GPT-OSS-120B` add no material benefit over self-written ones, the method matches full-solution self-distillation on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens, and `MMLU-Pro` and a fourteen-metric `FinTrust` compliance audit show no material regression.

papers.title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
papers.abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.
papers.summary: LLM agents that curate clinical cohorts should absorb changes to eligibility criteria without reprocessing requirements that have not changed. `CohortFlow` represents each natural-language correction as a localized update to a structured cohort specification and reconciles it with a persistent execution graph whose explicitly recorded semantic dependencies allow only the affected computations to be invalidated while valid prior results are kept. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria with 126 correction turns, localized steering with the same 8B model reaches 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration, a difference that is not statistically significant, while **cutting mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion** and 44.3% during execution with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept on `MIMIC`, all 13 cohort states execute successfully and correction trajectories show unaffected computations being preserved while changed or dependent nodes are recomputed.

papers.title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.
papers.summary: Tools exposed to LLM agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are described in natural-language metadata, which creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this tool-poisoning setting, `Log-To-Leak` is an additive attack whose injected directive induces one extra attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate tool call, targeting the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response, and is operationalized through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure components. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, drawn from five MCP servers and four LLM agents, the attack **achieves an attack success rate of 62.64 to 100%** with conditional logging accuracy of 76.55 to 95.64%, while 16 pairs see target-task completion change by at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual success above 55% on `GitHub MCP` with `GPT-4o`, and an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign tool descriptions, which the authors take as motivation for host-controlled authorization of secondary tool calls.

papers.title: Dirichlet Process Mixtures within Semiparametric Bayesian Networks: A Novel Conditional Density Estimation Approach
papers.abstract: Semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBNs) are flexible probabilistic graphical models for representing joint distributions of continuous variables through lower-dimensional conditional probability distributions (CPDs). Existing SPBN models use kernel density estimators (KDEs) for non-parametric CPD modeling, but their one-component-per-observation mixture representation can lead to increased inference costs and density estimation errors, which can be limiting. In this work, we define a new CPD modeling approach for non-parametric components based on Bayesian non-parametric Dirichlet Process Mixtures (DPMs) within SPBNs. DPMs provide a data-adaptive clustering of observations, yielding a more compact representation while retaining the flexibility of non-parametric density estimation, unlike KDE. This results in lower inference costs while improving density estimation performance. We implement the proposed DPM-based SPBN (DPM-SPBN) by extending the open-source PyBNesian package and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world data. For a given network structure, DPM-based CPDs significantly outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian network models for continuous variables in density estimation, achieving lower absolute log-likelihood errors on synthetic data. We further investigate the impact of the proposed CPD modeling on structure learning methods relying on CPD-based scores. DPM-based SPBNs achieve lower structure learning and density estimation errors than KDE-based SPBNs. Experiments on real-world data corroborate these findings, identifying DPM-based CPD modeling as the most effective alternative among the evaluated non-parametric approaches for continuous variables.
papers.summary: Semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBNs) represent joint distributions of continuous variables through lower-dimensional conditional probability distributions (CPDs), but their existing kernel density estimator (KDE) components keep one mixture component per observation, which raises inference cost and density estimation error. The authors replace these with Dirichlet process mixtures (DPMs), which cluster observations adaptively into a more compact non-parametric representation, and implement the resulting `DPM-SPBN` by extending the open-source `PyBNesian` package. For a fixed network structure, DPM-based CPDs **achieve lower absolute log-likelihood errors than state-of-the-art continuous Bayesian network models on synthetic data**, and inside score-based structure learning they give lower structure and density errors than KDE-based SPBNs, with real-world experiments corroborating both findings.

papers.title: Scaling and Renormalization in Neural Networks: An Effective Renormalization-Group Description of Grokking
papers.abstract: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization in deep neural networks (NNs). We examine whether scaling and renormalization group (RG) theories can describe this dynamics, establishing a quantitative physical framework for neural generalization transitions. For modular addition on a two-layer NN, an ensemble of trained models defines an order parameter (the squared weight norm) and fluctuation proxies for the heat capacity and the susceptibility, with training epoch and weight decay serving as thermal and field control coordinates. To bridge neural architectures to real-space RG, we construct an exact coupling matrix via a second-order expansion of the loss with respect to per-neuron norms and use its Fiedler vector to define an effective geometry. This spectral ordering yields a monotonic spatial decay of coupling strength that is absent under random permutations. We then execute real-space RG by block-spin aggregating adjacent neurons and parameterizing the coupling matrix into off-diagonal band strengths. Linearizing this local RG map yields relevant scaling exponents and five derived critical exponents, with direct empirical estimates matching RG predictions within 1-10%. Overall, our framework provides a consistent effective description of grokking, suggesting the scaling and renormalization group formalism as a tool to investigate NN dynamics.
papers.summary: Grokking is the delayed transition from memorization to generalization in deep neural networks (NNs), and this work asks whether scaling and renormalization group (RG) theory from statistical physics can describe that dynamics quantitatively. For modular addition on a two-layer network, an ensemble of trained models defines the squared weight norm as an order parameter with fluctuation proxies for heat capacity and susceptibility, treating training epoch and weight decay as thermal and field coordinates. A coupling matrix built from a second-order expansion of the loss in per-neuron norms is ordered by its Fiedler vector to define an effective geometry, which shows a monotonic spatial decay of coupling strength absent under random permutations, and real-space RG is then carried out by block-spin aggregating adjacent neurons. Linearizing the local RG map yields relevant scaling exponents and five derived critical exponents, with **direct empirical estimates matching the RG predictions within 1 to 10%**.

papers.title: Context Is a Pipeline, Not a Window: Information Attrition in LLM Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: LLM agents are judged by two numbers: the size of the context window, and how often the final answer is correct. Both numbers miss a third thing: how much of a tool's output is lost before the model ever sees it. We measured this loss in a real tool-using agent. The agent finds the cause of injected faults by reading Linux kernel traces. The context window was almost empty: across 720 runs, the single largest prompt used only 5.75% of it. Yet a third of all tool results (3,827 of 11,189) were cut before they reached the model, and every cut result became broken JSON. The harness cut each result by slicing its JSON text at a fixed length. This does not shorten a result evenly. It deletes whatever data sits near the end. One field reached the model in only 4.7% of calls. A second field, in the very same results, reached the model in 99.3% of calls. Which field held the fault's evidence depended on when the faulty process started: early or late in the trace. The agent's diagnosis accuracy matched this same split. So we ran controlled experiments to test one question: did the data loss cause the drop in accuracy? This paper makes four contributions. First, we model an agent's context as a five-stage pipeline, with a measured failure at each stage. Second, we replay 864 real tool results, including one from a production trace where the shipped cut deletes all 128 records of the fault's evidence. Third, a controlled experiment shows that the cut's real cost appears first as extra work, not as wrong answers: 43% more tool calls, twice the computation, and yield falling from 0.61 to 0.31. The agent still finds the right answer when it has another way to reach it. Fourth, a survey of seven agent frameworks finds two that cut tool output the same unsafe way. Whether the data cut truly causes the accuracy drop is still an open question.
papers.summary: Agent evaluations track context-window size and final-answer accuracy but not how much of a tool's output is discarded by the harness before the model ever sees it. Measuring an agent that diagnoses injected faults from Linux kernel traces, the authors find that although the largest prompt across 720 runs used only 5.75% of the window, **a third of all tool results (3,827 of 11,189) were truncated by slicing their JSON text at a fixed length**, every truncated result became broken JSON, and one field reached the model in only 4.7% of calls while another field in the same results reached it in 99.3%, a split that matched diagnosis accuracy. They model agent context as a five-stage pipeline with a measured failure at each stage, replay 864 real tool results including a production trace where the cut deletes all 128 records of the fault's evidence, and show in a controlled experiment that the cut first shows up as extra work (43% more tool calls, twice the computation, yield falling from 0.61 to 0.31) rather than wrong answers, since the agent still finds the answer when another route exists. A survey of seven agent frameworks finds two that truncate tool output the same way, and whether the truncation causes the accuracy drop is left as an open question.

papers.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
papers.abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.
papers.summary: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, the authors argue that the question of how humans should use AI in research can only be answered by first settling why humans should keep doing science at all. Taking durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values, as an indispensable aim of science, they derive **a two-part test for delegating a research task to AI**: a human-understanding condition requiring that the scientific community can still explain, defend, and contest the resulting claims and retain the skills to do so, and a human-direction condition keeping judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT), including peer review and the training of new researchers, yields recommendations that fields can tailor, and the framework is meant to hold even if AI outperforms humans rather than depending on current limitations. The paper closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

papers.title: When Connectivity Misleads: Guiding Agentic Search with Contrastive Evidence Paths
papers.abstract: Search agents can use cross-document graphs to discover sources through multi-hop connections and choose subsequent actions based on candidate rankings and relationships within a limited observation window. However, documents may rank highly because their numerous connections make them easier to reach, without necessarily providing more valuable evidence. Graph diffusion methods such as Personalized PageRank (PPR) aggregate propagation contributions from multiple sources, allowing highly connected distractor nodes to crowd the observation window. Flat node scores also obscure cross-document evidence trails, limiting continued exploration. We propose Contrastive Evidence Paths (CEP), which scores candidates by their strongest individual paths on a query-conditioned document graph and calibrates these scores against the same graph's background visitation distribution to mitigate structural bias. CEP ranks candidates by the calibrated scores and retains the corresponding source paths. Building on CEP, we develop Structured Corpus Interaction (SCI), which organizes candidates and their connecting paths into a structured Map, enabling agents to verify source documents and pursue missing information through expansion from anchor documents. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus and TREC-COVID show that SCI achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and nDCG@10 with the lowest generation cost. Compared with the strongest baselines by task performance, maximum reductions in tool calls and total generation costs exceed 50% and 40%, respectively. Further analysis confirms that SCI with CEP suppresses ranking inflation induced by structural connections and improves gold recall and exploration efficiency.
papers.summary: Search agents that navigate cross-document graphs can be misled because heavily connected documents rank highly simply by being easy to reach, and diffusion scores such as Personalized PageRank (PPR) let such distractors crowd the limited observation window while flat node scores hide the evidence trails between documents. `Contrastive Evidence Paths` (CEP) scores each candidate by its strongest individual path on a query-conditioned document graph and calibrates that score against the same graph's background visitation distribution to counter structural bias, retaining the source path for each candidate. `Structured Corpus Interaction` (SCI) builds on this by organizing candidates and their connecting paths into a structured map that lets agents verify source documents and expand from anchor documents toward missing information. On `BrowseComp-Plus` and `TREC-COVID`, SCI reaches state-of-the-art answer accuracy and nDCG@10 at the lowest generation cost, **cutting tool calls by more than 50% and total generation cost by more than 40%** relative to the strongest baselines, while suppressing connectivity-driven ranking inflation and improving gold recall.

papers.title: Physical structure as an organizing principle for universal Hamiltonian learning
papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) gives the electronic structure of materials, but its cost limits large-supercell calculations and materials screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonians bypass the self-consistent cycle but are usually system-specific; universal ones could cover new compositions and disordered solids. Such models must generalize across chemistry and keep downstream properties physical, while staying inexpensive for large cells. Here we introduce UniTB, a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian representation framework that integrates physical priors rooted in density-functional tight-binding theory with deep learning. UniTB's network, which corrects a prior Hamiltonian, generalizes across chemistry through a mixture of experts routed by that prior and a charge-equilibration head as in self-consistent-charge tight binding. A projection bounds band shifts from the prior, suppressing spurious states and keeping downstream properties physical. We provide the fastest SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network. The variant UniTB-Flash assembles its prior from two-center tables at $O(N)$ cost for $N$ atoms, against $O(N\log N)$ on a grid. Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB reaches a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements. Without amorphous training data, both models agree with DFT optics and conductivity of amorphous Ge-Sb-Te. UniTB-Flash ranks candidates with no significant difference from UniTB, whose property values are more accurate; together they screen 16,195 crystals for five application domains of industrial relevance.
papers.summary: Density functional theory (DFT) yields the electronic structure of materials but is too costly for large supercells and broad screening, and machine-learned Hamiltonians that skip its self-consistent cycle are usually tied to one system. `UniTB` is a universal E(3)-equivariant framework that learns a correction to a prior Hamiltonian grounded in density-functional tight-binding theory, generalizing across chemistry through a mixture of experts routed by that prior and a charge-equilibration head, while a projection bounds band shifts from the prior to suppress spurious states and keep downstream properties physical. The `UniTB-Flash` variant assembles its prior from two-center tables at linear cost in the number of atoms rather than the N log N cost of a grid, and the authors release fast SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network. Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB **reaches a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements**, both models match DFT optics and conductivity of amorphous Ge-Sb-Te without any amorphous training data, and together they screen 16,195 crystals for five industrially relevant application domains.

papers.title: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors
papers.abstract: Prompt optimization should improve the image a user receives without changing the scene the user requested. Yet stylistic rewriting can weaken object attributes and relations even when global text--image similarity remains high. We propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision. The graph exposes what should be preserved, while deletion, reordering, and insertion provide a token-aligned way to modify the prompt. This turns structural feedback from an external critique into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Learning from that signal requires handling both uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. StruPO retains grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple images for each edit before computing group-relative advantages. Experiments span three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, with comparisons to learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control. StruPO improves the faithfulness--aesthetics trade-off, with consistent gains in relational fidelity. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study provide complementary evidence, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity. Controlled ablations connect these gains to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning. The resulting policy produces reusable optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, without an iterative critique--rewrite loop.
papers.summary: Rewriting a text-to-image prompt for better aesthetics can quietly weaken the object attributes and relations the user asked for, even when global text-image similarity stays high. `StruPO` is a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph both to condition the editing policy and to supervise it from generated images, modifying the prompt through token-aligned deletion, reordering, and insertion; training keeps grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple generated images per edit before computing group-relative advantages. Across three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, it **improves the faithfulness-aesthetics trade-off with consistent gains in relational fidelity** over learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control, and a 15-annotator study shows human preference margins that grow with relation complexity. The learned policy produces optimized prompts in a single pass after graph calibration, with no iterative critique-rewrite loop.

papers.title: Replication or Corroboration? An Axiomatic Framework for Evidential Dependence in Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: In multi-agent debates, matching reports can arise for two different reasons: agents may repeat the same evidence (replication), or they may provide separate evidential roots that support the same claim (corroboration). A judge must distinguish these two cases. Counting report occurrences gives extra weight to relays, paraphrases, alias resubmissions, and excerpt splits, while merging all matching content avoids this only by also removing genuine corroboration. We formalize this tension as a minimal judgment game in which acquiring new evidence is costly, but replication is cheap. We show that root replication invariance (RRI) is exactly threshold-uniform replication immunity. Under RRI, replication-only deviations cannot change the verdict, and positive-cost replication is strictly dominated, whereas occurrence-sensitive and content-keyed judges admit profitable deviations. We also establish an information boundary: if a judge's observation interface cannot distinguish a replica from a matched fresh root, no judge can both ignore the replica and respond strictly to the fresh root. To preserve this distinction, we introduce the lineage quotient, which removes wording, identity, occurrence multiplicity, and arbitrary root names while keeping distinct roots separate. On orbit-connected domains, it is the coarsest representation sufficient for every deterministic judge invariant to replication and root-label renaming. We further lift this construction to quantitative bipolar argumentation frameworks (QBAFs), characterize strict fresh-root response, prove its propagation along sign-consistent paths under DF-QuAD, and derive a tight closed-form response modulus. Exhaustive audits over 28,224 direct-star profiles, 2,052 multi-layer DAGs, with matched interventions on 277 AVeriTeC-derived profiles, show the predicted separation between replication and corroboration under a supplied partition.
papers.summary: In multi-agent debate, a judge sees agents submitting matching reports and must decide whether they repeated the same evidence or independently corroborated a claim; counting occurrences rewards relays and paraphrases, while merging all matching content discards real corroboration. The authors formalize this as a judgment game where fresh evidence is costly and replication is cheap, and show that root replication invariance (RRI) is equivalent to threshold-uniform replication immunity, under which replication-only deviations cannot flip a verdict and positive-cost replication is strictly dominated. They introduce the lineage quotient, a representation that discards wording, identity, multiplicity, and root names while keeping distinct evidential roots separate, and lift it to quantitative bipolar argumentation frameworks (QBAFs) under `DF-QuAD` with a closed-form response modulus. **Exhaustive audits over 28,224 direct-star profiles, 2,052 multi-layer DAGs, and 277 `AVeriTeC`-derived profiles show the predicted separation between replication and corroboration.**

papers.title: Stratum: Repository Memory for Coding Agents Beyond the Context Window
papers.abstract: Context windows have grown a thousand-fold, yet coding agents still start every session with no memory of their past work. They re-read files, retry failed approaches, and forget root causes they established hours earlier. This is not a context-length problem but a memory-architecture problem. Our hypothesis: coding agents need persistent, experience-aware repository memory, so that knowledge survives from one session to the next. Three measurements on real repositories motivate the design. First, mid-size projects already exceed the largest production context windows, and storing knowledge inside the model's key-value (KV) cache costs $10^4$ to $10^5$ times more bytes than storing it as indexed text. Second, across 752 real bug-fix commits, the median fix edits two files, and these files plus their direct imports amount to less than 10% of the repository; the bottleneck is selection, not capacity. Third, even with transitive import reachability and test links, 47% of co-edited file pairs remain structurally disconnected; the knowledge needed for selection must be mined from history and experience. We sketch Stratum, a tiered memory that lives with the repository and serves it through page-safe tools: every response states what was returned, what remains, and what it cost. Retrieval over a store of one million nodes takes 1.7 ms at the median. In a multi-session experiment on eight real bugs, a fresh agent that inherited a prior session's memory, written by a different model, identified the root-cause file in 21 of 24 trials versus 6 of 24 for a retrieval-only baseline (Fisher $p<10^{-4}$), at 4.5x lower median token cost. With the notes of all eight investigations pooled in one store, success remained 8/8.
papers.summary: Coding agents start each session with no memory of prior work, so they re-read files, retry failed approaches, and forget root causes, which the authors argue is a memory-architecture problem rather than a context-length problem. Measurements on real repositories show that storing knowledge in the key-value (KV) cache costs 10,000 to 100,000 times more bytes than indexed text, that the median bug fix across 752 commits touches two files which, with their direct imports, amount to under 10% of the repository, and that 47% of co-edited file pairs remain structurally disconnected even through imports and test links. `Stratum` is a tiered memory that lives with the repository and is served through page-safe tools reporting what was returned, what remains, and what it cost, with median retrieval of 1.7 ms over a million-node store. **In a multi-session experiment on eight real bugs, a fresh agent inheriting a prior session's memory written by a different model found the root-cause file in 21 of 24 trials versus 6 of 24 for a retrieval-only baseline**, at 4.5x lower median token cost.

papers.title: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule
papers.abstract: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $\pi$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $\pi$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented language models must reconcile retrieved context with parametric knowledge when the two disagree, and existing methods resolve the conflict with a rule fixed at design time, such as always following the context or always trusting memory. A decision-theoretic analysis shows that any fixed rule scores linearly in the share of reliable contexts while the optimal score is convex, so every fixed rule loses somewhere, and that the symmetric divergence used by adaptive decoding carries no information about which source is right. The proposed system has the model write its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and uses a selector that commits or abstains under a prior on context reliability applied as an exact prior shift. **With the prior set to the true share of correct contexts, the system beats the best baseline at every mixture of `GRACE` contexts by up to 26 points**, scoring 45.3 and 35.0 on `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` and `Llama-3.1-8B` versus 29.4 and 27.5, and beating `CK-PLUG` and `TCR` on `ClashEval` by 12 and 26 points, though the gains vanish where the model lacks the underlying knowledge.
papers.highlight_summary:
Retrieval-augmented language models answer from two sources, the retrieved context and their own parametric knowledge, and when the two disagree every existing method commits to a direction fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to a divergence, or trust memory. The authors argue from a decision-theoretic model that any such fixed rule has an expected score that is a straight line in the share of right contexts while the attainable optimum is a convex curve above it, so resolving a conflict requires calibrated evidence about each source plus an explicit prior on how often the context is right.

- `GRACE`, a new benchmark built from `LC-QuAD 2.0` and Wikidata, holds each question fixed and intervenes only on its knowledge-graph context (clean, broken, wrong_branch, competing), and across 13 methods on `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` and `Llama-3.1-8B` every baseline is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones but never both.
- The theory predicts that a symmetric divergence detects a conflict but cannot resolve it, and `AdaCAD` confirms this empirically: its Jensen-Shannon weight is identical whether the model knows the answer or not (**0.375 vs 0.367** on Llama), and on wrong contexts the model could answer alone it returns a wrong answer **70%** of the time against 20% for a plain reader.
- The proposed system elicits the model's knowledge as notes before it reads the context, voices each note with a calibrated confidence from a small learned policy (a closed-form log-odds shift of a Brier-optimal forecast), answers in two voices through a frozen reader, and lets a gradient-boosting selector shift context-sourced candidates from the training prior of 0.25 to a user-stated prior before committing only above a probability of one half.
- On `GRACE` development data the system scores **45.3 and 35.0 C−W** (percent correct minus percent wrong) on Qwen and Llama against **29.4 and 27.5** for the best baseline, stays above the best baseline at every mixture of right and wrong contexts by **up to 26 points**, and on preregistered `ClashEval` beats same-backbone `CK-PLUG` and `TCR` by **12 and 26 points**.
- The gains vanish where the model lacks the knowledge (on `Housing Statute QA` it scores 2.0 against 11.4 for the plain reader), the selector's calibration does not transfer off graph-style contexts (it states 0.49 confidence on `ClashEval` for answers right only 18% of the time, where `GenRead` wins on Llama by abstaining on 62% of questions), and `GRACE` is the authors' own development set so its numbers are an upper bound.

papers.title: Learning Human Sports Motion Feasibility via Quantile Regression on Tracking Data
papers.abstract: We study time-to-arrival (TTA) in sports: the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach an arbitrary location on the pitch given their current kinematic state, estimated as the lower envelope of observed locomotion times. Rather than modeling space ownership through position density estimation or closed-form physics-based models, we cast TTA as a conditional quantile regression problem, estimating the lower quantile of locomotion time so the model learns a player's lower-envelope arrival time. We train the model on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the PFF FC FIFA World Cup 2022 dataset, and evaluate a lightweight multilayer perceptron against six player-motion models from the literature, re-expressed as TTA predictors, and a learned reachable- hull baseline. Across our evaluation metrics, the MLP consistently outperforms every physics-based baseline. To probe the generality of the learned locomotion model, we further evaluate it on basketball tracking data and a single-game NFL tracking dataset, analyzing the transferability of player motion dynamics across sports. Our project is available at https://github.com/mguti97/TTA-Quantile.
papers.summary: Time-to-arrival (TTA), the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach a location on the pitch given their current kinematic state, is estimated here as the lower envelope of observed locomotion times rather than through position-density or closed-form physics models. The authors cast TTA as conditional quantile regression, training a lightweight multilayer perceptron on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the `PFF FC FIFA World Cup 2022` dataset to predict a low quantile of arrival time. **The multilayer perceptron consistently outperforms six physics-based player-motion models re-expressed as TTA predictors and a learned reachable-hull baseline across all evaluation metrics.** Transfer experiments on basketball tracking data and a single NFL game probe how far the learned locomotion dynamics carry across sports.

papers.title: Can AI Guide Testing Without Generating Tests? A Comparative Study of AI-Assisted Unit Testing
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled assistants to generate increasingly sophisticated executable unit tests. However, novices may accept these outputs without independently identifying what to test, evaluating test-suite completeness, or verifying correctness, potentially limiting opportunities to develop essential testing skills. Although prior work has explored AI-assisted test generation and feedback-oriented programming tutors, little is known about whether AI can support novices' testing practices without generating tests for them. To investigate this, we introduce TestCompass, a generative AI tutor that provides targeted feedback on weaknesses in students' test suites without generating executable tests. In a classroom study with 18 students, we compared TestCompass with a general AI assistant across two Java unit-testing tasks, examining students' testing behaviors, test-suite quality, and subjective experiences. We found that participants using the general-purpose AI assistant produced more tests, whereas TestCompass participants spent more time developing and verifying tests themselves. However, most test-suite quality measures were comparable between conditions, and TestCompass participants achieved similar requirement coverage with significantly fewer test methods ($p=0.012$) in one task. Neither group reported short-term improvements in perceived testing knowledge or confidence. These findings suggest that feedback-oriented AI can support meaningful testing outcomes while preserving opportunities for hands-on testing practice, offering a complementary approach to AI-assisted testing education.
papers.summary: Generative AI assistants can write executable unit tests, but novices who accept them may never learn to decide what to test or judge suite completeness. `TestCompass` is a generative AI tutor that gives targeted feedback on weaknesses in a student's test suite without producing any tests, and a classroom study with 18 students compared it against a general-purpose AI assistant on two Java unit-testing tasks. Students using the general assistant produced more tests, while `TestCompass` users spent more time writing and verifying tests themselves; **most test-suite quality measures were comparable between conditions, and `TestCompass` users reached similar requirement coverage with significantly fewer test methods (p=0.012) on one task.** Neither group reported short-term gains in perceived testing knowledge or confidence.

papers.title: Skill Dreaming: Evolving Repository Skills through Pull Request Streams
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on reusable skills for complex software engineering tasks, making skill libraries essential for repository development and maintenance. However, repository-specific skills must evolve with changing code structures, implementation conventions, and maintenance requirements. Pull requests (PRs) provide a natural source of such knowledge by recording how repositories evolve through implementation and review. Meanwhile, new PRs must follow repository-specific implementation patterns, modify related components consistently, and ensure that existing tests continue to pass while adding coverage for new functionality. This creates a mutually reinforcing cycle: PRs provide knowledge for updating skills, while these skills improve future PRs, maintain repositories, and support further skill evolution. To enable this co-evolution of PRs, repositories, and skills, we propose Skill Dreaming, a framework that learns from PR streams to guide continuous repository development and maintenance. Given a repository and its PR history, Skill Dreaming builds a repository-specific skill library by extracting executable knowledge from validated PRs and continuously refines the skills as new PR information becomes available. These skills guide coding agents not only in implementing requested features but also in maintaining associated tests, documentation, compatibility, and repository conventions. By integrating PR analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming provides an end-to-end workflow for applying learned skills to repository changes and incorporating subsequent PR outcomes into future skill updates.
papers.summary: Repository-specific skills used by large language model (LLM) agents must track changing code structure, conventions, and maintenance requirements, and pull requests (PRs) record exactly how a repository evolves through implementation and review. `Skill Dreaming` is a framework that builds a repository-specific skill library by extracting executable knowledge from validated PRs and continuously refines those skills as new PRs arrive, so that skills guide agents in implementing features while also maintaining tests, documentation, compatibility, and conventions. **The framework integrates PR analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration into an end-to-end loop in which learned skills shape new PRs and PR outcomes feed back into future skill updates.**

papers.title: Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models
papers.abstract: Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow. We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 x 256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.
papers.summary: Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space for flow-based image generation is slow and hard, and the authors find that coarse second-order image statistics, in the form of frozen Wiener estimates, ease the task with gains beyond the linear predictions they provide. Wiener-informed Decoding (`WiD`) adds a trainable Wiener prediction path plus coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return predicted coefficient corrections, with all new parameters initialized from data statistics and trained jointly under the original velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures it accelerates training, smooths gradient trajectories, and stays effective alongside representation alignment. **On `ImageNet` 256x256, `PixelDiT-XL` with `WiD` reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, matching `PixelDiT` quality with 37.5% fewer training epochs.**

papers.title: count-catcher: Lean Theorems from Model Counting Certificates
papers.abstract: We present count-catcher, a tool that turns a CPOG certificate of a count by the exact model counter d4 into a Lean theorem that a CNF formula defined in Lean has exactly N models over V variables. With an encoding lemma, this theorem becomes a theorem about the number of combinatorial objects. A CPOG certificate consists of a Boolean circuit equivalent to the formula and a proof of equivalence. count-catcher checks in Lean that the formula implies the circuit (forward check) and the circuit implies the formula (reverse check). For the forward check, lrat-catcher streams a refutation through the LRAT checker of Lean's standard library. The reverse check and the validity check of the circuit are computations proved correct in Lean. Lean runs all three checks as compiled code, so the theorem depends on Lean's kernel, compiler and runtime, as does CPOG's verified checker. We combine the theorem with results from Mathlib, for instance with Burnside's lemma to count graphs up to isomorphism. We prove the number of Latin squares of order 8 as a weighted sum of hundreds of certified counts from about eight terabytes of certificates. We turn about half of the 2022 Model Counting Competition formulas into theorems, with the three checks taking about a quarter of the time of CPOG's verified checker. We found that CPOG's unverified checker reported wrong counts, and removed its verified checker's dependence on two unproved lemmas. End to end, a theorem costs about the same as a checked count.
papers.summary: `count-catcher` converts a CPOG certificate produced by the exact model counter `d4` into a Lean theorem stating that a CNF formula defined in Lean has exactly N models over V variables, which with an encoding lemma becomes a theorem about a count of combinatorial objects. The certificate's Boolean circuit is checked in both directions: `lrat-catcher` streams a refutation through the LRAT checker in Lean's standard library for the forward direction, while the reverse check and circuit validity are computations proved correct in Lean and run as compiled code. Combined with `Mathlib` results such as Burnside's lemma, the tool proves counts of graphs up to isomorphism and the number of Latin squares of order 8 as a weighted sum of hundreds of certified counts from about eight terabytes of certificates. **About half of the 2022 Model Counting Competition formulas become theorems, with the three checks taking roughly a quarter of the time of CPOG's verified checker**, and the work also exposed wrong counts from CPOG's unverified checker.

papers.title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
papers.abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love eagles", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, remain near chance. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.
papers.summary: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) holds that post-training selects a persona already learned during pre-training, and subliminal learning work has shown that models can embed covert traits into unrelated outputs such as number strings. Persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE) scores such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header to decode and classify the hidden signal. **PHLE distinguishes number sequences from a model prompted to love owls versus eagles, and separates answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove visible misalignment, from those of an unprompted model, while prompted classifiers including the generating model itself stay near chance.** The signal partly transfers across families, with the `Qwen` base model reading signals produced by `Olmo` and vice versa, suggesting a practical route for auditing hidden objectives.

papers.title: Concorde: Geometry-Aware Link Prediction via Decoupled Energy Minimization
papers.abstract: Link prediction remains difficult in sparse graphs, where diffusion heuristics lack connectivity and geometric methods suffer spectral instability when coupling learned representations with diffusion operators. We introduce Concorde, an energy-based framework that resolves this by decomposing link likelihood into three structurally decoupled branches: (i) a parameter-free spectral anchor that establishes permutation-invariant topological stability; (ii) a mixed-curvature residual on a learnable $\mathbb{H}^{d_h}_{c_h} \times \mathbb{S}^{d_s}_{c_s}$ product manifold, regularized by a feature-aware Ollivier-Ricci curvature proxy; and (iii) a continuous vector field on the tangent bundle of hyperbolic space for non-local structural alignment across topological gaps. The branches are fused via learned gating and trained with an N-pair ranking loss aligned with retrieval-style evaluation. Across five benchmarks spanning sparse, dense, featureless, and attributed regimes, Concorde establishes state-of-the-art early retrieval precision, nearly doubling P@10% over leading baselines in sparse settings.
papers.summary: Link prediction in sparse graphs suffers because diffusion heuristics lack connectivity and geometric methods become spectrally unstable when learned representations are coupled with diffusion operators. `Concorde` is an energy-based framework that decomposes link likelihood into three decoupled branches: a parameter-free spectral anchor for permutation-invariant stability, a mixed-curvature residual on a learnable hyperbolic-spherical product manifold regularized by a feature-aware Ollivier-Ricci curvature proxy, and a continuous vector field on the tangent bundle of hyperbolic space for non-local alignment across topological gaps. The branches are fused by learned gating and trained with an N-pair ranking loss matched to retrieval-style evaluation. **Across five benchmarks spanning sparse, dense, featureless, and attributed graphs, it sets state-of-the-art early retrieval precision, nearly doubling P@10% over leading baselines in sparse settings.**

papers.title: Counterfactual Profile Perturbations for Recommendation Explanations: A Reproducibility Study
papers.abstract: This reproducibility paper explores the counterfactual explanation technique known as Learning to eXplain Recommendations (LXR). Prior work has shown that LXR can reliably identify perturbations that, if applied to a user's profile, cause the user's top ranked item to no longer be recommended, thereby explaining the item's recommendation as a function of the user's rating choices. In this paper, we extend this work in multiple ways. We expand the scope of the original LXR study to look at explanations for items other than the most highly recommended item, finding that LXR is also effective at this version of the task. We consider alternate baselines for LXR, including item popularity and latent factor similarity, and we see that for some tasks these alternatives work surprisingly well. We also examine the impact of item popularity, finding that LXR offers better explanation quality (shorter perturbations) when less popular items are being explained. Finally, we conduct a brute-force exploration of a subset of the perturbation space in order to estimate a lower bound for optimal perturbation size against which LXR and other such methods can be compared.
papers.summary: Learning to eXplain Recommendations (LXR) explains a recommended item by finding small perturbations to a user's profile that would remove the item from the top of the ranking, and this reproducibility study extends the original evaluation in several directions. The authors show LXR also works for explaining items ranked below the top position, compare it against alternative baselines including item popularity and latent-factor similarity, and find that **for some tasks these simple baselines work surprisingly well.** They further find that LXR yields shorter perturbations when explaining less popular items, and they brute-force a subset of the perturbation space to estimate a lower bound on optimal perturbation size as a reference point for future methods.

papers.title: Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.
papers.summary: Structure predictors such as `ESMFold` fold proteins through dense neural computation whose mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure remains poorly understood. The authors train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the folding trunk's intermediate representations and proceed in three steps: a pilot analysis across modules and recycles locates where spatial computation happens, the learned dictionaries reveal a division of labor in which the single representation carries inherited sequence semantics while the pair representation computes pairwise geometry, and a reasoning language model interprets the dictionary at scale with gradient-based attribution tracing how concepts compose across blocks. **The concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality**, and following the interpreted features to the folding output shows where the computation agrees with or departs from known biochemistry.

papers.title: Directional Statistics on Circles and Spheres: A New Angle on Data
papers.abstract: Two compass bearings near north can have an ordinary arithmetic mean pointing south: the difficulty is that angles live on a circle, not a straight line. Using real wind observations, diffusion-MRI orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning, this article introduces circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres. The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.
papers.summary: Angles live on a circle rather than a line, so the arithmetic mean of two compass bearings near north can point south. This tutorial introduces circular and axial averages, measures of directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres, illustrated with real wind observations, diffusion-MRI fiber orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning. **The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.**

papers.title: Agent or Human? Detecting Commits by AI Coding Agents in the Absence of Authorship Signatures
papers.abstract: AI coding agents such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot coding agent, and Cursor now commit directly to open-source repositories. Empirical studies of these agents identify their commits through authorship signatures, such as bot accounts and Co-authored-by trailers. These signatures are optional, can be removed, and are often attached to pull requests rather than to individual commits. Hence, it is unclear whether Agent commits can be told apart from Human commits once the signatures are gone. We investigate the signals and limits of signature-free detection using 7,837,946 commits from 1,226 repositories, covering five coding agents and Human commits. After signatures are masked, detectors rank Agent commits above Human commits with a ROC AUC of up to 0.859, and most of this signal comes from message verbosity and change size rather than from the code itself. On the shared sample, gpt-6-sol without fine-tuning reaches AUCs similar to XGBoost and TF-IDF. At the observed Agent share, however, the best detector on the full test set reaches a precision of only 0.332. Detection transfers poorly to held-out Claude Code and Copilot, with TF-IDF reaching an AUC of only 0.524 for Claude Code. Temporal changes also depend on the agent, e.g., Copilot AUC drops and later recovers, while more training history helps Claude Code but not Copilot. These results indicate that signature-free detection can prioritize commits for review but cannot replace recorded attribution, and that studies relying on signature-based labels should treat them as a lower bound on agent activity.
papers.summary: AI coding agents now commit directly to open-source repositories, and empirical studies identify their commits through authorship signatures such as bot accounts and Co-authored-by trailers that are optional, can be removed, and are often attached to pull requests rather than to individual commits. Using 7,837,946 commits from 1,226 repositories spanning five agents, the authors mask these signatures and test whether detectors can still tell agent commits from human ones. **Detectors reach a ROC AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of up to 0.859, but most of the signal comes from message verbosity and change size rather than the code, and at the observed agent share the best detector's precision is only 0.332.** Detection transfers poorly to held-out agents, with `TF-IDF` reaching an AUC of just 0.524 on `Claude Code`, and `gpt-6-sol` without fine-tuning matches `XGBoost` and `TF-IDF`, leading the authors to conclude that signature-free detection can prioritize commits for review but cannot replace recorded attribution.

papers.title: MARQ: A Modular, LLM-Agnostic Requirement Quality Assessor Infused with Systems Engineering Knowledge
papers.abstract: Requirements engineering (RE) is foundational to systems engineering (SE), as requirement defects can propagate downstream and adversely affect development outcomes. Although large language models (LLMs) are promising for requirement quality assessment, prior work shows that off-the-shelf models miss a large share of expert-identified defects, perform unevenly across quality criteria, and vary across executions. This study investigates whether infusing expert-derived SE knowledge can improve LLM-based requirement quality evaluation beyond off-the-shelf capability. We present MARQ, a modular, LLM-agnostic prototype that supplements LLMs with a criterion-specific knowledge stack operationalizing INCOSE requirement quality criteria and evaluated against off-the-shelf baselines on an expert-labeled NASA requirement set using Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the open-weight Gemma 3 12B, with 100 executions per model. MARQ achieves median F1 scores of 0.80 for Claude Opus 5, 0.62 for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 0.53 for Gemma 3 12B, compared with off-the-shelf baselines of 0.55, 0.52, and 0.18, respectively. However, the nature of these gains is model-dependent. Claude Opus 5 improves defect detection and false-alarm control; GPT-5.6 Sol gains detection and better execution-level consistency at the cost of more false alarms; and Gemma 3 12B reaches the performance of off-the-shelf proprietary models, although it remains highly variable. Criterion-level analysis shows gains concentrated in Correctness and Conformance, trade-offs between misses and false alarms within individual criteria, and model-dependent responses across several criteria. These findings position SE knowledge infusion as a promising model-agnostic pathway for strengthening trustworthy LLM-based RE support while underscoring the need for criterion-specific interventions and human-in-the-loop review.
papers.summary: Requirement defects propagate downstream in systems engineering (SE), and off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) miss many expert-identified defects when assessing requirement quality. `MARQ` is a modular, LLM-agnostic prototype that supplements a model with a criterion-specific knowledge stack operationalizing INCOSE requirement quality criteria, evaluated against off-the-shelf baselines on an expert-labeled NASA requirement set across 100 executions each with `Claude Opus 5`, `GPT-5.6 Sol`, and `Gemma 3 12B`. **Median F1 rises to 0.80, 0.62, and 0.53 respectively, compared with 0.55, 0.52, and 0.18 off the shelf**, with the open-weight `Gemma 3 12B` reaching the level of unaided proprietary models though with high variance. The gains concentrate in the Correctness and Conformance criteria and differ by model, with `Claude Opus 5` improving both detection and false-alarm control while `GPT-5.6 Sol` gains detection and consistency at the cost of more false alarms.

papers.title: BehaveRec: When Does Long-Term Behavioral History Help Sequential Recommendation? A Study with Session, History, and Community Signals
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation models typically predict a user's next action from recent session interactions, which limits personalization when short-term signals are weak or ambiguous. Rather than assuming that incorporating longer-term history and community signals is universally beneficial, we study when it actually helps. We propose BehaveRec, a three-signal framework combining a causal session transformer, a bidirectional User History Encoder over a 90-day window, and a GraphSAGE module over a user-user graph built from behavioral embedding similarity rather than item co-occurrence; a learned gate blends the three signals per user. On an industrial dataset of 137M sequences from 12.6M users, BehaveRec improves R@5 by +3.2% over SASRec, with a larger-capacity SASRec baseline (more parameters than BehaveRec) still trailing by +2.5%, ruling out capacity as the explanation. More importantly, a user-level stratification by history length reveals a clear dose-response relationship: BehaveRec's advantage is negligible below roughly 10 interactions and grows monotonically with history richness, reaching +0.017 R@5 for users with 101+ events. This pattern is corroborated across one industrial and three public datasets spanning history-rich to history-sparse regimes, where session-only models remain preferable. These headline results, and the resulting deployment threshold, are established for category-level intent prediction; a preliminary, single-run check on the full item-level vocabulary yields a directionally mixed result and is scoped as an open question rather than a claim. We use these results to derive a practical deployment rule -- roughly 20 interactions per user -- for when long-term history and behavioral-graph signals are worth their added complexity. Despite this added complexity, BehaveRec remains lightweight: it uses 5.67M parameters and trains on a single GPU in under two days.
papers.summary: Sequential recommenders usually predict the next action from the current session alone, and rather than assuming longer histories and community signals always help, this work asks when they do. `BehaveRec` combines a causal session transformer, a bidirectional user-history encoder over a 90-day window, and a `GraphSAGE` module over a user-user graph built from behavioral embedding similarity, with a learned per-user gate blending the three. On an industrial dataset of 137M sequences from 12.6M users it improves R@5 by 3.2% over `SASRec`, and a larger-capacity `SASRec` still trails by 2.5%; **stratifying by history length reveals a dose-response pattern in which the advantage is negligible below roughly 10 interactions and grows monotonically with history richness**, yielding a deployment rule of about 20 interactions per user. These results hold for category-level intent prediction across one industrial and three public datasets, while a preliminary single-run item-level check is directionally mixed and left as an open question.

papers.title: Freeze, Don't Clone: Fine-Tuning with Expressive Policies Without Retaining Offline Data
papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning uses offline pretraining to accelerate subsequent online learning. While many methods assume the offline dataset remains available throughout fine-tuning, there are many settings where this is not the case. Prior work attributes failures in this setting primarily to critic recalibration under distribution shift. We identify a complementary actor-side failure: once the offline data disappears, continued behavioral cloning (BC) no longer preserves the offline behavior distribution and instead refits the behavioral model to the agent's limited, and nonstationary, online experience. We demonstrate that stopping online behavioral fitting while preserving the pretrained expressive prior substantially improves no-retention fine-tuning across implicit flow Q-learning (IFQL), flow Q-learning (FQL), and action-chunked RL (QC) on seven OGBench domains. We trace this failure to a behavioral feedback loop: continuing online behavioral cloning rapidly erases the pretrained prior, inducing representational collapse and action diversity loss that starves the critic of useful exploration. Freezing the prior breaks this cycle, preserving offline coverage while allowing value learning to drive continuous improvement.
papers.summary: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning often assumes the offline dataset stays available during fine-tuning, and prior work blamed failures in the no-retention setting mainly on critic recalibration under distribution shift. The authors identify a complementary actor-side failure: once offline data is gone, continued behavioral cloning (BC) refits the behavioral model to the agent's limited, nonstationary online experience instead of preserving the pretrained distribution, creating a feedback loop that erases the prior, collapses representations, and starves the critic of diverse exploration. **Freezing the pretrained expressive prior while letting value learning drive improvement substantially improves no-retention fine-tuning across implicit flow Q-learning (`IFQL`), flow Q-learning (`FQL`), and action-chunked RL (`QC`) on seven `OGBench` domains.**

papers.title: cuArms: GPU-Accelerated Conflict-Based Planning for Multi-Arm Manipulation
papers.abstract: Multi-arm manipulation has the potential to dramatically improve the throughput, efficiency, and dexterity of many manipulation tasks. Recent work coordinates multiple robot arms in a shared workcell by allocating and scheduling tasks for greater parallelism, jointly planning multi-arm motions, or directly learning multi-arm policies. So far, these approaches are either too slow, rely on domain-specific assumptions, or scale poorly with the number of robots and task horizon. Thus, we introduce cuArms, a conflict-based planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that efficiently decomposes the search space using reusable multi-modal roadmaps for individual robots and resolves conflicts and deadlocks through a lazy search. To jointly optimize task assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation skills, we integrate a high-level scheduler that proposes candidate skeletons for cuArms to ground into coordinated manipulation plans. Experimental results show that our method establishes a new state of the art, with real-time initial solutions and anytime improvements in both motion quality and scheduling, without days of domain-specific training required by learning approaches. Videos of both simulated and real-world industrial tasks are available on https://cuarms.github.io/.
papers.summary: Coordinating multiple robot arms in a shared workcell promises higher throughput, but existing approaches are too slow, depend on domain-specific assumptions, or scale poorly with robot count and task horizon. `cuArms` is a conflict-based planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that decomposes the search using reusable multi-modal roadmaps per robot and resolves conflicts and deadlocks through lazy search, paired with a high-level scheduler that proposes candidate task skeletons for the planner to ground into coordinated plans covering assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation skills. **It produces real-time initial solutions with anytime improvement in both motion quality and scheduling, without the days of domain-specific training that learning-based methods require**, demonstrated on simulated and real-world industrial tasks.

papers.title: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.abstract:
Hospitality service in online marketplaces has become increasingly popular over the past few years, not only because it helps people easily rent short-term lodging but also because it empowers travelers to connect with locals and feel belonging. A typical pattern of these industries is a central platform mediating the economic interactions between guests and hosts, where a successful booking experience is the key to user satisfaction. However, one of the biggest challenges is the possible delay of response and chance of rejection when guests try to book a request-to-book listing. Previously, we enabled the instant book feature to allow hosts to instantly accept qualified guests and guests to confirm bookings immediately. Yet the symptom has not been alleviated given mixed request-to-book and instant book listing supply in search results. One possible solution is to promote all instant book listings in search results; however, booking rate will be damaged due to some improperly promoted low quality listings.
  In this paper, we present a novel smart instant book filter system that applies the instant book filter intelligently and shifts request-to-book to instant book without hurting booking rate. Compared with traditional two-sided markets research that targets finding strategies to maximize a single overall social welfare goal, our proposed system aims to maximize the instant book rate with the constraint that booking rate should not decrease, forming a dual-objective optimization problem.
  We show A/B testing results for our system exposed to global users, demonstrating that our model performs better than previous human-expert-tuned models in terms of both instant book rate and overall booking rate. We also achieved improved metrics such as the host instant book adoption rate. The proposed system has been deployed to production and is serving millions of users every day.
papers.summary: On short-term lodging marketplaces, guests booking request-to-book listings face response delays and possible rejection, and simply promoting every instant-book listing in search would hurt booking rate by surfacing low-quality listings. The proposed smart instant book filter applies the instant-book filter selectively, framed as a dual-objective problem that maximizes instant-book rate subject to the constraint that overall booking rate does not decrease, in contrast to two-sided-market work that optimizes a single welfare objective. **In global A/B tests the model beat the previous human-expert-tuned models on both instant-book rate and overall booking rate**, also raising host instant-book adoption, and it now serves millions of users daily in production.

papers.title: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) are increasingly applied to Reverse Engineering (RE) workflows. RE, however, differs from common LLM coding tasks as it requires models to reason about low-level program behavior. Furthermore, the deployment of tooling in resource-constrained sandboxed RE environments limits the ability to use frontier-scale solutions. We examine whether a targeted LLM training approach can transfer distinct RE skills to open models via inverse basic-block execution: given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. Fine-tuning \texttt{Qwen3-1.7B} and \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2\% to 85.3\% and from 63.3\% to 95.2\%, respectively. Frontier models still score highest (up to 99.2\%), but our fine-tuned \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} comes within four points at a fraction of the parameter count. We release both fine-tuned models and the training dataset.
