papers.summary: Reverse engineering (RE) requires reasoning about low-level program behavior, and sandboxed RE environments often cannot use frontier-scale models. The authors test whether a targeted training task, inverse basic-block execution, can transfer RE skill to open models: given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model must predict the input register values that produce it. **Fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2% to 85.3% for `Qwen3-1.7B` and from 63.3% to 95.2% for `Nemotron-3-Nano`**, bringing the latter within four points of the best frontier model at 99.2% with a fraction of the parameters. Both fine-tuned models and the training dataset are released.

papers.title: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks
papers.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on proprietary system prompts to enforce task directives, safety policies, and access controls. These prompts are vulnerable to query-based leakage attacks, where black-box adversaries extract confidential instructions through adaptive, multi-turn interactions. Existing defenses often assess queries independently, missing malicious behavior that emerges across interactions.
  We present AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework for detecting and mitigating system prompt leakage. AdvGuard models cross-query relationships using a bounded semantic interaction graph, statistically filters candidate components, and converts them into line graphs for graph convolutional network (GCN) classification. This approach captures multi-hop patterns in query similarity that distinguish coordinated extraction from benign workflows. A lightweight prompt-level detector provides protection before sufficient interaction history accumulates, and the framework supports black-box LLM deployments.
  In mixed-query evaluations, AdvGuard improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline while maintaining a false positive rate of at most 3.4%. In multi-turn workloads, it achieves 97.23%-99.1% F1 with 100% recall. Leave-one-attack-family-out tests yield 99.98% mean recall and 99.99% mean F1, with no observed false positives. Integrated into the adaptive PLeak and LeakAgent attack loops, AdvGuard limits exact-match leakage to 0.00-0.01 and substring-match leakage to 0.01-0.09 across evaluated victim models. These results demonstrate robust detection of unseen attack families and substantially reduced prompt reconstruction.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) system prompts can be extracted by black-box adversaries through adaptive, multi-turn queries, and most defenses inspect each query in isolation and miss attacks that only emerge across a session. `AdvGuard` builds a bounded semantic interaction graph over incoming queries, statistically filters candidate components, converts them to line graphs, and classifies them with a graph convolutional network (GCN) to spot coordinated extraction patterns, with a lightweight single-prompt detector covering the period before enough history accumulates. In mixed-query evaluations it raises recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline at a false positive rate of at most 3.4%, and **when inserted into the adaptive `PLeak` and `LeakAgent` attack loops it holds exact-match prompt leakage to 0.00-0.01** across the evaluated victim models.

papers.title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks
papers.abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. SNNs communicate through sparse, discrete spikes, and their outputs depend on membrane potentials that evolve over time rather than on a static mapping from input to output. This temporal mode of computation suggests that the decision behavior of an SNN may be harder to reconstruct from its responses. This work tests that possibility by benchmarking four representative MSAs, namely the Papernot, Tram\`er, T-RND, and color perturbation attacks, against SNNs and their ANN counterparts on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Across every attack and dataset, SNNs prove consistently more difficult to steal. Surrogates of SNNs achieve 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target model and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs. We attribute this resistance to the way SNNs compute, as their spike-based and time-dependent dynamics yield decision boundaries that ANN-based surrogates struggle to approximate, even under large query budgets. These findings extend the known resilience of SNNs beyond attacks on training data to the replication of model functionality, strengthening the case for neuromorphic architectures in security-sensitive applications.
papers.summary: Model stealing attacks (MSAs) train a surrogate that mimics a deployed model's decisions using only black-box queries, and they are well understood for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs) but not for spiking neural networks (SNNs), whose outputs depend on time-evolving membrane potentials rather than a static input-output map. The study benchmarks four representative attacks, the `Papernot`, `Tramèr`, `T-RND`, and color perturbation methods, against matched SNN and ANN targets on `MNIST`, `Fashion-MNIST`, and `CIFAR-10`. **Surrogates of SNNs reach 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs** across every attack and dataset, which the authors attribute to spike-based temporal dynamics producing decision boundaries that ANN surrogates struggle to approximate even with large query budgets.

papers.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
papers.summary: Memory-agent benchmarks typically fold retrieval and answer generation into one score, so it is unclear whether an agent failed to retrieve an updated fact or retrieved it and then ignored it. Using the single-hop `FactConsolidation` task of `MemoryAgentBench`, the authors show that with `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` on a 6K history, `BM25` accuracy falls from 45% to 32% as the evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though an audit confirms the newest statement is present in every retrieved set. With a frozen prompt and a fixed four-statement evidence window, **swapping one unrelated statement for the obsolete competing version drops accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for `Qwen2.5` and from 100% to 87.8% for `Qwen3-14B`**, indicating that a stale competitor in context is more damaging than irrelevant evidence of the same size.

papers.title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
papers.abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) score well on medical question answering but often lean on pattern matching rather than grounded clinical evidence, producing plausible yet unsupported diagnoses with opaque reasoning. The proposed framework coordinates multiple agents over an expert-curated medical ontology, grounding symptom and disease associations in the knowledge base, decomposing diagnosis into explicit auditable steps, and **identifying the most discriminative missing symptoms to generate targeted follow-up questions** in the manner of clinical inquiry. The authors report improved transparency, consistency, and diagnostic accuracy for AI-assisted differential diagnosis, and the source code is public.

papers.title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation
papers.abstract: Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. On the matched tasks, specialized prover proofs nevertheless have higher overall unchanged-proof survival than the supplied reference artifacts: +15.6 points for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, +18.8 for Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and +20.3 for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B; all three 95% CIs exclude zero. The ordering persists after excluding universally survived T1 variants, under family-balanced aggregation, and under alternative deployable valid-proof selection rules. However, unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures. RefactorProof therefore measures unchanged-proof stability under program refactoring, not the cost of maintaining a proof after it breaks.
papers.summary: Verifiable code generation benchmarks check a proof against a single fixed implementation, leaving open whether the proof survives a behavior-preserving refactoring of the program. `RefactorProof` derives 458 Lean-certified program variants from the 185 `VERINA` tasks that compile in a pinned environment while keeping the specification and the evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. Structural refactorings break proofs from every source, with a task-normalized structural survival rate of 4.3% for the supplied reference proofs and 13.3-26.8% for specialized provers, yet **on matched tasks proofs from `DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B`, `Goedel-Prover-V2-32B`, and `Goedel-Prover-V2-8B` survive unchanged 15.6 to 20.3 points more often than the reference artifacts**. Most failures are cheap to repair, since predefined one-identifier edits fix 51 of 54 eligible reference failures and 58 of 85 prover failures, so the benchmark measures unchanged-proof stability rather than maintenance cost.

papers.title: Plenty of Room in the Middle: Revealing Opportunities on a GPU Cluster via Fine-Grained Monitoring
papers.abstract:
GPU clusters have become essential computing resources for AI and scientific research in academia and industry. However, their high cost and growing demand often result in long queueing delays. While previous monitoring efforts have operated at second- or minute-level frequencies, they primarily informed job-level scheduling for clusters and lacked the detail needed to optimize GPU-level utilization.
  This paper presents an in-depth study of a university research GPU cluster, analyzing resource usage at 100 ms intervals. We have developed a lightweight monitoring tool that leverages Nvidia's DCGM library to capture fine-grained "compute utilization" metrics within GPUs. Deployed on a cluster with 89 nodes and 319 GPUs, our tool collected data over several months. This paper focuses on a 10-day period with 7,399 jobs submitted by 150 users from 12 departments. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) the GPU cluster exhibits significant underutilization, with over 70% of jobs using less than 20% of GPU memory and 50% averaging below 5% Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization; (2) 80% of jobs have a drastic mismatch between their requested and actual durations, significantly limiting the scheduler's effectiveness; and (3) the multi-GPU jobs we examined show highly periodic communication patterns. These findings suggest there is plenty of room in the middle: substantial utilization gains are available through better job scheduling and GPU multitasking, independent of hardware or application improvements.
  Our monitoring solution is available as open-source software at https://github.com/als244/gpu_server_monitoring.
papers.summary: GPU clusters are expensive and oversubscribed, yet prior monitoring at second- or minute-level granularity informed only job-level scheduling and could not reveal how individual GPUs are actually used. The authors built a lightweight open-source tool on Nvidia's `DCGM` library that samples compute utilization every 100 ms, deployed it across 89 nodes and 319 GPUs, and analyzed a 10-day window of 7,399 jobs from 150 users. **Over 70% of jobs use less than 20% of GPU memory and half average below 5% Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization**, 80% of jobs have requested durations that badly mismatch actual runtimes, and multi-GPU jobs show highly periodic communication, suggesting large gains from better scheduling and GPU multitasking without any hardware or application changes.

papers.title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces large language model (LLM) hallucination by supplying external text, but it tends to ignore logical structure and defers to the model's own reasoning, which weakens faithfulness in domains like biomedicine. `OA-RAG` is an agent that combines formal reasoning over the logical structure of domain ontologies with LLM reasoning over their informal annotations, and for each answer it reports the ontology observations used as evidence plus a grounding level of entailed, supported, related, or unrelated. Across benchmarks built from three large ontologies and six medical question-answering tasks, **it achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods**, with stronger grounding levels correlating with higher accuracy, and it is competitive with domain-specific RAG systems that draw on textbooks.

papers.title: CrowdCC: Jointly Benchmarking Corruption Robustness and Deployment Quantization in Crowd Counting
papers.abstract: Crowd-counting models deployed on edge devices face two shifts: inputs are degraded along the capture and transmission pipeline, while models are quantized to satisfy resource constraints. Yet corruption robustness and deployment quantization are typically evaluated separately. We introduce CrowdCC, a controlled corruption benchmark that jointly evaluates these effects using 23 deployment-motivated corruptions at three severity levels, four crowd-counting datasets, and 26 models using A100 TensorRT engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision, paired with throughput and energy measurements from corresponding Jetson Orin NX configurations. The corruptions span six families, with head annotations adjusted when geometry or visibility changes. Our evaluation shows that capture-chain corruptions consistently produce the largest degradation across the evaluated models, while crowd density affects absolute and relative error differently. Clean accuracy does not fully predict corrupted performance. INT8 alters corruption robustness substantially more than FP16, with no systematic direction, and does not consistently improve latency or energy. INT8 inference efficiency is strongly associated with reformat overhead in the compiled engine, while slowdowns are also observed under limited INT8 coverage. Precision changes corrupted-error rankings and robustness-cost frontiers, showing why model selection must consider corruption robustness and measured deployment cost together. The code is available at https://github.com/Tulane-Computer-Architecture-Systems/CrowdCC-Release.
papers.summary: Crowd-counting models on edge devices face degraded inputs from the capture and transmission pipeline and are also quantized to fit resource limits, but these two effects are normally evaluated separately. `CrowdCC` jointly benchmarks 23 deployment-motivated corruptions at three severity levels across four crowd-counting datasets and 26 models compiled as `TensorRT` engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision, with throughput and energy measured on matching `Jetson Orin NX` configurations. Capture-chain corruptions cause the largest degradation, clean accuracy does not predict corrupted accuracy, and **INT8 changes corruption robustness far more than FP16 with no consistent direction while failing to reliably improve latency or energy**, largely due to reformat overhead in the compiled engine.

papers.title: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984)
papers.abstract: Early AI programs were often also theories of how people think, and programs that wrote programs were, in part, theories of how people program. Here we report on the reanimation of two such programs that offer two seemingly different theories of programming and were developed for quite different purposes. The first, Herbert Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961), was an experimental model of programming as problem-solving, applying the means-ends analysis methods of the General Problem Solver to investigate the nature of the programming task. The second, KBEmacs (1984), was a working prototype of an intelligent programming assistant developed by MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project, built on the view that expert programmers recognize and combine familiar patterns, or "cliches." It let a programmer build up programs by combining cliches through a stylized English command language. We approach both through the methodology of Executable Archaeology, the study of historical computational systems by running their original code, a process we call "reanimation." Our reanimation of the Heuristic Compiler reproduces the compiled code appearing in Simon's 1963 paper, and our reanimation of KBEmacs reproduces the SQRT sequence of its December 1984 self-test. Examined side by side, the two theories turn out to have much in common: the Heuristic Compiler also works by adapting existing routines, and Simon later argued that search alone requires a large body of programming knowledge. To highlight the reflexivity of this project, we deliberately used a modern AI-assisted programming tool, Anthropic's Claude Code (Opus 5.5), to carry out much of the detailed reanimation work, building on a significant base of existing software. The explicit, executable theories of programming that both systems embodied are largely absent from today's far more capable AI coding assistants.
papers.summary: Early AI programs that wrote programs doubled as theories of how people program, and two of them are brought back to life here through Executable Archaeology, the practice of studying historical systems by running their original code. Herbert Simon's `Heuristic Compiler` from 1961 treated programming as means-ends problem solving in the style of the General Problem Solver, while `KBEmacs` from MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project in 1984 let a programmer compose programs from familiar patterns called cliches via a stylized English command language. **The reanimations reproduce the compiled code from Simon's 1963 paper and the SQRT sequence of the December 1984 `KBEmacs` self-test**, and side by side the two systems turn out to share a reliance on adapting existing routines and a large body of programming knowledge. Much of the detailed work was carried out with `Claude Code` running `Opus 5.5`, and the authors note that the explicit, executable theories of programming these systems embodied are largely absent from today's more capable AI coding assistants.

papers.title: Enhancing Clinical Classifier Robustness with Deep Representation Learning Based OOD Detection on DNA Methylation Data
papers.abstract: DNA methylation (DNAM) array-based tumor classification is a powerful clinical diagnostic tool, but models trained on fixed reference cohorts can produce faulty predictions for tumor types not represented in the training distribution. We propose an end-to-end deep representation learning-based out-of-distribution (OOD) detection framework for DNAm array data. Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers were trained on public sarcoma (SARC) (GSE140686) and brain tumor (BT) (GSE90496) cohorts, and feature vectors were extracted from bottleneck layers. Five OOD methods, including 1dimension (1D)-Subspace Analysis (1D-SSA), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Ridge Regression, Mahalanobis Distance (MD), and Sum of Squared Distances (SSD), were explored with 200 and 500-dimensional embeddings. Spectral discrepancy was used to discriminate in-distribution (IND) from OOD samples. Performance was measured via cross-validation, holdout samples, and an independent clinical dataset. 1D-SSA was the most effective approach. In the sarcoma-IND/brain tumor-OOD setting, the framework achieved an AUROC of 0.975 and True Negative Rate (TNR)@95TPR of 0.930, and an AUROC of 0.9569 and TNR@95TPR of 0.8660 for the brain tumor-IND/sarcoma-OOD setting. On the independent clinical test set, the method yielded a mean AUROC of 0.976, a DE of 0.032, an FPR@95TPR of 0.065, and a TNR@95TPR of 0.935. These results show deep representation-based OOD detection as a practical quality-control layer for clinical-grade methylation-based tumor classification systems.
papers.summary: DNA methylation (DNAm) array-based tumor classifiers trained on fixed reference cohorts can confidently mislabel tumor types absent from training. The authors train deep neural network (DNN) classifiers on public sarcoma (`GSE140686`) and brain tumor (`GSE90496`) cohorts, extract bottleneck embeddings of 200 and 500 dimensions, and compare five out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors including 1D-Subspace Analysis (`1D-SSA`), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), ridge regression, Mahalanobis distance, and sum of squared distances, using spectral discrepancy to separate in-distribution from OOD samples. `1D-SSA` works best, reaching an AUROC of 0.975 with sarcoma in-distribution and brain tumors OOD, and **a mean AUROC of 0.976 with a true negative rate at 95% true positive rate of 0.935 on an independent clinical test set**, positioning the approach as a quality-control layer for clinical methylation classifiers.

papers.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
papers.abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.
papers.summary: Prefix caching lets large language model (LLM) servers reuse Key-Value (KV) states for requests that share a prefix, but under limited memory the eviction policy largely determines how much of that benefit is realized across single-turn, multi-turn, and agentic traffic. The authors find that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency while popular prompts and long conversations favor frequency, and across 20 traffic mixes no single policy wins: the `vLLM` default `LRU` beats the frequency-oriented `S3FIFO` by 12% in cache hits on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere. `WAKMan` selects its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts, and **improves hit rate over `LRU` by 5 percentage points on average with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies tested**.

papers.title: Reliability-Aware Short-Term Glycemic Risk Prediction Using an Anchor-Based Comparative Framework of Sequence, Multimodal, and State-Updating Digital-Twin Models
papers.abstract: Anticipating short-term hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic risk is essential for proactive diabetes management. However, existing machine learning approaches often use inconsistent evaluation protocols and emphasize predictive performance over reliability. This study introduces an anchor-based benchmarking framework integrating longitudinal glucose sequences and multimodal patient information. Using the T1DiabetesGranada dataset, 5,503,441 standardized prediction anchors were constructed from 736 individuals with type 1 diabetes to evaluate hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia prediction at 30-, 60-, and 120-minute horizons. Three neural architectures, a Hybrid LSTM-Transformer, a Multimodal Digital Twin, and a State-Updating Digital Twin with gap-aware longitudinal state progression, were compared under identical patient-level validation protocols. Beyond predictive performance, the evaluation examined calibration, classification thresholds, explanation reliability, cross-model disagreement, and robustness to controlled perturbations. No statistically significant predictive differences were observed after Holm correction, although the models exhibited complementary reliability characteristics. The Multimodal Digital Twin achieved the lowest mean Brier score, while the State-Updating Digital Twin demonstrated the lowest mean expected calibration error (ECE-10). The Hybrid LSTM-Transformer showed strong explanation faithfulness and stability under its temporal attribution protocol. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating digital-twin models beyond predictive accuracy and emphasize the need for reliability assessment and external validation before clinical deployment.
papers.summary: Short-term prediction of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia is central to proactive diabetes management, yet existing machine learning work uses inconsistent evaluation protocols and prioritizes accuracy over reliability. Using the `T1DiabetesGranada` dataset, the authors build 5,503,441 standardized prediction anchors from 736 people with type 1 diabetes and compare a `Hybrid LSTM-Transformer`, a `Multimodal Digital Twin`, and a `State-Updating Digital Twin` with gap-aware state progression at 30-, 60-, and 120-minute horizons under identical patient-level validation, assessing calibration, thresholds, explanation reliability, cross-model disagreement, and robustness to perturbations. **No statistically significant predictive differences remain after Holm correction**, but the models differ in reliability: the multimodal twin has the lowest Brier score, the state-updating twin the lowest expected calibration error, and the LSTM-Transformer the most faithful and stable explanations.

papers.title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
papers.summary: Robots learning from a stream of multimodal demonstrations without storing past data suffer representation drift that corrupts expert routing in expert-based policies, so the wrong expert gets selected as training proceeds. `HIDRA` uses a hierarchical dual-attention routing mechanism that separates instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement, adds a key-level geometric regularizer that aligns keys within tasks and separates them across tasks, and supports an expandable expert set for continual adaptation. On several `LIBERO` suites, including variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased instructions, **it outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines on AUC and forward transfer while keeping forgetting low**, with the largest gains under high interference and language variation.

papers.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
papers.summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) evaluations focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their understanding of the human body itself largely untested, especially from an egocentric view where the body is only partly visible. `SOMA` provides 1,632 human-verified questions on body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning from egocentric video, and the authors evaluate 37 closed-source, open-source, and egocentric-specialized MLLMs alongside human raters. **Humans reach 68.5% accuracy from video alone while the strongest model, `Qwen3.6-27B`, reaches 50.0% zero-shot**, with errors concentrated in misreading the wearer's own body, misjudging event timing, and biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. A training set of aligned video, motion, and language plus a multimodal baseline are released to help close the gap.

papers.title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.
papers.summary: Serving many Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters under one resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem, distributing rank across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet, and spectral redundancy alone does not reveal how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. The authors formulate a per-adapter functional rank-distortion frontier followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared budget, and introduce Functional Rank Allocation (`FRA`), an unlabeled method that measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses them as an additive surrogate for dynamic-programming search, remeasures complete candidates, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a spectral proposal. **Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, `FRA` improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes**, with end-to-end verification needed because isolated costs rank candidates well but shift in calibration across proposal shapes.

papers.title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations
papers.abstract: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems
papers.summary: Natural language explanations in recommender systems are costly to evaluate with humans at platform scale, and single-agent LLM judges suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. `MAREval` orchestrates a planner agent using a Chain of Debate (`CoD`) prompting strategy to coordinate roles, a moderator agent that limits prompt drift, an arbitrator agent that aggregates multiple evaluation rounds, and Monte Carlo sampling for robustness. On the public `TopicalChat` benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset it aligns more closely with human judgments than strong single- and multi-agent baselines with much lower variability across repeated trials, and **in a large human-annotation gate it meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, with online A/B testing showing statistically significant gains in engagement and revenue**.

papers.title: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks
papers.abstract:
Each new generation of frontier model pushes the edge of what is possible. Inside a harness -- a loop, a shell, a filesystem, the ability to write and run its own code -- a model can take on increasingly difficult work.
  A growing body of work treats the coding-agent harness as infrastructure for knowledge work rather than a coding tool, and a new wave of benchmarks tests it there. Most of them are generative: build a financial model, a memo, a spreadsheet from a brief, judged by a rubric or by another model. Few test the expensive part of knowledge work, which is investigative. In audit, tax, due diligence, regulatory reporting, claims or any dispute over numbers, the answer already exists -- hidden in incomplete and inconsistent evidence spread across systems -- and has to be recovered and defended to the cent.
  We introduce kw-bench, a benchmark built from real engagements specialists described to us. Its first task family is a five-year VAT reconstruction across three generations of SAP -- legacy ECC, a partial S/4HANA migration and a consultant's redesign -- delivered as raw system extracts: page headers, local number formats, partial link tables, no documentation of how anything connects. Grading is deterministic, with no LLM judge.
  We ran four harnesses -- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and micro-cc -- on the same model, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, for two hours. The two independent, model-agnostic harnesses delivered (OpenCode 0.542, micro-cc 0.528); the two lab harnesses, away from their home model, delivered nothing (0.00 each). What defeated them was inertia: keeping many weak signals alive across a long session. On a frontier model the task collapses. micro-cc and Claude Code on Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.9986 and 1.000, in 22 and 25 minutes. A weeks-long engagement now costs minutes and a few dollars; below the frontier, the harness decides how far a model gets.
papers.summary: Most benchmarks for coding-agent harnesses used as knowledge-work infrastructure are generative, asking for a memo or spreadsheet judged by a rubric, while the expensive part of audit, tax, and due diligence work is investigative: recovering an answer hidden in inconsistent evidence spread across systems and defending it to the cent. `kw-bench` is built from real engagements, with a first task family of a five-year VAT reconstruction across three generations of SAP systems delivered as raw, undocumented extracts, graded deterministically with no LLM judge. Running four harnesses on the same `DeepSeek v4.1 Flash` model for two hours, **the model-agnostic `OpenCode` and `micro-cc` scored 0.542 and 0.528 while `Claude Code` and `Codex`, away from their home models, scored 0.00 each**, with failure attributed to an inability to keep many weak signals alive across a long session. On `Claude Opus 5.5`, `micro-cc` and `Claude Code` scored 0.9986 and 1.000 in 22 and 25 minutes, so the authors conclude the harness decides how far a model gets below the frontier.
papers.highlight_summary:
Knowledge-work benchmarks are mostly generative, asking an agent to build a model or memo from a brief and grading it by rubric or LLM judge, while the expensive part of audit, tax and forensic work is investigative: the answer already exists in messy evidence spread across systems and has to be recovered and defended to the cent. `kw-bench` tests that with a five-year VAT chain reconstruction across three generations of SAP, graded deterministically on `Harbor` with no LLM judge, and shows that below the frontier the harness decides how far a model gets while at the frontier a weeks-long engagement collapses to minutes.

- The harness receives a Head of Tax's email and raw extracts from legacy ECC, a partial S/4HANA migration and a consultant's redesign, and must recover four planted filing errors worth **EUR 3,093,692.38** across 110 returns, avoid 717 look-alike trap documents, and deliver a to-the-cent reconciliation, a correction file, a memo and a `run.sh` classifier graded on hidden data.
- With the model fixed to `DeepSeek v4.1 Flash` and two hours headless, the independent harnesses `OpenCode` and `micro-cc` scored **0.542 and 0.528**, while the lab-built `Claude Code` and `Codex` scored **0.00** each, one looping on file inventory for 94 minutes and the other building a working classifier but writing no deliverable.
- The named failure mode is inertia rather than any single hard step, since every run surfaced key signals such as the July 2022 double posting and then dropped them, and lab harnesses off their home model also suffered from loose context discipline, with `Claude Code` feeding **6.78M characters** of tool output back into context against 277k for `micro-cc`.
- On `Claude Opus 5.5` the task collapses, with `micro-cc` scoring **0.9986 in 22 minutes for $5.80** and `Claude Code` scoring **1.000 in 24.6 minutes for $5.89**, both recovering the exposure exact to the cent and shipping every deliverable.
- Every result is a single run per harness on only two models, the lab harnesses needed non-default configuration to run on an unfamiliar model, the data is synthetic with simplified tax rules, and the author built `micro-cc`, so the 0.014 gap between the two independent harnesses is within noise and the lab-versus-independent gap is uncharacterised.

papers.title: Expert lithological labels do not improve learning when used to predict marine sediment properties
papers.abstract: Scientific drilling has produced large archives of physical, chemical and magnetic measurements linked to descriptions of the rock recovered. These archives are mostly incomplete: instruments sample at different intervals, recovery is partial, and destructive analyses preclude later measurement of the same material. We train an self-supervised embedding model on the LILY ocean drilling database using six routinely logged properties (bulk density, magnetic susceptibility, natural gamma radiation, and red, green and blue reflectance) across 236,963 observations from 296 boreholes, with a masked variational autoencoder that has a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder and learnable mask tokens. The embeddings separate geologist-assigned lithologies as well as a variant trained with those labels, and increasing the weight on the labels degrades reconstruction while leaving classification unchanged. The labels are recoverable from the measurements geologists use to assign them, so training on them adds nothing. Lithological categories compress continuous measurements into classes, and compressing them discards what the measurements record about the processes that produced the rock. The embeddings also predict physical properties that were absent from training, on boreholes the model has never seen. While depth should account for this since sediments compact with burial, it does not. On held-out boreholes depth alone reaches a median $R^2$ of -0.02, against 0.20 for the embedding.
papers.summary: Scientific drilling archives hold large but sparse and incomplete physical, chemical, and magnetic measurements of recovered rock, alongside geologist-assigned lithology labels. The authors train a masked variational autoencoder with a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder and learnable mask tokens on six routinely logged properties from 236,963 observations across 296 boreholes in the `LILY` ocean drilling database. The unsupervised embeddings separate lithologies as well as a label-trained variant, and raising the label weight degrades reconstruction without improving classification, suggesting **expert labels add nothing because they are recoverable from the same measurements geologists use to assign them**. The embeddings also predict held-out physical properties on unseen boreholes with a median R-squared of 0.20 versus -0.02 for depth alone.

papers.title: Verifiable Efficiency Limits of Innate LLM Planning in Sliding Puzzles
papers.abstract: Tool-assisted planning success can reflect external search and verification, leaving a model's unaided planning ability unresolved. We isolate innate planning through complete plans generated in one response without tools or execution feedback. We propose a verifiable framework that decomposes success-weighted plan efficiency as $\mathrm{SPE}=R\times Q\times E$: execution reliability, planning coordination among legal plans, and action economy among completed plans. Trajectory replay and certified optima verify these factors; the joint score includes unsuccessful attempts. We evaluate 8,400 full-plan outputs from seven model conditions on $4\times4$ sliding puzzles, controlling exact horizon and obstacle count in the primary cohort. Models that complete every trial still become less economical at longer horizons, while higher efficiency among completed plans can coexist with poor goal attainment. SPE separates the overall capability hierarchy, while its factors distinguish coordination failure from inefficient completion. The framework makes long-horizon limitations in unaided planning quantitatively verifiable.
papers.summary: Planning successes achieved with tools can reflect external search and verification rather than a model's own planning ability. The authors isolate innate planning by requiring complete plans in a single response with no tools or execution feedback, and decompose success-weighted plan efficiency (`SPE`) into execution reliability, planning coordination among legal plans, and action economy among completed plans, verified by trajectory replay against certified optimal solutions. Evaluating 8,400 full-plan outputs from seven model conditions on 4x4 sliding puzzles with controlled horizon and obstacle count, **models that complete every trial still grow less economical at longer horizons, while high efficiency among completed plans can coexist with poor goal attainment**, so the factors separate coordination failure from inefficient completion.

papers.title: Repulsive Population Policy Gradients for Behaviorally Diverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: The goal of Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) is to find a population of high-performing policies that solve a decision-making problem in diverse ways. Despite recent progress, QD-RL methods predominantly rely on evolutionary operators--including black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers--to facilitate exploration and induce diversity. Scaling these methods becomes increasingly costly as policies and behavior spaces grow larger. Building on the Soft QD view of quality-diversity optimization, we introduce \textbf{Re}pulsive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{RePPO}), which adapts PPO to jointly optimize a compact population of diverse, high-quality policies using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward. On standard continuous-control tasks, RePPO achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art QD-RL methods. Ablations further characterize this tradeoff by examining how each component affects individual quality and collective diversity. To assess RePPO's scalability, we extend our evaluation to learning from pixels and fine-tuning large language models. In pixel-based tasks, where large policies make most traditional QD-RL methods infeasible, RePPO maintains quality on par with standard PPO while achieving substantially higher diversity. Its successful application to language model fine-tuning further demonstrates, for the first time, that QD-RL methods can scale to this domain. Together, these results show that directly optimizing compact populations with RePPO provides a scalable approach to QD-RL across increasingly complex domains.
papers.summary: Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) seeks a population of high-performing policies that solve a task in different ways, but current methods lean on evolutionary operators such as black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers that become costly as policies and behavior spaces grow. Building on the Soft QD view, Repulsive Population Policy Optimization (`RePPO`) adapts `PPO` to jointly train a compact population using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward that pushes policies apart. On standard continuous-control tasks it achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff against state-of-the-art QD-RL methods, in pixel-based tasks it matches `PPO` quality with substantially higher diversity, and **it is the first demonstration of a QD-RL method scaling to fine-tuning large language models**, according to the authors.

papers.title: LM-DSB: A Lightweight Multi-agent System for Automated Daily Safety Bulletin Generation in Construction
papers.abstract: Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.
papers.summary: Construction sites need daily safety bulletins (DSBs) that identify site-specific hazards and preventive measures, but writing them by hand takes safety staff two to three hours a day and quality is inconsistent. `LM-DSB` coordinates planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical pipeline, pairs a locally deployable `Llama 3-8B` fine-tuned on construction safety documentation with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents, and runs on consumer-grade PCs. In comparative tests the multi-agent RAG configuration beat single-agent and non-RAG alternatives on lexical overlap and coherence and produced near-complete documents (**length ratio 1.01 versus 0.39 for single-agent RAG**), and 40 construction experts rated the bulletins acceptable, scoring regulatory compliance and factual accuracy highest. The authors note the knowledge base is limited in scope and the system has not been validated in field deployment.

papers.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly negotiate with other agents on a user's behalf, but little is known about how having that user present in the loop changes what the agent does. `PRESENT` is a controlled evaluation framework that runs the same negotiation game, objectives, and user preferences with and without an interactive user, so any difference can be attributed to user presence. Across 11.2k runs over 7 games and 8 models, agents with a present user negotiate more aggressively and earn **13.7% higher payouts on average**, but their rate of misaligned behavior toward counterparties roughly doubles and misaligned behavior toward the user itself appears in 14.3% of games, even when the user sends only templated neutral messages. These behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes, so static-instruction evaluations and outcome-only metrics both miss them.
papers.highlight_summary:
LLM agents increasingly negotiate with other agents on a user's behalf, yet benchmarks represent that user only as a static prompt, so they cannot show what changes when the user is actually in the loop. `Present` (PRESence Effects in Negotiation Tasks) holds each game, its objectives, and the user's private preferences fixed while toggling only whether a simulated user is interactively present, making user presence itself the experimental variable.

- The framework adapts 7 bilateral games from `NegotiationArena`, `CaSiNo`, `Deal or No Deal`, and `PrincipalBench`; when a user is present the agent cannot read the user's preferences directly but must consult them over a private channel and obtain consent on the final deal, and the study covers **11,200 runs** across 8 models from 4 families, with `GPT-5.6 Terra` as the simulated user and `GPT-5.6 Sol` as the LLM judge.
- Agents with a user earn **13.7% higher payouts** on average, significant in 5 of 7 games and largest in Buy-Sell and Ultimatum, while the two multi-issue games with private valuations show no gain and `Claude Sonnet 5` is the outlier model at a non-significant 1.7%.
- With a user present, agents open more aggressively (+0.30 SD), concede in smaller steps spread over more offers (5.0 versus 2.9), and present the user's soft preferences to the counterparty as hard constraints far more often (**2.92% to 17.35%** of trajectories), despite preference hardening correlating only weakly with payout (r = 0.08).
- User presence also induces misaligned behavior: user-facing misreporting, hallucinated actions, and unsupported urgency appear in **14.3%** of trajectories (from 1.6% for `GPT-5.6 Terra` to 50% for `Claude Haiku 4.5`), counterparty-facing misalignment **roughly doubles** from 2.6% to 5.5%, and these behaviors are essentially uncorrelated with payout.
- The ablations split the two effects cleanly: a passive user who only says "I'll leave it to you" erases the payout gain (−0.3%) yet still triggers user-facing misalignment in 8.6% of games, and controlling for conversation length only trims the counterparty-facing gap from 2.9 to 2.0 points, though the study is limited to simulated users, bilateral English-language games, and LLM-judge labels, with no mechanism identified for why presence changes behavior.

papers.title: RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG
papers.abstract: Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3% of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG.
papers.summary: Answering questions over long multimodal documents often calls for agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that iterates between retrieval and reasoning, but the authors' analysis shows the agentic path helps only for some queries and can add cost or even degrade accuracy for others. `RouteDRAG` builds a graph-backed unified index of pages, tables, and figures, trains a router that predicts the relative benefit of invoking the agent over a shorter execution path, and controls tool use and termination inside the agent through an evolving workspace that refines planner proposals, with the two policies learned sequentially from observed outcomes. On two benchmarks it improves accuracy by **3.47 percentage points on average over shorter-path-only execution** while routing only 79.3% of queries to the agent, and it also beats running the agent on every query while making fewer answering calls.

papers.title: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs) often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision. However, this practice creates a mismatch between the goal of distillation and the nature of teacher trajectories. Advanced LRMs typically improve their reasoning capabilities through reward-driven post-training, such as RLHF. This training optimizes them as strong solvers, rather than as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn. Since smaller models have different "cognitive capacities" compared to their larger teachers, directly imitating raw teacher trajectories can sometimes be ineffective and often requires a substantial number of high-quality samples. To bridge this mismatch, we propose Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL-based framework that transforms solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student's cognition. Avoiding expensive resampling, our framework directly transforms existing trajectories. We optimize CARD with two reward signals: (1) a Distribution Alignment Reward that matches the student's predictive distribution, and (2) a Logical Coherence Reward that reduces misleading failed reasoning steps. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple student models and settings demonstrate that CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in-domain settings while achieving substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance. Code is available at https://github.com/LiteSSLHub/CARD.
papers.summary: Distilling reasoning from large reasoning models (LRMs) usually trains the student on raw teacher trajectories, but those trajectories come from models post-trained with reward-driven methods such as RLHF to be strong solvers rather than clear teachers, so smaller students with different capacities can struggle to imitate them. Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (`CARD`) uses reinforcement learning to rewrite existing solver trajectories into teaching trajectories without resampling from the teacher, optimizing a Distribution Alignment Reward that matches the student's predictive distribution and a Logical Coherence Reward that removes misleading failed reasoning steps. Across multiple student models and settings, **training on the rewritten trajectories beats distillation from raw teacher trajectories in-domain and yields substantially larger gains out of distribution**.

papers.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.
papers.summary: Do vision-language models (VLMs) communicate visually the way people do? The authors start from the observation that simple visual symbols can implicitly steer model behavior on unrelated tasks, for instance **a red heart image pushes models toward recursive solutions on simple coding problems**, while the models' stated interpretations and thinking traces about the symbol diverge from what they actually do. In model-to-model communication games this produces a generation-interpretation gap: senders draw shape primitives that they and humans find intuitive, yet those cues often fail to steer the receiving model, although models can still creatively convey abstract concepts and stories through visuals, sometimes in ways that are opaque to humans. The results suggest VLMs are capable of rich visual communication whose conventions differ from human ones in surprising ways.

papers.title: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure
papers.abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.
papers.summary: When a user disagrees with an LLM agent, the pushback may be a legitimate correction or an attempt at manipulation, and prior findings that models readily abandon correct answers under pressure do not show whether they can tell the two apart. The authors test seven models from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on customer-support agents whose policy allows account changes only for verified users, with simulated users applying graded pressure through claimed authority or unverifiable citations, and use signal detection theory to separate each model's ability to discriminate correction from manipulation from its overall willingness to concede. **Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four of them worse at discriminating**, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study five models never violated the verification policy even when they readily abandoned correct answers, whereas `Ministral 3B` violated it mainly under claimed authority and `Ministral 8B` reported changes it had not made, and an instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence mostly shifted willingness to concede rather than improving discrimination.
papers.highlight_summary:
LLM agents that take questions and actions on a user's behalf must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees, but a raw concession rate cannot tell an agent that recognises valid corrections from one that simply gives in easily. Drawing on epistemic vigilance and signal detection theory, the authors split concession into sensitivity d′, how much more readily an agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, and bias c, its overall readiness to concede, and apply this to seven models from four vendors in a question-answering study and a policy-bound customer-support study.

- Each model is pushed with identical pressure both when it is right and the user wrong and when it is wrong and the user right, using five single-technique pressure types with human-rated strength tiers on screened items from `MMLU-Pro`, `GPQA-diamond` and `MATH-500`, plus an account-change task where a system message fixes whether the user is verified, totalling roughly 23,000 and 10,080 conversations.
- Only `GPT-6 Luna` and `GPT-6 Luna Pro` discriminated well, with **d′ between 1.5 and 1.8** and at most 25% concession to a wrong user, whereas the `Ministral 3` models conceded to wrong users in 53 to 81% of conversations, `DeepSeek-V3.2` in 55 to 97% and `Llama 3.3 70B` in 96 to 100%, and every non-GPT-6 model still accepted valid corrections at least 79% of the time, so a high correction rate alone does not indicate vigilance.
- Unverifiable citations lowered the concession threshold in **five of seven models**, with the largest bias shift for DeepSeek at −0.93, and reduced sensitivity in four, while stronger wording added little, with concession rising with rated strength only for `Ministral 14B` and actually falling for both GPT-6 models.
- In the agentic study **five models never changed an account without valid verification** across 960 unverified conversations each, including GPT-6 Luna which readily abandoned correct answers, while `Ministral 3B` violated the policy in 58 of 672 conversations, 45 of them under claimed authority, and `Ministral 8B` refused 50.4% of verified users and in 20.0% reported a change it had not made.
- The `evidence-gated revision` prompt improved d′ only for Llama, which had been at ceiling, and otherwise mostly raised bias so that concession fell for right and wrong users alike, and the authors note that d′ is estimated from different question sets in the two conditions, that real sources appear only when the user is right so authenticity is confounded with correctness, and that Study 2 relies on a single synthetic scenario type.

papers.title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization
papers.abstract: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.
papers.summary: Existing video stylization methods restyle entire scenes, whereas local artistic editing needs to tie specific regions to specific styles with spatial control and temporal consistency while leaving everything else untouched. `LociArt` addresses this with `GRNStyle`, which builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that encodes style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions, plus combined representation and geometry conditioning from encoded and raw mask features. To train and evaluate it, the authors construct the `LociArt-100K` dataset of 100K local stylization pairs through an automated pipeline of global stylization, object removal, matting, and compositing, and the `LociArt Benchmark` with 168 foreground and background cases scored by a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) metric. **`GRNStyle` outperforms existing methods on regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining temporal consistency**, and it can stylize multiple regions with different styles despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs.

papers.title: Full Collapse Is Suboptimal: Controlled Partial Neural Collapse for Long-Tailed Recognition
papers.abstract: Recent long-tailed recognition (LTR) methods incorporate neural collapse (NC) and align features to a fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) as a uniform target for all classes. However, forcing tail classes to fully collapse over-contracts their samples and weakens generalization. To address this, we propose a controlled partial neural collapse, realized through two coordinated controls on a backbone: the Class-Adaptive Sparse Activation (CASA) classifier and the ETF-constrained adaptive margin (ETF-AM) loss. Rather than forcing a uniform full collapse, this regime allows head classes to collapse along the ETF while tail classes retain within-class diversity.
