This prevents the tail from being forced into full collapse, which is suboptimal under imbalance. To set the dimensionality of collapse, CASA induces class-related node specialization through feature-conditioned gating so that tail classes occupy their own feature directions. For the clearance axis, ETF-AM applies a frequency-adaptive margin, with smaller margins for head classes and larger for tail classes. On CIFAR100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and iNaturalist-2018, our method achieves the best overall accuracy over prior methods. In the empirical analysis, within-class spread increases monotonically from head to tail classes, consistent with tail classes retaining variability rather than fully collapsing.
papers.summary: Recent long-tailed recognition methods push the features of every class toward a fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) following the neural collapse phenomenon, but forcing rare tail classes to collapse fully over-contracts their few samples and hurts generalization. The proposed controlled partial neural collapse combines a Class-Adaptive Sparse Activation (`CASA`) classifier, which uses feature-conditioned gating so tail classes occupy their own feature directions, with an ETF-constrained adaptive margin (`ETF-AM`) loss that assigns smaller margins to head classes and larger ones to tail classes, letting head classes collapse along the ETF while tail classes keep within-class diversity. **The method reaches the best overall accuracy among prior approaches on `CIFAR100-LT`, `ImageNet-LT`, `Places-LT`, and `iNaturalist-2018`**, and measured within-class spread increases monotonically from head to tail classes as intended.

papers.title: When to Intervene? An Empirical Study of Errors and Self-Recovery in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents interact with Web services to perform tasks on users' behalf. Errors during these interactions can disrupt execution and prevent task completion, motivating external intervention. However, agents may self-recover through continued execution, raising the question of when to intervene and when to wait for self-recovery. We present an empirical study of errors and self-recovery in LLM agents. We construct ReInBench, a dataset containing 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events across computer-use and Web tasks. Our study examines how often and how quickly agents self-recover, how self-recovery relates to subsequent execution and task completion, and whether self-recovery can be predicted when an error occurs. We find that 725 error events self-recover, often within a few steps, with self-recovery performance differing across Execution LLMs. Self-recovery can also help agents recover from subsequent errors of the same type and support overall task completion. Intervention should therefore prioritize errors unlikely to self-recover, while allowing agents to continue when self-recovery is likely. Building on these empirical findings, we propose ReCoF, a method that predicts whether an error will self-recover to inform whether additional intervention is needed. ReCoF achieves an average relative improvement of 9.02% in Macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on ReInBench. Our code and data can be found at https://method-notes.github.io/ReCoF/.
papers.summary: LLM agents acting on web services and computers hit errors mid-task, and operators must decide whether to intervene or let the agent keep going in the hope it recovers on its own. The authors build `ReInBench`, a dataset of 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events across computer-use and web tasks, and study how often and how quickly agents self-recover, how recovery relates to later execution and task completion, and whether recovery can be predicted at the moment an error occurs. **725 of the 1,403 error events self-recover, often within a few steps**, with rates varying by the execution LLM, and recovering from one error helps agents handle later errors of the same type and finish tasks. Building on this, `ReCoF` predicts whether a given error will self-recover so that intervention can be reserved for errors unlikely to resolve, improving Macro-F1 by 9.02% relative to the strongest baseline on `ReInBench`.

papers.title: FIDES-Live: Evaluating Behavioral Concordance in Sequential Trading Agents
papers.abstract: Sequential trading agents produce decisions, orders, execution receipts, account states, and reports that need not agree, even when the final portfolio value is correctly computed. We present FIDES-Live, an operational extension of FIDES from generated strategy concordance to the audit of sequential agent traces. The protocol separates structured decision validity, optional numerical commitment adherence, execution and ledger reconciliation, and receipt- grounded reporting, with explicit coverage and unscorable outcomes. We retrospectively audit ten requested inference routes over 7,299 cryptocurrency account-rounds and a 310-round equity pilot, using real market observations and local paper execution. Cryptocurrency decision validity is 97.35% and structured reporting accuracy is 90.81% among scorable responses, but route-level decision and reporting performance can diverge sharply. Commitment adherence is 94.36% overall; it falls to 62.63% on constraints emitted with nonempty order proposals, compared with 97.56% for valid empty proposals. All retained cash and position transitions reconcile with recorded fills, while execution controls and unavailable quotes explain separate rejection populations. Short-window marked returns provide descriptive context rather than a new test of whether concordance predicts alpha. These observations motivate reporting concordance, evidence coverage, activity, and financial outcomes separately. They do not establish long-run trading skill, semantic faithfulness of explanations, or causal benefits from audit feedback.
papers.summary: A sequential trading agent emits decisions, orders, execution receipts, account states, and reports, and these artifacts can contradict one another even when the final portfolio value is computed correctly. `FIDES-Live` extends the earlier `FIDES` concordance protocol from generated strategies to audits of live agent traces, separately checking structured decision validity, adherence to numerical commitments, reconciliation of executions against the ledger, and whether reports are grounded in receipts, with explicit coverage and unscorable outcomes. A retrospective audit of ten inference routes over 7,299 cryptocurrency account-rounds and a 310-round equity pilot finds 97.35% decision validity and 90.81% structured reporting accuracy, but **commitment adherence drops to 62.63% on constraints emitted alongside nonempty order proposals versus 97.56% for valid empty proposals**, and routes diverge sharply on decision and reporting quality. The authors stress these audits say nothing about long-run trading skill or whether the agents' explanations are semantically faithful.

papers.title: Proposing Better Rollouts for On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model post-training by letting the student learn from its own sampled trajectories under teacher supervision, aligning the training process with inference-time behavior. However, the rollout policy in OPD is usually treated as fixed: each round samples directly from the current student. We show that this choice can create a compounding teacher--student mismatch, because it requires the teacher to provide effective supervision on whichever trajectories the student samples, including ones less reachable by the teacher itself. On such trajectories, teacher supervision can become noisy or even misleading, leading to undesirable student patterns such as repetition. Moreover, since the updated student in turn defines the rollout policy of subsequent rounds, these patterns persist and potentially amplify over training. This failure mode suggests that improving OPD requires treating the rollout policy itself as an optimization target, rather than only modifying the distillation objective. We propose Mixture Proposal On-Policy Distillation (MPOPD), which derives a student-anchored, teacher-guided rollout distribution from a local trust-region objective based on relative teacher support. The resulting target is a geometric mixture of the student and teacher policies, and we introduce a proposal policy that approximates this mixture, enabling rollout generation in a single forward pass. Experiments on 16 math, knowledge, and medical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over OPD and recent variants. On math reasoning, our method improves average accuracy by 6.91 over OPD on Qwen3-4B-Base while reducing average generation length by 41%, suggesting that rollout policy design provides an effective way to improve OPD.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own sampled trajectories under teacher supervision, but sampling rollouts purely from the current student can produce trajectories the teacher itself would rarely reach, where its supervision becomes noisy or misleading and induces patterns such as repetition that compound across rounds. Mixture Proposal On-Policy Distillation (`MPOPD`) treats the rollout policy as the optimization target: it derives a student-anchored, teacher-guided rollout distribution from a local trust-region objective based on relative teacher support, which turns out to be a geometric mixture of student and teacher, and approximates that mixture with a proposal policy that generates rollouts in a single forward pass. Across 16 math, knowledge, and medical reasoning benchmarks it consistently beats OPD and recent variants, and **on math reasoning with `Qwen3-4B-Base` it raises average accuracy by 6.91 points over OPD while cutting average generation length by 41%**.

papers.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments
papers.abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.
papers.summary: Claims about LLM cognition are usually tested by converting behavioral experiments into text prompts, skipping the visual interfaces and time pressure human participants face, while browser-capable agents that can complete online studies raise concerns about contaminating behavioral-science datasets. `CogArena` packages ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences so that agents complete them through a standard web browser with the same stimuli and response interfaces as human participants, and scores sessions at three levels: whether the task was completed, how accurately, and whether the data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Running four multimodal models ten times per task, **many sessions failed to finish, and those that did reproduced some human signatures reliably and others not at all**, showing that completing an experiment and behaving like a human participant are distinct. The tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard are released.

papers.title: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation
papers.abstract: Cross-modal translation requires models to capture shared semantics across modalities while preserving the fine-grained structure required by the target modality. Yet in real-world scientific domains, paired data are often imperfect, while obtaining clean pairs at scale is costly. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) directly optimizes cross-modal translation through categorical token-level supervision, but this objective is sensitive to errors in the target sequences. JEPA offers a complementary representation-space objective, but most existing formulations focus on prediction within a modality rather than translation across modalities. We introduce Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (AC-JEPA), an SFT-compatible plug-in that predicts masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions using paired data. The joint-embedding objective targets cross-modal structure predictable from context, while the causal SFT path retains direct token-level supervision for the target sequence. During self-training, AC-JEPA learns from continuous latent targets derived from imperfect pseudo-labeled pairs, offering intrinsic tolerance to local data errors without promoting pseudo-tokens to hard categorical supervision. Using optical chemical structure recognition as a testbed, AC-JEPA trained on clean pairs achieves 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of the WildMol benchmark, compared with 67.40% for SFT alone. Using the same pseudo-labeled data for both approaches, AC-JEPA-based self-training further raises accuracy to 80.23%, whereas accuracy under direct SFT drops from 67.40% to 63.47%. These results support SFT-anchored joint-embedding prediction as an effective strategy for cross-modal translation under both curated and imperfect supervision.
papers.summary: Translating images into symbolic sequences in scientific domains, such as reading a chemical structure drawing into a molecular string, relies on paired data that is often noisy, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with token-level supervision is sensitive to errors in those targets. Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (`AC-JEPA`) is a plug-in for SFT that adds a joint-embedding predictive objective predicting masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions, so the model learns cross-modal structure in representation space while the causal SFT path keeps direct token supervision, and during self-training it learns from continuous latent targets of pseudo-labeled pairs rather than promoting them to hard labels. On optical chemical structure recognition, **`AC-JEPA` trained on clean pairs reaches 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of `WildMol` versus 67.40% for SFT alone**, and self-training on pseudo-labeled data lifts it to 80.23% while the same data drops plain SFT to 63.47%.

papers.title: ProCerDCL: Query-Efficient Black-Box Probabilistic Verification of Deep Learning Compiler Optimization
papers.abstract: We present \tool, a query-efficient framework for black-box probabilistic verification. Given a fixed, sampleable input distribution and a binary property oracle, \tool assesses the property's violation probability $p$ against a threshold $\theta$. Under independent sampling and stateless oracle behavior, acceptance asserts $p\le\theta$, rejection asserts $p>\theta+\eta$ for a user-specified separation margin, and an inconclusive verdict indicates insufficient evidence for either conclusion. The probability of each type of erroneous verdict is bounded by its specified error budget. To support this three-valued contract efficiently, \tool uses a single sequential test, eliminating the interval family required by the baseline. The test accounts for repeated sampling checks through either corrected exact binomial confidence intervals or an anytime-valid confidence sequence. We apply \tool to probabilistic local model semantic consistency, where the property oracle detects decision-level inconsistencies between reference and compiled executions under a specified perturbation distribution. Our evaluation covers 24 tasks across TorchInductor and TensorRT and examines sampling efficiency, conclusiveness, and diagnostic behavior. For sampling efficiency, we use paired one-model clean-label radius searches: the baseline requires 3.6-4.2 times as many unique samples under matched numerical parameters while providing a weaker decision contract. For model semantic consistency, checks at $\theta=10^{-3}$ yield 817 acceptances, 19 inconclusive verdicts, and 4 rejections across 840 input--backend instances from 21 tasks. Case studies of two documented compiler faults further demonstrate what these local verdicts can diagnose.
papers.summary: Checking whether a deep learning compiler such as `TorchInductor` or `TensorRT` preserves a model's decisions under input perturbations is naturally a probabilistic question, and existing black-box verifiers need many samples and offer weak guarantees. `ProCerDCL` treats verification as a query-efficient sequential test against a property oracle: given a sampleable input distribution it accepts when the violation probability is at most a threshold, rejects when it exceeds the threshold plus a user-set margin, or returns inconclusive, with each kind of erroneous verdict bounded by an error budget, using corrected exact binomial intervals or an anytime-valid confidence sequence to account for repeated checks. In paired radius searches **the baseline needs 3.6 to 4.2 times as many unique samples while providing a weaker decision contract**, and across 840 input-backend instances from 21 tasks at a violation threshold of one in a thousand the tool returns 817 acceptances, 19 inconclusive verdicts, and 4 rejections, with case studies showing what the local verdicts reveal about two documented compiler faults.

papers.title: Do AI Scientists Know What's New?
papers.abstract: A major challenge facing AI scientific discovery pipelines is how to determine when a generated idea is meaningfully novel. Ideally, novelty checks in these pipelines must be able to reject non-novel ideas while not rejecting too many novel ideas, and they should also be able to distinguish which parts of a proposal are non-novel, as opposed to opaquely discarding entire proposals. We design an analytical framework for evaluation of novelty checks with temporal ground truth at both the proposal- and claim-level, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals built from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas matching ones the field went on to publish. Auditing existing novelty checks with this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are later realized by human researchers, and observe that checks built to evaluate proposals as a whole can point to claim-level prior art only by rejecting the whole proposal. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module. ClaimNov catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate, and its claim-level novelty profile cuts the LLM judge's false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%. Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, ClaimNov also keeps proposals that build on established contributions, rejecting only 3% of ICLR-accepted proposals with a reviewer-disputed contribution and keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced prior contribution, against 76 for the strongest existing check. Code and data are available at https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov.
papers.summary: Automated scientific discovery pipelines need a novelty check that rejects ideas already in the literature without discarding genuinely new ones, and that can point to which specific claims in a proposal are not new rather than rejecting the whole thing. The authors build an evaluation framework with temporal ground truth at both proposal and claim level from four datasets totaling 1,060 proposals, drawn from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas that the field later published, and find that existing checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also raise many false alarms on ideas humans went on to realize. Their claim-level module `ClaimNov` **catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate** and cuts an LLM judge's false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%, while rejecting only 3% of ICLR-accepted proposals that contained a reviewer-disputed contribution and keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced-in prior contribution, versus 76 for the strongest existing check.

papers.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
papers.abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.
papers.summary: Locally deployed language models increasingly answer medical questions, and once deployed their behavior on ethical trade-offs is governed largely by the constitution they are given, yet existing medical benchmarks test factual accuracy or treat ethics as a fixed property of the model. `MedConstBench` makes the deployment constitution a controlled variable, organizes evaluation around Beauchamp's four principles of biomedical ethics, scores responses with human-calibrated multi-model peer review, and includes `MedDilemma`, a new dataset of clinical dilemmas. Evaluating ten open-source models under four constitutions shows that **a constitution's effect is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and no single constitution is best for every model**, which motivates a do-no-harm adaptive selector that picks a constitution per model, matches the per-model oracle, guarantees a worst-case floor, and generalizes cheaply to unseen models.

papers.title: RoboAuto: Autonomous Robot Program Search through Multi-Level Physical Understanding
papers.abstract: Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have shown strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions. In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy lets these agents search over modular and editable robot programs. However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail. Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved. We introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three components. First, a hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, learned from embodied data and online task solving. Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities. Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties. RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. We further show that the knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with its size. Project page: https://roboauto-ai.github.io/
papers.summary: LLM-based agents can iteratively generate, test, and refine executable robot programs under the Code-as-Policy paradigm, but effective search requires understanding how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why an interaction failed, which execution feedback alone does not supply. `RoboAuto` organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through a hierarchical knowledge base that pairs executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects learned from embodied data and online task solving, scene grounding that ties this knowledge to the current environment, and multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments that verify each stage's expected physical effect and test competing hypotheses. It **reaches an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon `LIBERO-PRO` tasks and more than doubles the mean success rate of `ASPIRE` on `LIBERO-PRO Long` and `LIBERO-Plus`**, beats `ASPIRE` and `π0.5` on three long-horizon real-robot tasks, and its knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments with performance scaling in its size.

papers.title: ATEMPO: Amortized Transfer Entropy Model Per-lag Over-Time
papers.abstract: When one time series informs another, the delay at which that information arrives determines if models can utilize this relationship effectively. A source may be strongly predictive at one delay but uninformative at neighboring lags. Therefore, fixed input windows may obscure this structure by bundling informative and irrelevant history together. Transfer entropy (TE) can recover these delays by measuring how much a source's past tells us about a target beyond the target's own history. However, existing TE estimators require separate fits across source and conditioning depths, with further estimation on local windows to track delays over time. We introduce ATEMPO, a diffusion-based transfer entropy estimator amortized over lags and time. ATEMPO samples source and conditioning depths during training and conditions explicitly on temporal position, allowing a single score network to estimate the full TE surface without refitting. Differencing this surface recovers when information arrives. Across synthetic datasets with ground-truth TE, ATEMPO achieves the lowest mean relative error among baselines, and on datasets with known lags, ATEMPO achieves $0.98\pm0.04$ lag-detection accuracy. ATEMPO requires a single fit across source depths $K=6$ and target depths $L=3$, whereas existing estimators require 18 separate fits to evaluate the same $K \times L$ grid. On three systems with time-varying lag, ATEMPO is the only estimator to maintain perfect lag-detection accuracy across all evaluated window lengths. These recovered delays improve downstream forecasting: ATEMPO-selected inputs reduce MSE on WEATHER-5K by 7.25%, while 120 selected inputs outperform the benchmark's 240-feature default by 4.6%. Across three brain-computer interface tasks, using ATEMPO-selected lags achieves the highest or equal-best $R^2$, improving mean $R^2$ by 4.1% relative to the strongest competing baseline.

papers.title: Monitor Accuracy Isn't the Answer: A Decision-Value Framework for Evaluating AI Agent Restart Monitors
papers.abstract: Classification accuracy and true-positive and false-positive rates alone do not determine whether restarting an AI agent improves success. Using an exact alarm-to-action identity for an independent clean restart with zero monitoring overhead, we show analytically that a monitor with fixed 90% accuracy can swing from a five-percentage-point loss to a 35-point gain in success rate, depending solely on the replacement attempt's residual-budget success probability. We introduce two techniques for evaluating monitors and progress signals in decision terms. First, a decision-sufficiency criterion, a binary-action specialization of Blackwell's comparison of experiments, identifies which progress representations or context compressions preserve the information needed to choose optimally between the specified actions, independent of trace reconstruction fidelity. Second, a finite-sample, model-free decision audit uses simultaneous binomial intervals over existing agent traces, without additional model calls, to certify a preference for "restart" or "continue" under stated sampling assumptions, or return "abstain" when evidence is insufficient. In a study of 194 externally evaluated model executions on 19 selected SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified, with a retrospective audit of 130 of these traces, we find a 2.29-point apparent restart gain traced to a single surviving failed attempt, a 42.29-point loss on a second model, no positive replication of the initial gain on prospective task cohorts, and zero of 103 live comparisons meeting the specified certification bar. These results motivate evaluating agent monitors through recovery opportunity, decision value, and statistical support, rather than classification performance alone.
papers.summary: Whether restarting a struggling AI agent on a monitor's alarm actually improves success cannot be read off the monitor's classification accuracy. Using an exact identity linking alarms to actions for an independent clean restart, the authors show that **a monitor with fixed 90% accuracy can yield anywhere from a five-point loss to a 35-point gain in success rate**, depending only on how likely a replacement attempt is to succeed within the remaining budget. They introduce a decision-sufficiency criterion, a binary-action specialization of Blackwell's comparison of experiments, that tests whether a progress representation or context compression preserves the information needed to choose between restart and continue, plus a finite-sample, model-free audit that uses simultaneous binomial intervals over existing agent traces to certify a preference for either action or abstain. In a study of 194 externally evaluated executions on 19 `SymPy` issues from `SWE-bench Verified`, an apparent 2.29-point restart gain traced to a single surviving failed attempt, a second model showed a 42.29-point loss, the gain did not replicate on prospective task cohorts, and none of 103 live comparisons met the certification bar.

papers.title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation
papers.abstract: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.
papers.summary: Unified conditional image generation asks one model to keep selected aspects of an input image while producing a target that follows a text instruction, and pretrained video models are a natural starting point because they encode visual transformations over time, but prior work pins the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. `FrameForge` instead models the condition-target relationship as an input-adaptive virtual temporal relation: a Mixture of Temporal Experts (`MoTE`) chooses among temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals to represent how far the target lies from the condition, and Chain of Temporal Reasoning (`CoTR`) routes the transformation through a latent intermediate state using a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask. On `DreamBench`, `COCO2017`, and `GEdit-Bench`, **`FrameForge` outperforms the compared methods on subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing**.

papers.title: REACH: An RL-based Hierarchical Humanoid Crawling Framework for Adaptable Confined Space Traversal
papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.27--0.50m in bipedal locomotion and 0.50--0.20m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/REACH/.
papers.summary: Humanoid robots moving through confined spaces must adjust body height continuously across distinct locomotion modes, yet most prior approaches stop at height-adjustable bipedal walking. The authors train a hierarchical set of reinforcement learning policies for a `Unitree G1` humanoid that regulate body height across complementary command ranges, with bipedal walking covering 1.27 to 0.50 meters and **crawling extending traversal down to 0.20 meters of clearance, beyond the limits of crouched walking**. A history-conditioned latent representation built from proprioceptive observations captures terrain and contact context during crawling, and a bidirectional transition policy bridges the large kinematic and contact discontinuities between the two modes. A LiDAR-based planner converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands with proactive height targets, and real-world experiments show accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, and reliable mode transitions through height-constrained environments.

papers.title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization
papers.abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.
papers.summary: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) covers problems where gradients are unavailable or expensive, as in simulation-based and experimental settings where each black-box evaluation is costly, so the core difficulty is choosing informative evaluation points under a tight budget. `NextEval` pairs a large language model agent with a numerical environment that exposes tools for analyzing past evaluations and running classical DFO methods, keeps a shared evaluation history and per-method state so the agent can switch methods mid-run, and lets the agent pick tools, set their parameters, and allocate the remaining budget. The accompanying `NextEval Bench` protocol compares agent configurations on shared tasks with identical tools, budgets, and information constraints, and **on low-dimensional problems the solver outperforms state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency**.

papers.title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using language agents increasingly modify external systems, yet most runtime safeguards allocate scrutiny by generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics. We introduce CASEL (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer), a model-agnostic runtime allocation policy that combines calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness to choose, for each proposed tool call, among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, approval, and abstention by minimizing a per-mode cost. We formalize direct execution as selective prediction and state and test the validity conditions of a finite-sample threshold and a trajectory risk ledger. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, in which every method has the same intervention menu and the same compute cost, CASEL reduces harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75 percent for an uncertainty-ranked gate to 7.02 percent and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123. A gate ranked by the product of failure probability and consequence reaches similar harm (5.82 percent, 0.120) but sends 45 percent more actions to human approval, and removing reversibility-aware routing raises the rate to 15.53 percent. A trajectory-level risk budget, in contrast, increases harm at equal cost (11.82 percent). Intervention effectiveness is assumed, not measured: the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.
papers.summary: Tool-using language agents increasingly make changes to external systems, but most runtime safeguards decide how much scrutiny to apply using generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics. `CASEL` (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer) is a model-agnostic policy that scores each proposed tool call on calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness, then picks the lowest-cost option among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, human approval, and abstention, with direct execution formalized as selective prediction under a finite-sample threshold and a trajectory risk ledger. In a controlled simulation of 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, **harmful-side-effect trajectories fall from 14.75 percent under an uncertainty-ranked gate to 7.02 percent**, while a gate ranked by failure probability times consequence reaches similar harm but routes 45 percent more actions to human approval, and removing reversibility-aware routing pushes harm back up to 15.53 percent. The authors stress that intervention effectiveness is assumed rather than measured, so the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

papers.title: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses to diverse user requests, yet streaming may expose users to harmful content before generation is complete. Existing guardrails face two limitations in this setting. First, post-hoc moderation at response or chunk boundaries delays intervention, risking harmful exposure when content is released before verification. Second, even with token-level detection, coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, while fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. To address these limitations, we introduce ADTGuard, which checks each token before release, progressively refines token-level training targets, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. ADTGuard models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. To adapt the choice of observation layers to the current prefix, we propose the Causal Depth Router (CDR). With only response-level labels available, we further develop Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) to progressively construct token-level training targets for both components. Through extensive experiments across multiple safety benchmarks, we demonstrate that ADTGuard consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and maintaining competitive per-token latency.
papers.summary: Streaming responses from large language models (LLMs) can expose users to harmful text before generation finishes, and existing guardrails either moderate after the fact at response or chunk boundaries or rely on fixed-layer readouts and response-level labels that do not pinpoint where harm begins. `ADTGuard` checks each token before release, modeling risk across both network depth and generation time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and accumulates it over successive tokens, while a Causal Depth Router (CDR) adapts which layers to read based on the current prefix. Because only response-level labels are available, Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) progressively constructs token-level training targets for both components. Across multiple safety benchmarks the system **matches or surpasses state-of-the-art safeguards in streaming detection with only 16M trainable parameters** and competitive per-token latency.

papers.title: Less is more: learning what to profile for GPU kernel optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models have recently shown strong potential for automatically optimizing GPU kernels, yet their effectiveness depends critically on the hardware information available to the kernel optimization model. Existing systems typically rely on predefined profiling strategies, leaving what to profile largely outside the optimization process. We show that effective profiling is not simply about collecting more information: increasing the number of profiling metrics does not monotonically improve kernel optimization, while the most useful profiling information varies across kernels. Our theoretical analysis further shows that, under such heterogeneous profiling utility, kernel-conditioned selection can outperform any single fixed profiling configuration. Motivated by this observation, we propose AutoProfiler, a feedback-driven framework for learning a deterministic profiling tree from optimization feedback. The tree is iteratively refined through REWRITE and SPLIT operations, with an LLM generating candidate modifications and empirical evaluation determining their acceptance. Once constructed, the tree quickly gathers the required profiling information for any kernel, allowing the LLM rewriter to be invoked only once. Experiments on KernelBench show that our approach improves kernel optimization over fixed profiling configurations under constrained profiling budgets. These results suggest that hardware profiling should evolve from static metric collection toward profiling reasoning, making profiling itself a new dimension for improving kernel optimization. The codes are available at https://github.com/Satissss/AutoProfiler.
papers.summary: LLM-driven GPU kernel optimization depends heavily on what hardware profiling information the model receives, yet existing systems fix the profiling strategy in advance and leave the choice of metrics outside the optimization loop. The authors show empirically that adding more profiling metrics does not monotonically improve kernel optimization and that the most useful metrics differ across kernels, and they argue theoretically that kernel-conditioned metric selection can beat any single fixed profiling configuration. `AutoProfiler` learns a deterministic profiling tree from optimization feedback, iteratively refining it through REWRITE and SPLIT operations in which an LLM proposes modifications and empirical evaluation accepts or rejects them, and once built the tree quickly gathers the needed profiling data for a new kernel so the LLM rewriter is invoked only once. **On `KernelBench` the learned profiling tree improves kernel optimization over fixed profiling configurations under constrained profiling budgets**, which the authors read as evidence that profiling should become a reasoning step rather than static metric collection.

papers.title: Follow the Herd: A Data-Driven Approach for Actionable Recourse
papers.abstract: As machine learning systems make increasingly greater decisions about people's lives, it is critical to provide users with actionable recourse about how they can achieve their desired outcomes. This problem is currently tackled by relying on expensive human supervision which involves hand-designing a cost function before searching for low-cost actions that achieve the desired outcome. In this paper, we propose \textit{``Data-Driven Action Recourse"} (DDAR), the first approach for providing action recourse without requiring costly supervision from humans about action costs. We build upon the notion that highly likely trajectories in the historical user data should be associated with lower costs. With this, DDAR first builds a dynamics model of historical user trajectories. Under this model, it then searches for trajectories that achieve the desired outcome. In experiments, we find that this simple approach recommends plausible action recourse without requiring human supervision, achieving lower action costs than the existing approaches.
papers.summary: Actionable recourse tells people subject to machine learning decisions what they can change to reach a desired outcome, but current methods depend on hand-designed cost functions over actions, which requires expensive human supervision. Data-Driven Action Recourse (`DDAR`) removes that requirement by assuming that trajectories commonly observed in historical user data should be treated as low cost, fitting a dynamics model to those trajectories, and then searching under the model for a path that reaches the desired outcome. **In experiments the approach recommends plausible recourse without any human-specified costs and achieves lower action costs than existing methods.**

papers.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
papers.abstract: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.
papers.summary: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is difficult because stroke alters sleep-related neural activity and co-occurs with respiratory disturbances, and existing stroke-specific models handle only sleep staging while adapting pretrained EEG encoders creates a mismatch between embeddings seen during training and those of unseen patients. `MM-Net` addresses the mismatch with cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment, then fuses sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling to perform sleep staging and respiratory-event detection jointly. On `iSLEEPS` (99 subacute stroke patients) under ten-fold patient-independent evaluation it reaches **76.3 percent staging accuracy and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC**, outperforming matched baselines, with embedding alignment adding 1.4 percentage points of staging accuracy over a frozen encoder versus 0.2 points without alignment. The model also achieves 86.4 percent staging accuracy on `Sleep-EDF` and 80.3 percent staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on `ISRUC-I`, and the stroke-trained model retains respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on `ISRUC-I` and 0.841 on `UCD` without retraining.

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Behaviorally Adequate Test Generation from Software Requirements
papers.abstract:
As large language model agents increasingly compile natural-language requirements into repository-level code, requirement-to-test generation grows in importance to provide validation constraints (or harness) to guide code generation. Yet it remains unclear whether current agents can generate tests that validate the required behavior when the implementation of that behavior is withheld. Existing test-generation benchmarks mostly focus on white-box testing, whereas the requirement--test-related study usually requires evaluation on semantic alignment between the given documents and the generated tests.
  We introduce Req2Test-Bench, a benchmark containing 5,086 execution-validated instances recovered from developer-authored behavior-driven development (BDD) artifacts in 8 open-source projects, spanning 5 programming languages and 4 BDD frameworks. Each instance pairs a natural-language requirement in Gherkin with its developer-written Test Implementation. Given the requirement, target interfaces of the required behavior, an agent must generate a complete, potentially multi-file Test Implementation. Evaluation of 8 agent--model--reasoning configurations reveals a substantial gap between execution success and behavioral adequacy, which is measured strictly as kill-completeness: a kill-complete test kills every mutant that the ground-truth test kills. The best-performing configuration, Codex with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, produces passing tests for 82.8% of instances, yet only 33.8% are behaviorally adequate. We find that (1) scaling up agents yields sharply diminishing returns in behavioral adequacy relative to generation cost; (2) under-specified requirements cause the information gap, including ambiguous setup and implicit expected outcomes; and (3) requirement-grounded harnesses that steer agent non-determinism offer a promising direction for improvement.
papers.summary: As LLM agents increasingly turn natural-language requirements into repository-level code, generating tests from requirements becomes a way to constrain and validate that code, but it is unclear whether agents can write tests that check required behavior when the implementation is withheld. `Req2Test-Bench` contains 5,086 execution-validated instances recovered from developer-authored behavior-driven development (BDD) artifacts across 8 open-source projects, 5 programming languages, and 4 BDD frameworks, each pairing a Gherkin requirement and target interfaces with the developer-written test implementation that an agent must reproduce as a complete, possibly multi-file test suite. Behavioral adequacy is scored strictly as kill-completeness, meaning the generated test must kill every mutant the ground-truth test kills, and across 8 agent, model, and reasoning configurations **the best setup, `Codex` with `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`, produces passing tests for 82.8 percent of instances but only 33.8 percent are behaviorally adequate**. The authors find sharply diminishing returns from scaling agents relative to generation cost, trace much of the gap to under-specified requirements with ambiguous setup and implicit expected outcomes, and point to requirement-grounded harnesses that steer agent non-determinism as a promising direction.

papers.title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?
papers.abstract: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
papers.summary: Coding agents are starting to work on the production infrastructure that trains and serves large models, but existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. `InfraDev` comprises 36 tasks built from real pull requests to `Megatron-LM`, `vLLM`, and `verl`, each requiring a multi-file change that runs correctly across many GPUs, graded by jointly synthesized hidden probes that enforce requirements the original tests leave unchecked and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution, with a shared execution environment that cuts storage by 52 to 57 percent and build time by 13 to 14 percent. Across six frontier models **the best resolves only 38.9 percent of tasks, the probes reject 32 percent of submissions that pass every official test, and no model solves a single task when given the original pull request descriptions as prompts**. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents rarely test memory, time, or traffic, and packaging these lessons as an agent skill raises a frontier model's resolved rate on the `Megatron-LM` tasks by 10.5 percent.

papers.title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.
papers.summary: Decision models choose quickly among supplied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models handle open-ended tasks through slow sequential generation, and many workloads provide no well-defined candidate list because they expect a generative backend to decide what is possible. The authors bridge this gap with a small candidate formalizer, trained on offline teacher-generated lists, that constructs explicit validated alternatives from task context so that a frozen decision model can select among them. A motivating comparison on 200 `CALVIN-D` test episodes reports 11 percent success with generic motions versus 46.5 percent with `DeepSeek V4 Flash` pose candidates, and in a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 `CALVIN-D` validation annotations **a locally deployed decision model reaches up to 52.6 percent task success with the fine-tuned formalizer versus 11.8 percent without it**, at 2.09 seconds end-to-end latency compared with 3.67 seconds for `Qwen3.5-27B` in the same setup.

papers.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
papers.abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
papers.summary: `Mamba-2` compresses its entire context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth, and existing compressors quantize or prune that state one coordinate at a time in the native basis. Examining trained states, the authors find that energy is almost rank-one and concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output actually reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace misaligned with the state coordinates, so even output-aware per-coordinate scores miss the directions that matter. They propose a post-training transform that performs balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians, applying the rotation exactly through the scalar-identity transition of `Mamba-2`, together with `HARP`, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than the released `GHOST` protocol, and **halving the state dimension costs an average of 0.3 points (1.8 percent) of `WikiText-2` perplexity across 130M to 2.7B models versus 1.6 points (9.3 percent) for `GHOST`**, with the gap widening at 25 percent retention.

papers.title: Dream-COP: Guiding Algorithm Discovery for Combinatorial Optimization Problems in an Experience World
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable algorithm discovery for combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) through iterative program generation and evaluation. A central challenge is how to organize search to discover better algorithms within a limited budget. Our key insight is that past search trajectories and their recorded outcomes form an experience world, which can be used to facilitate the COP solving through replay. We introduce Dream-COP, in which a \emph{policy agent} learns executable policies through \emph{dreaming} in this experience world to guide a \emph{discovery agent} in generating and refining COP programs. Specifically, policy replay provides feedback on the quality of the programs revealed and the search steps used, to guide policy selection more effectively. Across five COPs, \textsc{Dream} discovers better algorithms than fixed exploration in both heuristic component design and complete solver generation. Particularly, it matches the optimal values on KP and reduces the gap on OBPP from 2.112\% to 1.199\% while using 42.5\% fewer search requests. Moreover, the learned exploration policies transfer effectively across different COPs with the assitance of the experience world.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can discover algorithms for combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) by iteratively generating and evaluating programs, but organizing that search to find good algorithms within a limited budget remains the central challenge. `Dream-COP` treats past search trajectories and their recorded outcomes as an experience world in which a policy agent learns executable exploration policies by replaying, or dreaming through, prior searches, and those policies then guide a discovery agent that generates and refines COP programs, with replay providing feedback on both program quality and the search steps consumed. Across five COPs the method finds better algorithms than fixed exploration for both heuristic component design and full solver generation, **matching optimal values on `KP` and cutting the `OBPP` gap from 2.112 percent to 1.199 percent while using 42.5 percent fewer search requests**, and the learned exploration policies transfer across different problems with help from the experience world.

papers.title: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving systems batch requests dynamically, so the same input may run alongside different requests across runs, and if GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI) the numerical output for an unchanged input can differ and break reproducibility, yet kernel generation agents optimize for correctness and speed while ignoring this property. The authors find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts and propose a plug-in component that combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts, inserted as successive acceptance gates in a kernel agent's optimization loop so that structurally risky or non-invariant candidates are rejected with feedback before performance benchmarking. Across three agent frameworks on real-world LLM serving tasks, **the BI pass rate rises from 67.6 percent to 91.9 percent while retaining 91.8 percent of the baseline geometric mean speedup**.

papers.title: Adapting Video Models for Robot Control via Motion-guided Asymmetric Prediction
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video generative models for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual observations and actions. The visual prediction objective plays a key role in adapting pretrained video representations to the target robot domain. Yet standard visual prediction inherited from video pretraining treats all visual regions uniformly, despite their differing relevance to robotic control. We therefore investigate the spatial allocation of visual supervision in WAMs and show that focusing supervision on dynamic regions can substantially improve policy performance. Building on this finding, we introduce Motion-Guided Asymmetric Prediction (MoGAP), which augments WAM training with motion-focused visual prediction. MoGAP allocates noise asymmetrically across regions, training the model to reconstruct more heavily corrupted dynamic regions using less corrupted static regions as context. MoGAP is trained alongside standard video-action prediction through a training-only auxiliary prediction path within the shared video diffusion backbone. It uses motion cues derived directly from training videos, requiring neither an external teacher nor additional modalities. Across robot manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP consistently improves policy performance, increasing success rates on the GR-1 tabletop benchmark from 38.8% to 47.5% for Fast-WAM (Wan2.2-5B) and from 52.3% to 62.3% for Cosmos3-Nano.
papers.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generative models to robot control by jointly predicting future frames and actions, but the visual prediction objective inherited from video pretraining supervises all image regions equally despite their very different relevance to control. The authors show that concentrating visual supervision on dynamic regions improves policy performance and introduce Motion-Guided Asymmetric Prediction (`MoGAP`), which adds a training-only auxiliary prediction path in the shared video diffusion backbone that corrupts moving regions more heavily than static ones and trains the model to reconstruct them from the less-corrupted static context, with motion cues derived directly from the training videos and no external teacher or extra modalities. Across manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures the method consistently helps, **raising `GR-1` tabletop success from 38.8 to 47.5 percent for `Fast-WAM` (`Wan2.2-5B`) and from 52.3 to 62.3 percent for `Cosmos3-Nano`**.

papers.title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.
papers.summary: Event cameras produce sparse responses that yield uneven keypoint errors, and the effect of those errors on spacecraft pose depends on correspondence geometry and on how reliable successive observations are. The proposed reliability-aware framework links polarity-time localization, geometric recovery, event-to-CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization, using a three-branch representation that fuses positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, an ordered semantic-point head that estimates relative correspondence precision for constrained pose recovery, event-edge and CAD-projection agreement for local refinement, and a ten-dimensional sequence-level descriptor that sets time-aligned observation weights. On the official `SPADES` challenge test set the full system **scores 0.0474 on the combined pose metric, about 5.4 percent lower than `PASAN+IRIS` on a scale where lower is better**, and validation ablations improve the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform `PnP` to 0.0514 for the complete cascade.

papers.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
papers.abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.
papers.summary: Generative AI has rapidly changed the public web, and the authors measure how much by analyzing a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages for AI-generated text. They run multiple AI detectors and fit a Bayesian hierarchical model that corrects for each detector's false positive and false negative rates, allows detector performance to vary across groups, and propagates uncertainty about error rates into the prevalence estimates. The share of pages containing AI-generated text has risen sharply but unevenly, with English-language pages and .com domains showing higher prevalence than other languages and .gov or .edu domains even after controlling for compositional effects. **AI-generated text is most common and growing fastest on the least central pages in the web graph, which drives most of the overall growth, while the most central tier is the least likely to contain it.**

papers.title: Tap2Listen: Instant Target Switching for Streaming Audio-Visual Speaker Extraction
papers.abstract: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) uses a target speaker's face to extract the speaker's speech from an input audio mixture in real time. However, existing systems fix the target speaker for an entire clip, while conversation demands frequent and immediate target switches. To address this problem, we propose Tap2Listen, a streaming AV-TSE model designed for instant response to target switches. The model separates computation by modality: the target-agnostic audio encoder processes only the mixture, while the target-specific visual cues of the selected face condition only the decoder. A switch requires only a 0.12ms re-projection and takes effect immediately. We also design component-wise losses: a prediction loss for the encoder and a supervised extraction loss for the decoder. For evaluation, we measure how quickly output quality recovers after a switch. On the standard LRS3-2mix test set, Tap2Listen improves SI-SNRi from 8.85 to 9.68 dB at a comparable parameter count. After a switch to a known face, the model produces full-quality output from the first frame, whereas the baseline needs about 1 second to recover. Finally, we show that the proposed streaming AV-TSE model runs in real time on a single CPU core.
papers.summary: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) uses a target speaker's face to pull their speech out of a mixture in real time, but existing systems fix the target for an entire clip even though conversation requires frequent, immediate switches. `Tap2Listen` separates computation by modality so that a target-agnostic audio encoder processes only the mixture while the selected face conditions only the decoder, which means a switch requires just a 0.12 millisecond re-projection and takes effect immediately, and component-wise losses train the encoder with a prediction objective and the decoder with a supervised extraction objective. On the `LRS3-2mix` test set the model improves `SI-SNRi` from 8.85 to 9.68 dB at a comparable parameter count, and **after switching to a known face it produces full-quality output from the first frame, whereas the baseline needs about 1 second to recover**, while running in real time on a single CPU core.

papers.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior.
