To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
papers.summary: Memory lets LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be wrong or applied in the wrong situation, and team-level success or failure alone cannot tell whether a memory needs fixing or simply should not have been used. `DiscernMem` is a training-free framework with two parts. Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with none to diagnose rule defects, then tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to avoid regressing previously useful behavior, while Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) logs each memory's past uses and effects so its owner role learns when to apply or avoid it given task context and incoming messages. With `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` on four benchmarks, the method achieves the highest average score on `AutoGen`, `CAMEL`, and `MacNet`, **beating the strongest reported baselines by 0.51 to 4.32 points**, and leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a `PDDL` score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on `CAMEL`.

papers.title: The View from Nowhere: Population-Centered Agent Evolution
papers.abstract:
Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents.
  These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness.
  Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. In our evaluation, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. These results suggest that treating the population as evidence--not merely as candidates for selection--provides a complementary principle for agent evolution.
papers.summary: Self-improving agent systems revise the harnesses that govern their own behavior, but existing methods improve only selected parent agents using their own evolutionary history and leave the rest of the population underused, producing a large gap between population coverage (tasks solved by at least one variant) and the best single agent's performance. The authors propose a principle they call the view from nowhere, under which an agent is improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification, and instantiate it as Population-Centered Evolution (`PCE`), which distills task records and modification histories from the whole population into a population block capturing recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of past modifications to guide edits to a selected parent's harness. Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, **`PCE` reaches 72.1 percent on `SWE-bench Verified` and 96.7 percent on `Polyglot`, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points**, and it shrinks the coverage-to-best-agent gap by one-third on `SWE-bench` and closes it on `Polyglot`.

papers.title: A Quantitative Approach to Asch Conformity in Frontier Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The Asch conformity experiment has recently gained considerable attention as a way of measuring conformity in large language models (LLMs). While previous studies have focused on demonstrating conformity in LLMs, our work adds a further quantitative layer to this approach. Instead of sampling a frontier LLM on a suite of questions, our approach samples a single question repeatedly, leveraging the probabilistic nature of LLMs to produce a distribution of answers. In doing so, we can compare the distributions of answers before and after the model is presented with the manufactured consensus. Our experiments confirm that frontier LLMs do conform, reinforcing prior literature, and, through our distribution-to-distribution comparisons, provide additional quantitative data on the conditions that lead to conformity and the degree to which it occurs.
papers.summary: The Asch conformity experiment, in which a subject is confronted with a manufactured consensus, has become a common way to probe conformity in large language models (LLMs), but prior studies mostly stop at demonstrating that conformity exists. Instead of asking a model one question each across a suite, the authors sample a single question many times to obtain a distribution of answers, then compare the distributions before and after the model is shown the manufactured consensus. **Frontier LLMs do conform under this protocol**, reinforcing earlier findings, and the distribution-to-distribution comparisons add quantitative detail on which conditions trigger conformity and how strongly it occurs.

papers.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
papers.summary: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) re-process every visual token at each denoising step, and visual tokens make up 89-97% of the input on the benchmarks studied, so most decoding compute goes to the same image over and over. Comparing `LLaDA-V` predictions with and without the image at every step shows that dropping the image changes which token gets unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average. `LOWN` exploits this by predicting masked tokens without the image and processing the image only when that prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned one; agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. Without training or a tuned threshold, **`LOWN` retains 99.6% of the base model's score across ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs**, transfers to other `LLaDA`-based DVLMs, and composes with visual token pruning and key-value caching.

papers.title: Learning Where to Trust: Reliability-Guided Expert Routing and Velocity Gating for 3D Deformable Registration
papers.abstract: Deformable image registration relies on accurate anatomical correspondences. However, explicitly coupling local matching reliability with spatial context selection and deformation update strength remains insufficiently explored in learning-based registration. This challenge is particularly pronounced in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions, where ambiguous matches may induce erroneous deformation updates. We propose ReliMorph, a reliability-routed symmetric framework for 3D deformable registration that couples correspondence assessment with spatial context selection and update strength.Local correlation distributions characterize correspondence ambiguity using shared anatomical features with modality-specific adaptation. These reliability cues guide spatial expert fusion and gate residual velocities during coarse-to-fine refinement. Updated inverse-inconsistency feedback guides routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. To our knowledge, ReliMorph is the first 3D deformable registration framework to jointly condition spatial expert routing and residual velocity gating on correspondence reliability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReliMorph consistently outperforms competing methods in anatomical overlap, highlighting its effectiveness across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.
papers.summary: Learning-based deformable image registration struggles in homogeneous, weakly textured, or heavily deformed regions, where ambiguous correspondences can drive erroneous deformation updates. `ReliMorph` is a symmetric 3D registration framework that estimates correspondence reliability from local correlation distributions and uses those cues both to route among spatial-context experts and to gate the strength of residual velocity updates during coarse-to-fine refinement, with inverse-inconsistency feedback steering routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. The authors describe it as the first framework to condition both expert routing and velocity gating on match reliability, and report that it **consistently outperforms competing methods on anatomical overlap** across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.

papers.title: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding
papers.abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.
papers.summary: The question is why macroscopic order parameters emerge from microscopic many-body systems, and the proposed answer borrows collective predictive coding (CPC), a theory of how language and symbols emerge from communication. Each atom is treated as an agent that infers and predicts the behavior of the others, and the macroscopic coordinate produced by this communication is called the collective predictive order. On two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic `Ising` models, a spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected `Sherrington-Kirkpatrick` spin glass, **the appropriate order parameters, including the replica overlap, emerge from observed spin configurations alone without any reference to the microscopic Hamiltonian**. For the Ising cases the equilibrium distribution of the learned coordinate also yields a potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution of a Landau potential.

papers.title: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
papers.abstract: Modern language models are trained on far more language than children experience, but we know much less about learning from small, naturalistic datasets. We train small GPT-2 models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (BabyView) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (TinyDialogues), varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data. Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. Much of this specialization is lexical and distributional: a simple 5-gram model reproduces the cross-child pattern (r=.91). Training on data from multiple children clearly improves prediction of pooled held-out language relative to training on a single child's input without a similarly clear improvement on grammatical benchmarks. Across data sizes, naturalistic and synthetic training inputs also produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, with important differences between grammatical phenomena. Together, these results show that small-data language learning depends not only on how much language a model sees, but on which environments it comes from and how well that input matches what the model is asked to predict.
papers.summary: Language models usually see far more text than any child hears, leaving open how learning behaves on small, naturalistic data. The authors train small `GPT-2` models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (`BabyView`) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (`TinyDialogues`), varying the amount, source, and diversity of the training data. Models trained on one child's environment predict that environment much better than other children's, and **a simple 5-gram model reproduces this cross-child specialization pattern with r=.91**, pointing to lexical and distributional causes. Pooling data from several children improves prediction of pooled held-out language but brings no comparable gain on grammatical benchmarks, and naturalistic versus synthetic input produces different grammatical and lexical-semantic profiles across data sizes.

papers.title: PsyJev: Psychological Analysis via System-1 Judgment
papers.abstract: Self-disclosures on the Web support diverse psychological analyses, from recognizing expressed experiences to identifying symptom-relevant information. We study a shared, question-conditioned decision interface for this heterogeneous problem in content analysis. We organize PsyJudgeBench, comprising 13 annotated datasets and 82 questions across six psychological areas, while preserving source-specific criteria and masks for unobserved labels. We introduce PsyJev, a System-1 model that directly produces distributions over answers specified in each request. Joint supervised training establishes the shared judgment function, followed by Judgment-Anchored RLCD (JA-RLCD), which adapts logit-space reward optimization to heterogeneous psychological judgments through balanced supervision, selective retention of correct SFT predictions, and question-group reward optimization. The Qwen3.5-based 2B, 4B, and 9B models achieve 64.33, 66.21, and 67.56 average test F1, respectively. The 9B model exceeds the strongest external comparison by 2.54 points. Controlled 2B comparisons examine the training stages and anchored refinement. Further analyses examine question-conditioned judgment, inference cost, and probability quality, complemented by qualitative comparisons across models.
papers.summary: Self-disclosures posted online support many kinds of psychological content analysis, from recognizing expressed experiences to identifying symptom-relevant information, but these tasks are usually handled with separate models. `PsyJudgeBench` gathers 13 annotated datasets and 82 questions across six psychological areas under one question-conditioned interface, keeping source-specific criteria and masking unobserved labels, and `PsyJev` is a System-1 model that directly outputs a distribution over the answers each request specifies. Training combines joint supervised fine-tuning with Judgment-Anchored RLCD (`JA-RLCD`), which adapts logit-space reward optimization through balanced supervision, selective retention of correct SFT predictions, and question-group rewards. The `Qwen3.5`-based 2B, 4B, and 9B models reach 64.33, 66.21, and 67.56 average test F1, and **the 9B model exceeds the strongest external comparison by 2.54 F1 points**.

papers.title: TOPS: Reshaping Flow Source and Transport for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation commonly share a single $\textit{Gaussian}$ source prior and a common linear transport path across tasks. However, reliably executing multiple tasks with distinct motion requirements remains challenging for a shared policy. We introduce $\textbf{TOPS}$ ($\textbf{T}$ask-$\textbf{O}$riented $\textbf{P}$riors and $\textbf{S}$chedules), which adapts the flow source prior and interpolation schedule to each task without modifying the network architecture. TOPS first constructs multimodal task sources from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, allowing language instructions to select where generation begins. Guided by source-target covariance mismatch, it then slows the transition toward expert actions early in denoising and accelerates it later along directions requiring expansion. Under a $\textit{Gaussian}$ endpoint model, our analysis shows that this schedule adjustment can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN demonstrate improved performance across in-distribution, perturbation and cross-environment settings, alongside better data efficiency. Using one integration step, TOPS raises LIBERO-10 success from $53.44\%$ to $69.67\%$ compared with ten-step Standard Flow Matching (FM), while reducing inference time to approximately one-sixth of the baseline. TOPS also yields consistent gains when transferred to the large-scale flow-based $\pi_{0.5}$ policy across all four evaluated settings. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improved task success, including an increase from $20\%$ with standard FM to $80\%$ with TOPS on the upper-drawer opening task.
papers.summary: Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation typically share one Gaussian source prior and one linear transport path across tasks, which makes it hard for a single policy to handle tasks with different motion requirements. `TOPS` (Task-Oriented Priors and Schedules) builds multimodal task-specific source distributions from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, so a language instruction selects where generation starts, and then reshapes the interpolation schedule using source-target covariance mismatch, slowing early denoising and accelerating later along directions that need expansion. Under a Gaussian endpoint model this schedule adjustment lowers an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. On `LIBERO`, `LIBERO-Plus`, and `CALVIN` the method improves in-distribution, perturbed, and cross-environment performance, and **with a single integration step it raises `LIBERO-10` success from 53.44% to 69.67% versus ten-step standard flow matching while cutting inference time to about one-sixth**; gains carry over to the large-scale `π0.5` policy and to real-world trials, where upper-drawer opening rose from 20% to 80% success.

papers.title: HeteGCD: Statistics-Aware Dual-Prototype Learning for Generalized Category Discovery on Heterophilous Graphs
papers.abstract: Heterophilous graphs are prevalent in real-world applications, where connected nodes often exhibit dissimilar attributes or belong to different classes, posing significant challenges to conventional graph learning methods based on homophily. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in generalized category discovery (GCD), which requires models to recognize known classes and discover novel ones using labels from known classes only. However, existing graph GCD methods typically rely on aforementioned homophily-based inductive biases, which are ill-suited to heterophilous graphs. Meanwhile, although current heterophilous graph learning methods exploit diverse neighborhood signals, their selection and fusion are often guided by supervision across all classes, including novel classes whose labels are unavailable in GCD. These limitations raise a key question: how can heterogeneous neighborhood information be effectively leveraged for category discovery without any novel-class supervision? To answer this question, in this study we propose HeteGCD, a new statistics-aware dual-prototype learning perspective for generalized category discovery on heterophilous graphs. The key idea is to examine both statistics of local attribute differences and neighborhood class distribution to extract discriminative information in feature and probability spaces simultaneously. Specifically, a gated dual-stream encoder integrates both node attributes and local attribute-difference statistics to learn informative node representations. Afterwards, a dual-prototype classifier combines feature-based similarity with distribution-based consistency to support category discovery. Experiments on five heterophilous graphs show that HeteGCD achieves competitive performance against 24 baseline combinations.
papers.summary: Generalized category discovery (GCD) asks a model to recognize known classes and discover novel ones using labels only for the known classes, and on heterophilous graphs, where connected nodes often differ in attributes or class, the homophily assumptions behind existing graph GCD methods break down. `HeteGCD` takes a statistics-aware dual-prototype approach: a gated dual-stream encoder combines node attributes with statistics of local attribute differences, and a dual-prototype classifier merges feature-based similarity with consistency against neighborhood class distributions, so discriminative signal is drawn from both feature and probability spaces without novel-class supervision. **Across five heterophilous graphs the method is competitive with 24 baseline combinations** that pair heterophilous graph learners with GCD techniques.

papers.title: Conservative Dueling Bandits: Preference Learning under Baseline Constraints
papers.abstract: Contextual dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons, the same feedback used to fine-tune language models from human preferences. Standard algorithms explore aggressively and can show users two poor options. We study conservative contextual dueling bandits, which require that, at every round, the cumulative score of the better displayed item stay above a $(1-\alpha)$ fraction of a trusted baseline's. An item's score is its probability of beating the best available item, so the constraint depends only on utility differences and needs no absolute rewards. This also changes how safety can be certified: we show that transferring the safety test of the conservative bandit algorithm CLUCB unchanged can incur linear regret, even when the baseline's utilities are known exactly. For linear utilities, we develop MaxInP-BC, which certifies scores through utility gaps and, when it must fall back, pairs the baseline with an informative partner so that fallback rounds still drive learning. It is safe with high probability at all times, with regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T}/\kappa)$ plus an additive cost of conservatism that does not grow with the horizon. For general utility classes, we develop BTIGW-BC, which turns the guarantee of an online logistic-regression oracle into cumulative safety certificates. It is safe at all times, makes finitely many fallbacks, and has sublinear regret whenever the oracle's logistic regret is sublinear. In experiments, both satisfy the constraint, which their unconstrained counterparts often violate, at a moderate cost in regret.
papers.summary: Contextual dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons, the same feedback used to align language models from human preferences, but standard algorithms explore aggressively and may show users two poor options at once. The conservative variant studied here requires that at every round the cumulative score of the better displayed item stay above a (1-α) fraction of a trusted baseline's, where an item's score is its probability of beating the best available item, so the constraint depends only on utility differences and needs no absolute rewards. The authors show that porting the safety test of the conservative bandit algorithm `CLUCB` unchanged can incur linear regret even with exactly known baseline utilities, then develop `MaxInP-BC` for linear utilities, which **is safe at all times with high probability and achieves regret of order d√T/κ plus a conservatism cost that does not grow with the horizon**, and `BTIGW-BC` for general utility classes, which turns an online logistic-regression oracle into cumulative safety certificates with finitely many fallbacks. In experiments both methods satisfy the constraint their unconstrained counterparts often violate, at a moderate cost in regret.

papers.title: From Voiceprints to User Entities: Online Speaker-Memory Construction for Multi-User Spoken Agents
papers.abstract: Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.
papers.summary: Personalized spoken agents must work out who is speaking before they can retrieve that user's memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume histories are already correctly attributed. Treating voiceprints as observations of identity rather than identities themselves, the authors formulate online speaker-memory construction and introduce `EvoSpeakerMem`, a training-free layer that performs causal speaker routing, selectively updates each user's acoustic state, and partitions memory writes and retrieval by identity on top of a replaceable text-memory backend. They also build `LoCoMo-ID`, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal `SMIIP-TV` data, a frozen near-enrollment threshold sees genuine-probe rejection climb from 29.8% to 55.6% over about a year, while on `LoCoMo-ID` **gated updating improves identity-gated question answering over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions with no wrong-user authorizations**, though the analysis also exposes a fragmentation-contamination trade-off that question-answering accuracy alone cannot capture.

papers.title: Generative Refinement Learning for Temporal Interpolation in Scientific Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Computationally expensive simulations and real-world observations often provide data at a lower temporal resolution than downstream tasks require. Averaging observations at fixed grid points can introduce errors, and motion estimates alone do not determine how the physical field values change. In this work, we study whether learning to correct a simple numerical interpolation improves the reconstruction of intermediate scientific fields. Our model, interpolative FLow EXpert (iFLEX), first estimates the missing field by taking a weighted average of the two observations at each grid point, giving more weight to the observation closer to the requested time. During training, subtracting this estimate from an observed intermediate field gives the residual that a conditional diffusion model learns to generate. Both observations condition the model, together with the target time, the interval between observations, and available physical parameters. To reconstruct an unobserved intermediate field, the generated residual is added to the weighted average. We evaluate iFLEX on Navier-Stokes Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature. Across these datasets, iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than the evaluated baselines, including optical-flow and diffusion models developed for video frame interpolation in computer vision. In a controlled turbulence comparison at a Reynolds number of 36,000, learning the residual reduces relative Frobenius norm error from about 13.7 for direct field generation to 10.5, with the diffusion backbone and training setup held fixed. Code is available at https://github.com/paulpuren/iflex.
papers.summary: Expensive simulations and real-world sensors often deliver scientific fields at coarser time resolution than downstream tasks need, and neither averaging at fixed grid points nor motion estimation alone recovers how field values change between observations. `iFLEX` (interpolative FLow EXpert) first forms a time-weighted average of the two bracketing observations at each grid point, then trains a conditional diffusion model, conditioned on both observations, the target time, the interval between them, and available physical parameters, to generate the residual between that estimate and the true intermediate field. On `Navier-Stokes` Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature it achieves lower reconstruction error than optical-flow and diffusion baselines built for video frame interpolation, and **in a controlled turbulence comparison at Reynolds number 36,000, learning the residual rather than generating the field directly cuts relative Frobenius error from about 13.7 to 10.5** with the backbone and training setup held fixed.

papers.title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution
papers.abstract: Gradient-based data attribution has become an important tool for high-quality data selection in the instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), as it estimates the contribution of training examples through their influence on model optimization. However, we find that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from surface-form bias: minor changes to semantically irrelevant details, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content remains unchanged. To address this issue, we propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA), a robust framework for instruction data selection. CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, thereby reducing formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. CIGA also reduces attribution cost, offering a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.
papers.summary: Gradient-based data attribution scores instruction-tuning examples by their influence on optimization, but existing global attribution methods turn out to be sensitive to surface form: trivial changes to wording or formatting can swing attribution scores even when the content is unchanged. Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (`CIGA`) addresses this by first selecting layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving perturbations, then dynamically fusing those gradient signals with semantic representations of the input. **Across multiple benchmarks `CIGA` yields more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance**, and it also lowers the cost of computing attributions.

papers.title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.
papers.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) close the loop between experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback, but wiring flexible robot control to the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurement streams of lab instruments remains an open execution-interface problem. The proposed framework has four parts: `LAM` (Lab Action Model), a measurement-conditioned policy that extends the vision-language-action paradigm to emit both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls; `OpenSDL`, an execution substrate that maps role-level operations onto heterogeneous devices and records timestamped causal events; `Safe-SDL`, a runtime gate combining pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution; and `L3-Bench` (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark), an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. **The contribution is an end-to-end design with an initial control implementation** that targets coordination and traceability in SDL workflows rather than reported experimental gains.

papers.title: The Vocabulary Is Already Here: Adapting Pretrained Interpretable Features for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) predicts the next item through its semantic ID (SID). Existing methods commonly fit SID vocabularies to pretrained language model (PLM) representations of item descriptions, incurring additional training costs and making vocabulary coverage dependent on the fitting domains. We observe that pretrained sparse autoencoders expose PLM features with human-interpretable semantic annotations, allowing feature indices to serve as a reusable SID vocabulary. However, reusing this vocabulary requires preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and learning to favor target items over candidates with shared dominant features. It also requires extending feature interpretability from item content to retrieval decisions. To address these challenges, we propose API, a framework that Adapts the Pretrained Interpretable vocabulary for effective and explainable GR without additional vocabulary learning. Within API, Pretrained Interpretable IDs (PIDs) retain selected feature indices and relative activation strengths for item discrimination. With PIDs as supervision, the Semantic Prediction Adapter (SPA) learns user preferences from interaction histories through joint feature-index and strength prediction. SPA combines both predictions to score candidate items, with item-level supervision encouraging the observed next item to outrank its alternatives. API further explains candidate score differences through feature contributions paired with their pretrained semantic annotations. Extensive experiments show that API achieves competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, while preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and enabling explainable retrieval.
papers.summary: Generative recommendation (GR) predicts the next item by generating its semantic ID (SID), and most methods learn a fresh SID vocabulary by fitting it to pretrained language model (PLM) representations of item descriptions, which costs extra training and ties coverage to the fitting domain. The `API` framework instead reuses the feature indices of a pretrained sparse autoencoder, which already carry human-readable semantic annotations, as the SID vocabulary: Pretrained Interpretable IDs (`PIDs`) keep selected feature indices plus their relative activation strengths to tell items apart, and a Semantic Prediction Adapter (`SPA`) learns user preferences by jointly predicting feature indices and strengths, with item-level supervision pushing the observed next item above competing candidates. **The approach reaches competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes without any vocabulary learning**, preserves item distinctions under compact token budgets, and explains score differences between candidates through feature contributions paired with their pretrained annotations.

papers.title: Beyond the Evidence Coherence Trap: Agent-Driven Evidence Selection for Temporally Disordered Fake News Detection
papers.abstract: Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. DelSA outperforms existing methods on ChronoFake, while remaining competitive on PolitiFact and GossipCop.
papers.summary: Temporally disordered fake news rearranges real events into a false chronology, so each event checks out on its own and retrieval can surface plausible but wrong-period evidence that lets an article pass verification, a failure the authors call the evidence coherence trap. To isolate this setting they build `ChronoFake`, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events that separates temporal manipulation from legitimate devices such as flashbacks. `DelSA`, a Document Selection Self-Updating Agent, iteratively refines its evidence-selection rules during training and applies a frozen rulebook in one pass at inference, using an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, a verifier-trained reranker to balance local relevance against timeline consistency, and a classifier that compares the article-implied chronology with the evidence-derived one. **`DelSA` outperforms existing methods on `ChronoFake`** while remaining competitive on `PolitiFact` and `GossipCop`.

papers.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) now solve many competition-level math problems, but whether they can verify natural-language proofs, especially long Olympiad proofs where every claim needs checking, is far less studied, and grading still relies on costly expert inspection. The authors release a human-curated set of `USAMO 2025` candidate solutions with expert grades, propose `TROJAN`, an iterative self-critique pipeline that generates high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale, and evaluate 20 models across seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, finding that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. They then introduce `MABGrader`, a multi-armed bandit framework that treats grading as arm selection over the discrete score space, and **it beats the previous state of the art `ProofGrader` by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%**.

papers.title: Batching the Reflective Optimization Loop: Parallel Proposals Make GEPA Faster and Better
papers.abstract: Reflective text optimization makes agentic systems better, but the optimization loop is itself a resource-hungry workload whose sequential structure leaves parallel evaluation capacity idle. We extend the open-source GEPA optimizer to propose and evaluate a batch of candidates on each optimization step instead of one candidate at a time. In our sweep on two tasks, most batched runs finished in half the wall-clock time or less, and the fastest in about a quarter to a third. Batched settings also achieved higher held-out test scores, from 68.9% to 72.1% on LiveBench-Math (with $2\times2$) and from 49.0% to 60.0% on HoVer (with $8\times1$). A simple runtime model explains the measured speedups under a finite worker pool, and batched settings also spend their metric-call and dollar budgets more efficiently. We frame the axes along which a reflective optimization step can scale in parallel, a first look at allocating a fixed optimization budget across them.
papers.summary: Reflective text optimization improves agentic systems, but the optimizer's sequential loop leaves parallel evaluation capacity idle. The authors extend the open-source `GEPA` optimizer to propose and evaluate a batch of candidates at each step rather than one at a time, and sweep batch configurations on two tasks. **Most batched runs finished in half the wall-clock time or less, and the fastest in about a quarter to a third**, while also reaching higher held-out scores: 68.9% to 72.1% on `LiveBench-Math` with a 2×2 batch and 49.0% to 60.0% on `HoVer` with 8×1. A simple runtime model explains the speedups under a finite worker pool, batched settings spend metric-call and dollar budgets more efficiently, and the paper frames the axes along which a reflective optimization step can be parallelized.
papers.highlight_summary:
Reflective prompt optimizers such as `GEPA` improve agentic systems by proposing textual mutations, scoring them with rollouts, and keeping the winners, but the loop is strictly sequential, so a run can take hours while parallel evaluation capacity sits idle. The authors extend `GEPA` to propose and evaluate a batch of candidates per step, which both shortens wall-clock time and, by committing to several proposals before adapting to the validation set, generalizes better to held-out tests.

- Standard `GEPA` extends one Pareto-frontier parent per step, whereas the `P×N` sampling strategy samples P parents, draws N reflective mutations of each from separate mini-batches, dispatches all P·N reflection calls and mini-batch screens concurrently, and then evaluates every accepted child on the full validation set in parallel before updating the frontier.
- At a fixed metric-call budget (5,000 on `LiveBench-Math`, 3,000 on `HoVer`, with `gpt-5-mini` as proposer and `gpt-4.1-mini` as solver), batched settings raised held-out test accuracy from **68.9% to 72.1%** on `LiveBench-Math` with `2×2` and from **49.0% to 60.0%** on `HoVer` with `8×1`, while 16-way widths cut wall-clock time by roughly **3 to 4×** and most batched runs finished in half the time or less.
- Speedups are sublinear because wider steps trigger full validation more often: on `LiveBench-Math`, `2×2` cut iterations 4.9× (219 to 45) but the share of iterations triggering full validation rose from 17% to 53%, yielding only a **1.9× speedup** (7.7 to 4.1 hours), which a simple runtime model with acceptance probability and a finite worker pool (512 workers on `LiveBench-Math`, 64 on `HoVer`) predicts well.
- The `2×4` setting is also more budget-efficient, reaching validation scores single mutation needs about 2,000 calls to match, beating it by **3.0 and 6.0 points** on the two test sets, and showing a validation-to-test gap of only 2 points versus 9 for single mutation on `LiveBench-Math`, with total LLM spend comparable at $12 to $16 per run.
- Evidence is limited to two tasks at one budget each, the best P versus N split is task-dependent (`2×2` on `LiveBench-Math`, `8×1` on `HoVer`), some batched settings did not beat single mutation on test, returns diminish with width, and the better-generalization explanation is offered as a hypothesis consistent with the data rather than tested directly.

papers.title: Dependency Graphs of Mathematical Arguments: Representation, Structural Measurement, and Proof Review
papers.abstract: We propose a source-grounded framework for representing and measuring mathematical arguments with assistance from large language models. It includes numbered and unnumbered statements, equations, assumptions, and constructions, distinguishing source occurrences from contextual states and inference records. Proposed dependencies retain source evidence and review status. A measurement contract fixes manuscript versions, boundaries, granularity, proof choices, and macro anchors. On a selected finite directed acyclic graph, depth is the longest prerequisite-path length, and bulk counts distinct ancestor edges. We give a union recurrence that accounts for shared subarguments and identify reachability conditions preserving depth and the macro skeleton; unrestricted refinement need not preserve depth or bulk. A standardized, versioned prompt protocol separates annotation discovery, deterministic recomputation, and review assistance. Cross-paper links support a research agenda on theorem co-use, rare combinations, and connections between dependency communities. These patterns motivate probabilistic premise suggestions and review of possible omissions or unchecked application conditions in human-written and AI-generated proofs. Further applications include source-linked reading support and comparison of individual and collaborative argument shapes. We provide an evaluation design rather than empirical evidence of these benefits. Suggested premises require mathematical validation, and the measures describe a specified representation rather than intrinsic mathematical difficulty, originality, or importance.
papers.summary: The goal is a source-grounded representation of mathematical arguments, built with assistance from large language models, that supports structural measurement and proof review. The representation covers numbered and unnumbered statements, equations, assumptions, and constructions, distinguishes source occurrences from contextual states and inference records, and attaches source evidence and review status to proposed dependencies, while a measurement contract fixes manuscript versions, boundaries, granularity, proof choices, and macro anchors. On the resulting directed acyclic graph, depth is the longest prerequisite path and bulk counts distinct ancestor edges; a union recurrence accounts for shared subarguments, and reachability conditions are identified under which refinement preserves depth and the macro skeleton. A versioned prompt protocol separates annotation discovery, deterministic recomputation, and review assistance, with proposed applications in premise suggestion and omission checking for human-written and AI-generated proofs, but **the paper provides an evaluation design rather than empirical evidence** of these benefits.

papers.title: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training
papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
papers.summary: Test-time training (TTT) lets a deployed language model write incoming context into a small set of fast weights instead of only attending over it, and `In-Place TTT` made this practical by reusing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as those fast weights. The authors find that `In-Place TTT`'s gains largely disappear on realistic web long-context question answering and attribute this to its uniform write schedule, where every chunk is written with equal strength and irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. `Select-TTT` scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query, computed with no new parameters or supervision as the probability mass the frozen output head assigns to the query tokens given the chunk's hidden states, then converted into learning-rate multipliers by a temperature-scaled softmax that leaves the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of `In-Place TTT` intact. **`Select-TTT` consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones**, and the authors suggest the same query-conditioned writes could help long-horizon agent tasks that pose multiple queries over evolving contexts.

papers.title: An Algebra of Transformers
papers.abstract: On the theoretic analyses on transforms, they mainly focus on the computability analysis, such the Turing-completeness of unbounded precision transformers, the advantage of parallelizability of unbounded precision transformers and the limitations of bounded precision transformers. This paper give transformers an algebra for reasoning, which relies heavily on the functional decomposition results of transformers. This algebra uses functional decompositions as atomic actions, includes sequential composition and parallel composition, recursion for feedback and abstraction for hidden layers. As we know, it is the first attempt to model transformers logically and can be used to verify the correctness of transformer based applications.
papers.summary: Existing theoretical analyses of transformers mostly concern computability, such as the Turing-completeness of unbounded-precision transformers, the advantages of their parallelizability, and the limitations of bounded-precision ones. Building on functional decomposition results for transformers, the authors define an algebra in which decompositions serve as atomic actions, combined through sequential and parallel composition, recursion for feedback, and abstraction for hidden layers. **The authors describe it as the first attempt to model transformers logically** and propose the algebra as a basis for verifying the correctness of transformer-based applications.

papers.title: SetGRPO: Calibrating Grader-Induced Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning uses fine-grained grader feedback to train large language models on open-ended tasks, but grader randomness can alter GRPO updates in ways that score discrepancies alone cannot characterize. Because GRPO jointly normalizes rewards within each response group and combines the resulting training coefficients with response-level gradients, a scoring discrepancy can shift the coefficients of the entire group and induce policy-dependent update changes. Selective execution further affects the direction-reversal risk of retained updates. To address this, we propose Set-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (SetGRPO). It comprises three modules: (a) Joint Reward Set Calibration constructs a joint uncertainty set for the training coefficients; (b) Geometry-Guided Safe Recovery maps candidate coefficients into the current policy's local update geometry and determines the largest safe recovery ratio for each response group; and (c) Selective Risk-Gated Optimization selects a global threshold through independent risk calibration to control the conditional direction-reversal risk of accepted updates while preserving the original GRPO objective. Under exchangeability, SetGRPO provides finite-sample marginal coverage for the joint coefficient set and simultaneous risk control across candidate thresholds. On ten open-ended benchmarks spanning three domains, SetGRPO achieves the highest macro average among all compared training methods on both Qwen3.5 and Llama3.2 model families.
papers.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning trains large language models on open-ended tasks with fine-grained grader feedback, but because Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) normalizes rewards within each response group and combines the resulting coefficients with response-level gradients, a single noisy grader score can shift the coefficients of the whole group and alter the policy update in ways that raw score discrepancies do not reveal. Set-Valued `GRPO` (`SetGRPO`) addresses this with three modules: Joint Reward Set Calibration builds a joint uncertainty set over the training coefficients, Geometry-Guided Safe Recovery maps candidate coefficients into the current policy's local update geometry to find the largest safe recovery ratio for each group, and Selective Risk-Gated Optimization picks a global threshold through independent risk calibration to bound the conditional risk that an accepted update reverses direction, all while keeping the original `GRPO` objective. Under exchangeability the method gives finite-sample marginal coverage for the coefficient set and simultaneous risk control across candidate thresholds, and **on ten open-ended benchmarks spanning three domains it achieves the highest macro average among all compared training methods on both `Qwen3.5` and `Llama3.2` model families**.

papers.title: An Incremental Knowledge-Graph Learner Digital Twin for Evidence-Grounded Early Warning
papers.abstract: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.
papers.summary: Early-warning systems in learning analytics flag students at risk of failing or withdrawing, but the alerts rarely expose which learning traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify them. The authors build an incremental learner digital twin as a lightweight knowledge graph that is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying activity and assessment records, deriving predictive features through graph queries while storing features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records as queryable entities. On a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol, **graph-mediated features preserve the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints**, and each alert is materialized as an evidence chain linking the risk decision back to raw platform records.

papers.title: TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control
papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.
papers.summary: Pretrained video generation models encode useful priors about physical interaction, but using them for robot control usually means expensive video generation at inference time or bolting on action heads that ignore most of the pretrained backbone. `TAPESTRY` (Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy) treats each robot action timestep as a single-patch token in the latent space of a pretrained video diffusion transformer, mapping actions through a linear projection into the VAE patch dimensions so they pass through the same patchifying layers and backbone as video. The shared model is trained with three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: video-only diffusion on robot and human videos, joint video-plus-action diffusion with a coupled timestep and an asymmetric attention mask, and action-only diffusion conditioned on clean image latents. At test time it generates an action chunk in a single DDIM step from pure noise, **producing smooth action chunks in 84 ms on consumer hardware**, and it achieves strong performance across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments at substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video-action policies.

papers.title: Who Knows What - and What Does It Support? Perspective-Bounded Evidence Calibration for Multimodal Theory of Mind
papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others' beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence. Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent's mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver. Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion. We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process. PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively.
papers.summary: Multimodal Theory of Mind (ToM) asks a model to infer an agent's beliefs, goals, and intentions from only the evidence that agent could access, yet existing LLM-based and Bayesian approaches reconstruct global event traces and let agent-inaccessible events or misaligned actions and utterances leak into the inferred mental state. The authors frame this as an evidence-admissibility problem, requiring that evidence be accessible to the relevant agent, preserve its information source, and be diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. `PIP-ToM` builds agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while leaving the underlying Bayesian inference intact. Paired with `GPT-4o`, it **reaches average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00% on `MuMA-ToM`, `MMToM-QA`, and `Hi-ToM`**, outperforming prior ToM methods.

papers.title: When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly depend on harnesses that govern interaction, memory, tools, and execution around large language models (LLMs). While recent work has begun to evolve these harnesses from execution experience, the supervision used to guide evolution often remains relatively static, making it difficult to track changing behavioral weaknesses across rounds and potentially limiting generalization to unseen tasks. To address this issue, we propose RuHarness, a rubric--harness co-evolution framework for continual agent self-improvement. RuHarness continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes the most relevant unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to guide targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse agent tasks and backbone models show that RuHarness outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, particularly on unseen held-out tasks. Further analyses show that adaptive rubric prioritization tracks shifting weaknesses and supports more sustained improvement and stable generalization across evolution rounds.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents rely on harnesses that govern interaction, memory, tools, and execution around a large language model (LLM), and recent work evolves these harnesses from execution experience, but the supervision guiding that evolution usually stays static and fails to track shifting behavioral weaknesses across rounds. `RuHarness` co-evolves rubrics and harnesses: it continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes the most relevant unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to drive targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Across diverse agent tasks and backbone models it **outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, with the largest gains on unseen held-out tasks**, and analyses show that adaptive rubric prioritization tracks changing weaknesses and sustains improvement over evolution rounds.

papers.title: Conservative Policy Iteration For Zero-Sum POSGs
papers.abstract: Occupancy-state reductions make dynamic programming possible for zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs). Existing point-based solvers usually optimise a central value function. This restores Bellman recursion, but it requires point-based updates over high-dimensional occupancy spaces. We introduce an approximate policy-iteration algorithm for finite-horizon zs-POSGs. The method maintains one policy per player and updates both jointly along occupancy trajectories induced by conservative policy updates. Instead of approximating a full central value function, each update uses a single supporting hyperplane induced by the current joint policy. The algorithm alternates local policy improvements, conservative updates, and persistent exploration. Computation is therefore concentrated on occupancy regions where the current joint policy is exploitable. On finite-horizon zero-sum POSG benchmarks, the method is competitive at small horizons and often improves the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons compared with PBVI, HSVI, and CFR+.
papers.summary: Zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs) can be solved by dynamic programming over occupancy states, but existing point-based solvers optimize a central value function and need point-based updates over high-dimensional occupancy spaces. The proposed approximate policy-iteration algorithm for finite-horizon zs-POSGs maintains one policy per player and updates both jointly along occupancy trajectories, using a single supporting hyperplane induced by the current joint policy instead of approximating the full central value function, and alternating local policy improvements, conservative updates, and persistent exploration so that computation concentrates where the joint policy is exploitable. On finite-horizon zero-sum POSG benchmarks it is competitive with `PBVI`, `HSVI`, and `CFR+` at small horizons and **often improves the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons**.

papers.title: Evolving Agent Teams
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.
papers.summary: Software engineering agents are increasingly pointed at open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization, but existing coding agents converge to local optima on expert-written production kernels such as those in `FlashInfer`. `Evolving Agent Teams` pairs a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents with a persistent file system holding a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, so restructuring is grounded in accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget it consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines, and with an extended budget it **writes a CUDA kernel from scratch that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production `FlashInfer` MLA paged decode kernel, winning on 36 of 47 `FlashInfer-Bench` production workloads**. The same framework delivers 3.01x over `vLLM` for KDA prefill on AMD MI350X, 3.44x over `FlashKDA` on NVIDIA B200, 30.3 tokens/s decode for `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` in 4-bit MLX on a 48 GB M4 Pro via MoE expert offloading, and 62.1 on `RoboDojo` held-out seeds versus 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry.

papers.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model's current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student's low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy. We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning (PICO), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.
papers.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) draws its learning signal from binary rewards on on-policy rollouts, so on problems beyond a model's current ability every rollout fails and group-relative estimators such as `GRPO` and `RLOO` collapse to zero advantage, while expert trajectories sit in the student's low-probability regions and tend to teach surface imitation rather than transferable reasoning. `PICO` (Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning) performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism keeps sampling within a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are both verified correct and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized alongside on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that corrects their distribution mismatch with importance sampling, and the method **consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines across diverse reasoning datasets and agentic benchmarks**.

papers.title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception
papers.abstract: Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) enables structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution. Most existing approaches rely on passive perception, which creates real2sim gaps due to imperfect observation. Inspired by how humans perceive actively through actions, we propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to align the Real2Sim2Real gap from interactions. ActiveAlign introduces two complementary modules: (i) ActiveAlign-Waving, which performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and (ii) ActiveAlign-Touching, which refines object alignment through tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level precision. Together, these capabilities enable strong real2sim alignment. We demonstrate that ActiveAlign-Waving can be used to curate simulation environments for open-sourced uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and demonstrate on a real Unitree G1 robot that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.
