papers.summary: Real-to-sim-to-real pipelines give robots structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution, but most rely on passive perception, so imperfect observations leave a gap between the real scene and its simulated copy. `ActiveAlign` closes that gap through interaction with two modules: `ActiveAlign-Waving` performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and `ActiveAlign-Touching` refines object alignment using tactile feedback. The waving module is used to curate simulation environments for open-source uncalibrated manipulation datasets, and on a real `Unitree G1` the full system **achieves millimeter-level alignment that enables fine manipulation such as pressing buttons and moving sliders**.

papers.title: AdaGround: Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming with Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement for GUI Grounding
papers.abstract: GUI grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming in is a common training-free remedy. However, most existing zooming pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally and never revisit a wrong answer. To address these issues, we propose AdaGround, a training-free framework with three components: (1) Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming, which sets the magnification, field of view and zoom depth of each sample from the model's own estimate of the target size; (2) Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement, which uses one marked-click Yes/No verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding and, with an existence query, decide when to abstain; and (3) Compositional Structure Grounding, which composes spreadsheet cells from their headers. On Qwen3-VL models, AdaGround surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, and its gains carry over to held-out UI-Vision. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/AdaGround
papers.summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming is a common training-free remedy, but existing zoom pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally, and never revisit a wrong one. `AdaGround` sets each sample's magnification, field of view, and zoom depth from the model's own estimate of the target size, uses a single marked-click yes/no verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding, and decide when to abstain, and composes spreadsheet cell locations from their headers. On `Qwen3-VL` backbones it surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, **improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on `OSWorld-G` and `ScreenSpot-Pro`**, with gains carrying over to the held-out `UI-Vision` benchmark.

papers.title: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA
papers.summary: Mobile GUI agents are usually fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that emit each action as text, so they decode token by token and keep a large model in the loop even when only scoring candidate actions. `GUI-JEPA` is a decoder-free policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA): an encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots produces a screen latent, an action- and region-conditioned predictor turns it into one latent per candidate action, and lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass without decoding a token. A randomly initialised predictor performs as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics, indicating the predictor is trained for the decision itself. On `AndroidControl` it runs **2.8 to 4.0x faster on the same GPU than a `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` agent fine-tuned on identical inputs while reaching 86 to 92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of the parameters**.

papers.title: RubricAtlas: Mining Type-Level Rubrics from Expert Reports to Evaluate Deep Research Agents
papers.abstract: Deep research agents conduct multi-step Web searches and synthesise retrieved information into analytical reports. Evaluating these outputs requires checking which analyses they deliver, beyond the presence of relevant facts. Query-specific binary rubrics make individual requirements explicit, but task-level checklists may leave the overall analytical structure underexamined. We introduce RubricAtlas, which derives type-level analytical requirements from expert reports on different objects within the same research type and organises detailed checks around recurring analytical questions. The requirements give related tasks a shared standard for what to analyse, without prescribing their answers. Our framework links binary checkpoints to report passages and evaluates completeness separately from argument validity. Built from 3,079 Chinese financial research reports, RubricAtlas covers 99 research types. Reference-report selection experiments show that individual reports cover only about half of their type's analytical questions, and that selecting requirements from different reports changes evaluation scores and agent rankings. Across ten agents, two judge pipelines achieve checkpoint agreement of $\kappa$ = 0.71 and agent-ranking agreement of Kendall $\tau$ = 0.87. Controlled deletions reduce scores on the affected analyses, while padding produces no detectable increase. These findings support type-level rubrics for comparing the analytical completeness of Web deep research outputs, with individual decisions traceable to report evidence.
papers.summary: Deep research agents run multi-step web searches and synthesise analytical reports, and evaluating them requires checking which analyses they deliver rather than just which facts appear, but query-specific binary rubrics can leave the overall analytical structure unexamined. `RubricAtlas` mines type-level analytical requirements from expert reports on different objects within the same research type, organises binary checkpoints around recurring analytical questions, links each checkpoint to report passages, and scores completeness separately from argument validity. Built from 3,079 Chinese financial research reports spanning 99 research types, it shows that **a single reference report covers only about half of its type's analytical questions**, so the choice of reference report shifts both scores and agent rankings. Across ten agents, two judge pipelines reach checkpoint agreement of kappa 0.71 and ranking agreement of Kendall tau 0.87, and controlled deletions reduce scores on the affected analyses while padding produces no detectable increase.

papers.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FAST.Farm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.
papers.summary: Wind farm noise mitigation usually just reduces turbine power output, ignoring wake interactions between turbines and the directional nature of noise emission, which produces over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. `Noise Steering` is a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power under a local noise constraint in a protected region, trained at reduced cost by coupling a low-fidelity acoustic model with the steady-state `FLORIS` simulator. On a six-turbine test farm the policy meets the 40 dB constraint across the full range of turbulent winds **with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, versus 17% for the industry-standard noise-reduced operation baseline**, and it largely retains its performance when deployed in the higher-fidelity `FAST.Farm` simulator.

papers.title: Natural Hard-Negative Mining from Positives for Instruction-Following Retrieval
papers.abstract: Instruction-following information retrieval (IFIR) requires retrievers to rank documents by both a query and its instance-specific instructions, yet instruction-conditioned contrastive supervision remains scarce. Existing synthetic methods typically fix a positive passage and generate additional negatives, overlooking the hard-negative potential of the original positive. We propose Natural Hard-Negative Mining (NHNM), which promotes convertible negatives under query-compatible instructions and repurposes original positives as natural instruction hard negatives. Its automated Candidate Cleaning, Reversal Construction, and Geometry Filtering pipeline produces compact, high-contrast supervision aligned with the pretrained retrieval space. Applied to MSMARCO, NHNM yields NHNM-MARCO, an IFIR training set of nearly 7K instances. On InstructIR and FollowIR, models with 568M to 4B parameters fine-tuned on NHNM-MARCO achieve strong instruction-following performance and match or surpass substantially larger retrievers in several settings. Controlled analyses and ablations attribute these gains to natural hard-negative supervision rather than model scale or training-data volume.
papers.summary: Instruction-following information retrieval (IFIR) requires ranking documents by a query plus instance-specific instructions, but instruction-conditioned contrastive supervision is scarce, and existing synthetic methods fix the positive passage and generate extra negatives, overlooking the original positive's potential as a hard negative. Natural Hard-Negative Mining (`NHNM`) promotes convertible negatives under query-compatible instructions and repurposes original positives as natural instruction hard negatives, with an automated pipeline of candidate cleaning, reversal construction, and geometry filtering that keeps the supervision compact and aligned with the pretrained retrieval space. Applied to `MSMARCO` it yields `NHNM-MARCO`, a training set of nearly 7K instances, and **retrievers of 568M to 4B parameters fine-tuned on it match or surpass substantially larger models in several settings on `InstructIR` and `FollowIR`**, with ablations attributing the gains to the natural hard negatives rather than model scale or data volume.

papers.title: Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.
papers.summary: Minority languages struggle to keep pace as large language models expand into multimodal spoken interaction. The first open speech language model for Basque adopts the `LLaMA-Omni` architecture with a `Latxa` backbone, transferring its Basque text capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules, and addresses data scarcity by translating the English `VoiceAssistant-400K` corpus into Basque and synthesising the audio with a Basque text-to-speech system. Evaluation gives **3.86 out of 5 for content quality, a 9.94% word error rate for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 `UTMOS` score for audio quality**, showing that modular architectures and synthetic data suffice to build low-latency end-to-end spoken interaction in a low-resource language.

papers.title: Vision-Language Agents Can Learn in Their Own Latent Worlds
papers.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
papers.summary: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) hold rich world knowledge, but that knowledge is rarely used to improve a policy through online interaction, partly because policy updates shift the interaction distribution and continually updating a large model as a world model is computationally expensive. `Dwell` is a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that recasts the VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator so it can predict, adjust, and act in its own latent space, serving as both world model and policy while learning from real interactions and from latent imagination. Across five interactive visual environments it **achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially cutting the compute needed for imagination**, suggesting that world models for VLM agents need to predict action-relevant futures rather than reconstruct them.
papers.highlight_summary:
Pretrained vision-language models hold rich world knowledge, but model-free RL burns environment samples, pixel-reconstructing world models are expensive, and their latents are often unusable by a VLM policy. `Dwell` turns a frozen VLM into a recurrent latent transition operator that serves as both world model and policy via two separate LoRA adapters, so the agent learns from imagined rollouts inside its own latent space.

- An observation-conditioned posterior and an action-conditioned prior update a set of latent slots, the prior is trained to match the stop-gradient posterior in a JEPA-style objective, the posterior is grounded to frozen `V-JEPA2` embeddings by slot-wise cosine distance, a reward head is trained on pure-prior lookaheads to limit compounding error, and PPO optimizes actor and critic on H-step imagined trajectories while the world model is refreshed from new real experience every cycle.
- On a `Qwen2.5-VL-3B` backbone across `Sokoban`, `FrozenLake`, `Navigation`, `PrimitiveSkill`, and `EB-ALFRED`, `Dwell` reaches an **overall success rate of 0.38** versus 0.28 for `GRPO`, 0.18 for `PPO`, 0.24 for the adapted `LeWorldModel`, and 0.10 for the untrained base, with the largest gains on `Sokoban` (**0.53**), `FrozenLake` (**0.51**), and `EB-ALFRED` (0.18).
- The win is only among trainable methods and is task-dependent: off-the-shelf `Claude 4.5 Sonnet` (0.60), `GPT-4o` (0.55), and `Qwen2.5-VL-72B` (0.48) all score higher without any training, and `GRPO` clearly beats `Dwell` on `Navigation` (0.73 vs 0.39), where the authors argue immediate observations already carry strong action cues.
- Ablations show the predictive dynamics loss matters far more than representation grounding, a frozen world model saturates early under policy-induced distribution shift, and replacing the shared latent interface with a learned adapter drops `Sokoban` from 0.53 to 0.38, while end-to-end GPU-hours fall **38 to 58%** relative to the generative `AdaWorld` and below `PPO`/`GRPO`, though `LeWorldModel` remains cheaper.
- Evidence is limited to a single 3B backbone and five simulated environments, several results are noisy over three seeds (`PrimitiveSkill` Align at 0.29 ± 0.508, `EB-ALFRED` with only 20 evaluation episodes), latent dynamics are deterministic with no uncertainty estimate, and grounding still depends on a frozen pretrained visual encoder.

papers.title: Beyond QASecClaw: Agent Scaling, Verifier Feedback, and Evidence Reliability in Software Assurance
papers.abstract: Can additional specialist language-model contexts improve software assurance when deterministic tool evidence is already available? We study this question through five experiments spanning authored Java warning controls, OWASP Benchmark assessment, Defects4J test generation, SV-COMP assertion verdicts, and deliberately misleading evidence packages. The evaluated systems use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, with a 1.5B sensitivity analysis, and complete 13,638 model requests. On eight related development warnings, increasing the context count from 1 to 50 increases token use 49-fold without improving unsafe clearance. On 160 OWASP cases, model configurations trade clearance against unresolved outcomes; the ten-context arm assesses only 96 cases. On 32 SV-COMP tasks, raw verifier feedback raises mean correct model verdicts from 12.7 to 22.0, but also raises incorrect verdicts from one to seven; a JBMC-plus-JVM validation baseline returns 26 correct verdicts and six unresolved outcomes. On two sets of 120 evidence packages, models reject 70-100% of applicable counterexamples, while construction-specific scope checks classify every package correctly. No target defect is discovered in three Defects4J bugs, one unsupported by the test adapter. These descriptive results support deterministic evidence admission for the tested settings, while exposing limits of verdict aggregation, feedback interpretation, and the available evaluation coverage.
papers.summary: Whether adding specialist language-model contexts improves software assurance when deterministic tool evidence is already available is tested across five experiments spanning authored Java warning controls, the `OWASP Benchmark`, `Defects4J` test generation, `SV-COMP` assertion verdicts, and deliberately misleading evidence packages, with `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct` as the main model across 13,638 requests. **Raising the context count from 1 to 50 increased token use 49-fold without improving unsafe clearance on eight related development warnings**, and on 160 OWASP cases the ten-context configuration assessed only 96. Raw verifier feedback on 32 SV-COMP tasks lifted mean correct verdicts from 12.7 to 22.0 but also raised incorrect verdicts from one to seven, while a JBMC-plus-JVM validation baseline returned 26 correct verdicts and six unresolved outcomes. Models rejected 70 to 100% of applicable counterexamples that construction-specific scope checks classified perfectly, no target defect was found in three Defects4J bugs, and the authors read these descriptive results as supporting deterministic evidence admission in the tested settings while exposing limits in verdict aggregation, feedback interpretation, and evaluation coverage.

papers.title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
papers.summary: Language models normally keep conversation history in external storage that grows with the dialogue, and this work asks whether a dialogue can instead be written into the model's parameters and later recalled with no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. Self-keyed in-parameter memorization (`SKIM`) is a closed-form method in which the model generates many varied questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as keys that retrieve the turn's content, so a later user question phrased differently can still match one of them. Evaluated on five language models, **`SKIM` recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions**, answering from the parameters alone.

papers.title: DCKV: Learned Transform Coding of the Prompt KV Cache in Hybrid Language Models
papers.abstract: Hybrid language models keep a key-value (KV) cache only in their few full-attention layers, but this cache is still the part of a prompt's state that grows with the prompt and that must be stored or moved to reuse it. We present DCKV, a differentiable codec for the KV cache and the first KV-cache codec that is trained end to end. Its transform, its quantizer and its entropy models, which are conditioned on the prompt tokens and on already decoded neighbouring positions, are optimized together against the frozen language model, both for the code length that the entropy models assign and for the change of the model's output. On Qwen3.5-2B, DCKV stores a compressed token in more than 55 times fewer bytes than bf16 at a loss of at most 1.8 points on three long-context benchmarks, and in more than 100 times fewer bytes at a loss of at most 3.6 points.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models keep a key-value (KV) cache only in their few full-attention layers, but that cache still grows with the prompt and must be stored or moved whenever a prompt's state is reused. `DCKV` is a differentiable codec for the KV cache trained end to end against the frozen language model: its transform, quantizer, and entropy models, conditioned on the prompt tokens and on already decoded neighbouring positions, are optimized jointly for the code length the entropy models assign and for the change in the model's output. On `Qwen3.5-2B` it **stores a compressed token in more than 55 times fewer bytes than bf16 at a loss of at most 1.8 points on three long-context benchmarks**, and in more than 100 times fewer bytes at a loss of at most 3.6 points.

papers.title: Dense Representation Learning and Differentiable Shape Modeling for Spine Landmark Detection
papers.abstract: Spine landmark detection from spinal X-ray is a key step for estimating spine deformation severity, for building biomechanical models, and for pre-operative planning. We reframe anatomical landmark detection as a pixel-level contrastive representation learning problem, matching dense pixel embeddings with landmark prototypes. Surprisingly, even with a generic U-Net backbone, this formulation results in more discriminative heatmaps compared to the traditional heatmap regression paradigm, leading to improved discrimination between vertebral corners on distinct vertebra. Furthermore, we combine the resulting heatmaps with learnable shape priors over the global configuration of spinal landmarks to resolve ambiguities in landmark locations, yielding a simple and practical approach to spinal landmark detection. Our approach is competitive, in terms of landmark accuracy and clinical parameter estimation, with the state-of-the-art on the public AASCE dataset and on two private spinal X-ray datasets. Our code and pre-trained weights are available at https://github.com/BioMedTP/Pix2Point.
papers.summary: Detecting anatomical landmarks on spinal X-rays underpins deformity severity estimation, biomechanical modeling, and pre-operative planning. The authors reframe landmark detection as pixel-level contrastive representation learning that matches dense pixel embeddings against landmark prototypes, then combine the resulting heatmaps with learnable shape priors over the global configuration of spinal landmarks to resolve ambiguities between corners of neighbouring vertebrae. **Even with a generic `U-Net` backbone, the contrastive formulation yields more discriminative heatmaps than traditional heatmap regression**, and the full approach is competitive with the state of the art in landmark accuracy and clinical parameter estimation on the public `AASCE` dataset and two private spinal X-ray datasets.

papers.title: PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval models have been increasingly adopted in search and recommendation systems. However, industrial generative retrieval models are commonly specialized to a fixed online scenario: they learn from scenario-specific interactions, support a narrow set of query forms and retrieval objectives. We study how to remove these couplings and build a unified end-to-end multimodal search system for open-ended image--text queries, heterogeneous shopping intents, and online scenarios with different resource constraints. We present \textbf{PailitaoMMSearch}, which directly generates product Semantic IDs from a raw query image and free-form instruction and scales along three dimensions. \textbf{Data scaling} uses a reusable toolset that can be composed into intent- and lifecycle-specific workflows for cold-start synthesis, quality control, real-traffic refinement, and continuous data production. \textbf{Intent scaling} progressively equips one model with e-commerce product knowledge, multiple retrieval relations, and adjustable reasoning budgets through continual pre-training (CPT), mixed-budget supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and unified reinforcement learning (RL). The RL stage combines intent-balanced optimization and Sample--Beam rollouts aligned with multi-candidate serving. \textbf{Scenario scaling} exposes quality--cost operating points across model capacity and reasoning budget. The system is deployed in multimodal search applications on Taobao Pailitao. A controlled online A/B test reports statistically significant improvements, including item page views $\textbf{+17.90\%}$, transactions $\textbf{+27.04\%}$, and gross merchandise value $\textbf{+8.94\%}$.
papers.summary: Industrial generative retrieval models are usually tied to one online scenario, learning from scenario-specific interactions and supporting a narrow set of query forms and retrieval objectives. `PailitaoMMSearch` generates product Semantic IDs directly from a raw query image plus a free-form instruction and scales along three axes: a reusable data toolset composed into workflows for cold-start synthesis, quality control, real-traffic refinement, and continuous production; intent scaling through continual pre-training (CPT), mixed-budget supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and unified reinforcement learning (RL) with intent-balanced optimization and sample-beam rollouts matched to multi-candidate serving; and scenario scaling that exposes quality-cost operating points across model capacity and reasoning budget. Deployed in Taobao Pailitao multimodal search, a controlled online A/B test reports **statistically significant gains of 17.90% in item page views, 27.04% in transactions, and 8.94% in gross merchandise value**.

papers.title: Do bots feel bad? Assessing empirical evidence for functional valence in LLMs
papers.abstract: Do LLMs have valenced states, i.e. states that feel pleasant or unpleasant? Recent empirical work has claimed to show that LLMs possess functional valenced states (e.g. ``functional pleasure and pain'' [Ren et al. 2026], ``functional emotions'' [Sofroniew et al. 2026], and ``functional welfare'' [Han et al. 2026]) that play the same causal role as valenced states in cognition and action, without necessarily being consciously experienced. But it remains unexplored how well the identified states fit the functional role of valence as understood in the philosophical and cognitive science literature. Here, I assess the current body of evidence, and argue (i) that key aspects of valence remain untested in LLMs, and (ii) that extant empirical paradigms inadequately distinguish (functional) valence from neighbouring constructs like preferences, value-judgments, valence attributions and role-play. I conclude by sketching some novel experimental approaches to better target (functional) valence itself.
papers.summary: Recent empirical work has claimed that large language models (LLMs) have functional valenced states, meaning states that play the causal role of pleasant or unpleasant feelings in cognition and action without necessarily being consciously experienced. The author examines how well the states identified in that work match the functional role of valence as characterised in the philosophy and cognitive science literature. **Key aspects of valence remain untested in LLMs, and existing paradigms fail to separate functional valence from neighbouring constructs such as preferences, value judgments, valence attributions, and role-play.** The author closes by sketching new experimental designs aimed more directly at functional valence itself.

papers.title: Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.
papers.summary: Proactive large language model (LLM) agents must anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history, but existing memory designs emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories and offer little support for validating recurring behavioral patterns or judging whether they apply to the current event. `ProactMem` organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities, checks trajectory facts against their source events, and tests regularities through historical replay before matching them to current conditions. The authors also build `ProactiveStream`, a longitudinal benchmark across three application scopes in which agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On it, **`ProactMem` reaches an overall F1 of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines**.

papers.title: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are extending agent-mediated commerce on the Web from shopping for consumers to operating businesses for sellers. In online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, decisions are issued through Web-based platforms but realized through costly physical execution. Evaluating such agents requires going beyond individual transactions to ask whether decisions made online turn into sustained economic returns. We introduce AutoVend, a benchmark in which one LLM agent manages 20 vending machines across five site types through a Web-based operating interface for 180 simulated days. Its data-grounded simulator combines a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. We evaluate five LLM agents against a rule-based inventory-control baseline and diagnose their site coordination, execution, and performance over time. Four of five evaluated LLM agents fall short of this baseline, and returns per dollar of inference cost rank models differently from returns alone. Operational analyses show that gains in individual metrics do not consistently yield stronger economic growth, as inventory and execution costs erode these gains. Trajectory analysis further reveals difficulties in grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and converting feedback into effective policy revisions.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are beginning to operate businesses for sellers in online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, where decisions are issued through web platforms but carried out through costly physical execution, so evaluation needs to ask whether online decisions turn into sustained economic returns. `AutoVend` has a single agent manage 20 vending machines across five site types through a web-based operating interface over 180 simulated days, with a data-grounded simulator covering a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. **Four of the five evaluated LLM agents fall short of a rule-based inventory-control baseline**, and ranking models by return per dollar of inference cost differs from ranking by return alone. Trajectory analysis points to difficulties grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and turning feedback into revised policies, while gains in individual metrics are often eroded by inventory and execution costs.

papers.title: Advancement or Acceleration? How Data Curation Improves LLM Training
papers.abstract: While data curation is widely credited with improving large language model training, a basic question remains unresolved: does curation expand what a model can ultimately learn, or merely reach the same solution faster? In this paper, we formalize this distinction between advancement (improving the attainable performance) and acceleration (reaching the same performance with less data). Through an analytic characterization and real-world LLM experiments, we show that advancement requires a correctable train-target gap. When the baseline training and target objectives coincide, no curation policy improves the endpoint, although curation may still accelerate training. This reframes advancement as a property of the curation task rather than the curation method. Under a common gap-centric view of data mixture and selection, we operationalize this condition as the $\Delta$-test, an observable discrepancy between the uncurated baseline's training and target losses that is computable prior to expensive curation. Across extensive experiments, an appreciably nonzero $\Delta$ predicts persistent gains, whereas gains near $\Delta=0$ tend to diminish as the training budget grows. Beyond individual methods, our findings recenter data curation on the task itself and point to target-set construction as a promising direction for shaping what curation can achieve.
papers.summary: Data curation is widely credited with improving large language model (LLM) training, but it has been unclear whether curation raises what a model can ultimately learn (advancement) or just reaches the same result with less data (acceleration). Through an analytic characterization and LLM experiments, the authors show that **advancement requires a correctable gap between the baseline training objective and the target objective; when the two coincide, no curation policy improves the endpoint**, though curation may still speed training. They operationalize this condition as the `Delta-test`, a discrepancy between the uncurated baseline's training and target losses that can be computed before any expensive curation. Across experiments, a clearly nonzero Delta predicts persistent gains, while gains near zero tend to fade as the training budget grows, which recenters curation on target-set construction rather than on the curation method.

papers.title: LearnPrunerV2: Learnable Progressive Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal capabilities but suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to the massive number of visual tokens. While token pruning is a promising solution, existing methods still suffer from two major drawbacks: 1) unreliable pruning criteria that fail to accurately localize task-specific regions due to inherent attention biases or query-agnostic designs, and 2) suboptimal pruning strategies that employ rigid, non-adaptive schedules, overlooking the dynamic evolution of token redundancy across different model depths. To address these challenges, we propose LearnPrunerV2, which extends the previous two-stage heuristic framework (LearnPruner) into a fully learnable architecture. Specifically, we integrate lightweight learnable modules into every layer of the VLM backbone, which estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with extrinsic query relevance captured via a shadow token. By uncovering a consistent staircase redundancy pattern across VLM layers, we further introduce Budget-Deterministic Pruning (BDP) to establish a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. Extensive experimental results across various benchmarks and VLMs demonstrate that LearnPrunerV2 consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods. Notably, LearnPrunerV2 preserves 99.8% of the original performance when pruning 77.8% of visual tokens on LLaVA-v1.5, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) carry heavy compute costs from their many visual tokens, and existing token pruning methods suffer from unreliable importance criteria and rigid, non-adaptive pruning schedules. `LearnPrunerV2` turns the earlier two-stage heuristic `LearnPruner` into a fully learnable design by adding lightweight modules at every layer that estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with query relevance captured through a shadow token. Observing a consistent staircase pattern of redundancy across layers, the authors add `Budget-Deterministic Pruning` (BDP), a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. **On `LLaVA-v1.5` the method preserves 99.8% of original performance while pruning 77.8% of visual tokens**, and it outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods across benchmarks and VLMs.

papers.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that ranks passages independently with dense retrieval can return redundant chunks, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and leave multi-hop questions with incomplete evidence. `SpectRAG` builds a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between large language model (LLM)-generated utility questions, then at query time seeds a high-recall candidate set with hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral coordinates, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. On `MultiHopRAG`, `UltraDomain`, and long-document question answering, **it improves broad evidence recovery and reaches competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, `HyDE`, `LightRAG`, and `NaiveRAG` baselines**. The results suggest graph-spectral structure helps most for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, with trade-offs in early precision, compute cost, and domain-dependent performance.

papers.title: Evaluating Priority Dispatch for Premium Membership in On-demand Taxi-sharing
papers.abstract: In this paper, we analyze the dispatch-level feasibility of introducing premium membership into an on-demand taxi-sharing service using a sequential optimal insertion method. We propose two dispatch-level methods: deadline shortening for premium users, and deadline shortening with dedicated premium vehicles. We compare them with a baseline dispatch method through SUMO-based simulations under three demand scenarios: steady uniform demand, time-varying demand with a peak period, and urban-focused demand with concentrated peak traffic. Our results show that the suitable priority mechanism depends on operating conditions and premium ratio, suggesting that condition-dependent method switching may provide premium benefits while keeping non-premium-user burden smaller for overall optimization.
papers.summary: On-demand taxi-sharing services may want to offer premium membership, but it is unclear how to prioritize premium riders at the dispatch level without unduly burdening other users. The authors propose two methods built on sequential optimal insertion, shortening deadlines for premium users and shortening deadlines combined with dedicated premium vehicles, and compare them against a baseline dispatcher in `SUMO` simulations under steady uniform demand, time-varying demand with a peak period, and urban-focused demand with concentrated peak traffic. **Which priority mechanism works best depends on operating conditions and the share of premium users**, suggesting that switching methods by condition could deliver premium benefits while keeping the burden on non-premium riders smaller.

papers.title: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.
papers.summary: Embedding-level scaling grows a language model's capacity through lookup-based memory rather than deeper or wider networks, but extending it to vision-language models (VLMs) is hard because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent rather than discrete tokens suited to n-gram lookup. `V-LUMEN` discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, forms spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals, and fuses the retrieved embeddings into the backbone through a gated residual pathway, with all addressing non-parametric. It substantially improves a frozen `Qwen3-VL-2B` on five reasoning-intensive benchmarks and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from training. **At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a `LoRA` or mixture-of-experts adapter's capacity into the lookup memory preserves accuracy on two backbones**, which the authors read as evidence that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis whose lookup cost is constant in table size and paid once at prefill.

papers.title: Crop Yield Prediction Using Regression Models: A Comparative Evaluation of Model Performance
papers.abstract: Reliable crop-yield prediction can support agricultural planning and resource allocation. This study evaluates five regression models for predicting crop yield from environmental, crop-related, and agricultural management variables. The dataset initially contained 1,000,000 observations and ten variables, with 231 observations having negative target values removed during preprocessing. Categorical variables were represented using one-hot encoding, and Boolean variables were converted into binary values. The models considered were multiple linear regression (LR), random-forest regression (RF), decision-tree regression (DT), ridge regression, and lasso regression. Their performance was evaluated using 80:20 and 70:30 training-testing splits based on the coefficient of determination (R-squared), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). Applying an 80:20 split, LR achieved a test R-squared of approximately 0.9130 and a test RMSE of 0.5008. Applying a 70:30 split, lasso regression yielded the highest test R-squared (approximately 0.9131) and the lowest test RMSE (approximately 0.5008), with performance almost identical to LR and ridge regression. DT also showed improved test performance under the 70:30 split, whereas RF exhibited a substantial gap between training and testing performance. These results indicate that the evaluated linear regression model provides competitive baselines for this dataset. Further experimentation, including validation testing, will help determine the models' performance and predictability.
papers.summary: Reliable crop-yield prediction can support agricultural planning, and this study compares five regression models on a dataset of about one million observations with ten environmental, crop, and management variables, after removing 231 rows with negative yields and one-hot encoding categorical features. Multiple linear regression, random forest, decision tree, ridge, and lasso were evaluated with 80:20 and 70:30 train-test splits using R-squared, mean squared error, and root mean squared error. **Linear regression and its regularized variants reached a test R-squared of about 0.913 and a root mean squared error of about 0.50 under both splits**, essentially tied with each other, while random forest showed a large gap between training and test performance. The authors conclude that linear models provide competitive baselines for this dataset and note that further validation is needed.

papers.title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.
papers.summary: Deep learning performs well at breast cancer diagnosis from histopathology, but limited interpretability holds back clinical adoption. The authors benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained architectures, including `ResNet50`, `DenseNet121`, `ConvNeXt`, `ViT`, and `Swin Transformer`, for benign-versus-malignant classification on the `BreakHis` dataset with a patient-level split, and explain predictions with `Grad-CAM`, `LIME`, `Integrated Gradients`, and `LRP`. **`DenseNet121` achieved 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999**, significantly outperforming every other model, with transformer-based models trailing the convolutional networks. The explanation maps consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance.

papers.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
papers.abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
papers.summary: Spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents, but synthesizing targeted training data for these tasks is difficult and costly. The authors argue both rest on a shared capability they call connecting evidence, meaning identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the right entities, recovering their relations, and composing an answer, and that data for this capability is far easier to synthesize. `EvidenceConnect` generates questions from zoomed views of related regions within a single image that require comparing, aggregating, or chaining visual evidence, keeping a reference answer only when independent vision-language models agree and discarding questions whose answer survives removal of the selected regions. Training base models on this data with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) yields `ZwZ2`, which **improves fine-grained and spatial perception and also gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning even though the data is not tailored to any benchmark**.

papers.title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning on mathematics and programming, but its rollouts tend to collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, shrinking the explored space. Building on evidence that thinking tokens at critical steps act as structural anchors in reasoning paths, `Guided-RLVR` adds a lightweight controller that injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, nudging the model to approach problems from multiple perspectives. **On mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks it consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.**
papers.highlight_summary:
RLVR rollouts tend to collapse onto the handful of reasoning paths the base model already favors, and a union-bound argument shows that trajectories with sampling probability well below 1/G get essentially no learning signal under a finite rollout budget. `Guided-RLVR` attaches a small learned Logic Controller that, at high-entropy sentence boundaries, boosts the logit of one semantically meaningful steering token such as "Wait", "Therefore", "However" or "If", and trains the controller jointly with the policy on the same group-relative advantages.

- The controller is an MLP over summed hidden states that fires only after sentence-final punctuation when next-token entropy exceeds a dynamic threshold, picks one of six categories (Reflection, Progression, Causality, Causal Reflection, Contrast, Hypothesis), raises that token to probability **0.5** before sampling, guides 8 of every 10 rollouts, and is cold-started on `DeepSeek-R1` traces from `OpenThoughts-114k-math`, with an auxiliary log-perplexity bonus granted only to correct rollouts where the steering token was actually sampled.
- Across `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` and `Qwen3-4B` with both `GRPO` and `DAPO`, it posts the best ten-metric average in all four pairings, beating the strongest of vanilla, `ENT` and `REP` by **1.1 to 2.8 points**, with the clearest case being `Qwen3-4B` + `GRPO` at **72.64** versus 69.82 for `REP` and 60.62 for vanilla, and `AIME2024` pass@128 of **83.33** versus 63.33.
- On `MATH` at k=128 it raises textual diversity to **0.70** from 0.60 and equational diversity to **0.16** from 0.13 while `ENT` and `REP` fall below vanilla `GRPO` on both, generations are shorter on the competition sets (1,088 versus 1,225 tokens on `AIME2024`), and RL-stage compute rises by **12.6%** (17.92 versus 15.92 GPU-hours).
- Ablations on `MATH` show every component matters, with random token choice dropping pass@1/pass@16 from 65.6/80.6 to 63.4/77.2, a fixed "Wait" token to 63.9/78.2, removing the entropy threshold to 62.1/79.2 (and policy entropy diverging during training), and removing the log-perplexity reward to 62.0/79.6.
- The `AIME` sets have 30 problems, so the headline pass@128 gaps amount to one or two problems, pass@1 is not uniformly better on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` (`AIME2025` 5.03 versus 5.99 for vanilla `GRPO`), the controller cold start is extra supervision no baseline receives, and policy updates consume guided samples without any importance correction.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Discovery of CNOT Decompositions for Quantum Permutations on Constrained Topologies
papers.abstract: Efficient quantum circuit compilation is challenging for quantum computers, where limited qubit connectivity can introduce substantial overhead in the implementation of logical operations. Recent AI-assisted synthesis methods have shown considerable potential for reducing circuit complexity, but their role in uncovering principles that can guide the design of new deterministic compilation algorithms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate this perspective for the synthesis of quantum permutations into CNOT circuits under constrained qubit connectivity. Using AlphaCNOT as an exploratory tool, we identify a recurring decomposition for remote transpositions that improves on the construction based on adjacent SWAP routing. For two qubits at graph distance $d>1$, the discovered pattern yields a topology-legal implementation using at most $6d-4$ CNOT gates, compared to the $6d-3$ gates required by the corresponding SWAP-based construction. We formalize this observation through a constructive proof to define Global Transpositions, a deterministic synthesis method that searches for a minimum-cost decomposition of an entire permutation into topology-aware logical transpositions. The resulting method subsumes optimal SWAP routing within its synthesis model and provides certified upper bounds on the topology-constrained CNOT cost. Our experiments also reveal circuits that cannot be expressed as concatenations of independently synthesized transpositions. Instead, these circuits exploit intermediate linear transformations that temporarily leave the permutation subgroup and combine partial effects of multiple logical operations, a mechanism we call intermediate CNOT fusion. Our results show that AI-assisted synthesis can support not only circuit optimization, but also the discovery of reusable identities, provable constructions, and hidden mechanisms in quantum circuit compilation.
papers.summary: Limited qubit connectivity forces quantum compilers to add routing overhead when implementing logical operations, and while AI-assisted synthesis can shrink circuits, its use for uncovering principles behind new deterministic compilation algorithms has been largely unexplored. Using `AlphaCNOT` as an exploratory tool for synthesizing quantum permutations into CNOT circuits, the authors identify a recurring decomposition for remote transpositions that beats adjacent-SWAP routing: **for qubits at graph distance d greater than 1 it needs at most 6d-4 CNOT gates versus 6d-3 for the SWAP-based construction**. They formalize this with a constructive proof into `Global Transpositions`, a deterministic method that searches for a minimum-cost decomposition of a whole permutation into topology-aware transpositions, subsumes optimal SWAP routing, and certifies upper bounds on CNOT cost. Experiments also surface circuits that temporarily leave the permutation subgroup and merge partial effects of several logical operations, a mechanism the authors call intermediate CNOT fusion.

papers.title: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Audit-based certification bounds the violation rate of an LLM agent by auditing a random fraction $\varepsilon$ of actions and reweighting the audited labels; its validity is meant to rest only on the defender's audit coin. We show that it also rests on a confidentiality property: the coin must not interfere with the agent's view before the action commits, at a time the agent chooses. We call this pre-commit noninterference (PNI) and measure its violation by $D_{\mathrm{A}}$, the total-variation distance between the agent's views under the two coin values. PNI is necessary and sufficient for an unbiased certificate against adaptive agents, the worst-case bias is $(1-\varepsilon)D_{\mathrm{A}}$, and no procedure that sees only audited labels can pay less. Leakage composes across steps, a resource shared across episodes opens a channel of computable size, and raising the audit rate cannot restore validity. On a monitor we built, a silent audit changes no output but adds latency that tool timestamps expose, and the agent can enlarge it. A real LLM agent follows an injection that names a visible audit notice (generic, tool, and timing clauses have no effect); over that channel the plain certificate fails on measured labels and, by a post-hoc analysis, in a live run on a pre-registered schedule, while a silent audit restores it. A fresh coin per audited call closes the timing channel; padding only narrows it.
papers.summary: Audit-based certification bounds an LLM agent's violation rate by auditing a random fraction epsilon of its actions and reweighting the audited labels, and its validity is meant to rest only on the defender's secret audit coin. The authors show it also rests on a confidentiality property they call pre-commit noninterference (PNI): the coin must not alter the agent's view before an action commits, at a time the agent chooses, with violation measured by the total-variation distance between the agent's views under the two coin values. **PNI is necessary and sufficient for an unbiased certificate against adaptive agents, the worst-case bias is (1 minus epsilon) times that distance, and raising the audit rate cannot restore validity.** On a monitor they built, a silent audit changes no output but adds latency that tool timestamps expose, a real LLM agent follows an injection naming a visible audit notice and thereby breaks the plain certificate on measured labels and in a pre-registered live run, and a fresh coin per audited call closes the timing channel where padding only narrows it.

papers.title: Exploring the Limits of the Delta Learning Hypothesis: Single-Pair Generator Biases in Direct Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) typically relies on preference pairs generated from diverse model pools and ranked by an external LLM judge. The recently proposed delta-learning hypothesis suggests that comparable supervision can instead be obtained from a single pair of models by treating the larger model's response as preferred. We investigate the limits of this approach across model families and scales. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that fixed model pairs introduce systematic, generator-dependent biases that are predictive of the preference label independent of response quality. Consequently, DPO trained on single-pair data consistently underperforms multi-model preference data, despite the larger generator producing higher-quality responses, and we trace this gap to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases. We further show that simply increasing the number of generators, even without an external judge, is enough to partially mitigate this effect. Our results highlight generator diversity as a critical factor in preference-data construction.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) usually relies on preference pairs drawn from diverse model pools and ranked by an external LLM judge, while the delta-learning hypothesis proposes that a single pair of models suffices if the larger model's response is simply treated as preferred. Testing this across model families and scales, the authors show theoretically and empirically that **fixed model pairs introduce systematic generator-dependent biases that predict the preference label regardless of response quality**, so DPO trained on single-pair data consistently underperforms multi-model preference data even though the larger generator writes higher-quality responses. They trace the gap to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases and find that adding more generators, even without an external judge, partially closes it.

papers.title: EnergyCal: Taming Loss Spikes in Muon-Family Optimizers for Sparse MoE Training
papers.abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training can exhibit large loss spikes with Muon-family optimizers. We introduce EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton-Schulz directions. EnergyCal leaves the spectral transform unchanged and adds no persistent optimizer state. We evaluate it on a 4B-parameter MoE model. Against a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, EnergyCal-MuonH reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%, with a modest throughput cost. With plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, the reduction in mean spike burden averages 95.98% across the two tested exponents, accompanied by small endpoint improvements. These findings support stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated setting.
papers.summary: Training sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models with Muon-family optimizers can produce large loss spikes. `EnergyCal` is a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton-Schulz directions, leaving the spectral transform unchanged and adding no persistent optimizer state. On a 4B-parameter MoE model, **`EnergyCal` on top of `MuonH` cuts mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%** against a development-selected lower-learning-rate `MuonH` recipe, at a modest throughput cost. With plain `Muon` at matched learning rate and weight decay, spike burden drops by about 96% on average across two tested exponents with small endpoint improvements, supporting stabilization both with and without Hyperball.

papers.title: Correctness Conditioning as Selection in Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Evaluation
papers.abstract: Restricting chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness evaluation to correctly answered instances changes the population being measured. We study this selection step in a seven-variable structural causal model and derive the exact observed gap $\Delta = \operatorname{Cov}(A, C)/P(C=1)$. The model distinguishes difficulty confounding from shortcut-induced collider bias and states the conditional-independence assumption needed to express the gap through latent response propensities. A protocol review of 18 papers distinguishes answer-correctness restrictions from agreement-based selection, benchmark construction, and training-data filtering. We evaluate four sub-ceiling deployments on arithmetic tasks and observe positive selection gaps in all four. The primary GLM-5.3 run yields a +7.4 percentage-point gap ($n = 1000$, $p < 0.0001$), and pooled Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel analysis gives OR = 1.70 ($p < 10^{-6}$). An assumption-free covariance decomposition assigns 42.8% of the GLM-5.3 gap to between-stratum variation in interventionable-operation count, leaving the majority unattributed. When counterfactual compliance is observable for every instance, evaluating all traces directly estimates population faithfulness without correctness filtering.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness evaluations often restrict analysis to correctly answered instances, which changes the population being measured. The authors study this selection step with a seven-variable structural causal model, derive the exact observed gap as the covariance between correctness and faithfulness divided by the probability of a correct answer, separate difficulty confounding from shortcut-induced collider bias, and review the protocols of 18 papers. On arithmetic tasks across four sub-ceiling deployments they observe positive selection gaps in every case; **the primary `GLM-5.3` run shows a +7.4 percentage-point gap on 1000 instances**, with a pooled Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio of 1.70. A covariance decomposition attributes 42.8% of that gap to between-stratum variation in the count of interventionable operations, and the authors note that when counterfactual compliance is observable for every instance, evaluating all traces estimates population faithfulness without correctness filtering.
papers.highlight_summary:
Restricting chain-of-thought faithfulness scores to correctly answered instances quietly changes which traces are being measured, and the paper argues this is a selection-bias problem rather than a detail of protocol. The `CoTsel` framework models the correctness filter as a selection step in a seven-variable structural causal model, derives the resulting gap in closed form, audits how 18 prior evaluations choose their reporting population, and measures the gap on arithmetic tasks where a symbolic oracle makes counterfactual compliance observable for every trace, including the ones answered wrong.

- The gap between correctness-filtered and all-trace faithfulness equals **Cov(A, C) / P(C = 1)** as an assumption-free identity, where A marks an appropriate answer change after an intervention on the reasoning chain and C marks answer correctness, and the model names two mechanisms that can make it positive: difficulty confounding, where harder tasks lower both accuracy and compliance, and a collider between CoT reliance and latent shortcut competence that conditioning on correctness opens.
- On arithmetic DAGs with intermediate-value interventions, all four sub-ceiling deployments show positive gaps, with the primary `GLM-5.3` run at **+7.4 percentage points** (n = 1000, p < 0.0001), `deepseek-v4-flash` at +6.0 pp (p = 0.046), and `glm-5.2` and `deepseek-v4-pro` positive but not significant at +1.6 pp and +2.4 pp.
- A pooled Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test gives **OR = 1.70** (p < 10⁻⁶) and survives dropping any single deployment, while two 100%-accuracy controls (`qwen3.8-max`, `Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite`) return exactly zero gap because the identity forces it, not as independent evidence.
- A covariance decomposition assigns **42.8%** of the `GLM-5.3` gap (bootstrap interval 26.8 to 69.1%, and 21.9% for flash) to between-stratum variation in interventionable-operation count, and inverse-propensity reweighting on that count removes only 23 to 34%, so the majority of the gap remains unattributed and the share itself depends on the covariate chosen.
- The shortcut detector records **0%** shortcut use under neutral framing, so the collider mechanism is theorized but untested here and the paper's own shortcut-mixture special case overpredicts the observed gaps by 6.4 to 11.7 times, and further limits include arithmetic-only evidence, no counterfactual oracle for natural-language tasks, a scoring convention that counts unparseable responses as non-compliant and enlarges the headline gap, and withheld raw API logs.

papers.title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents
papers.abstract: Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. This study developed OpenGray, a benchmark of planning tasks with known correct decisions. Materials and methods: OpenGray adds tasks with known answers to the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset, including two contradictions with dose goals proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal. Four systems, from a rule-based planning script to a full LLM agent, were evaluated on 30 patients, the LLM-based ones with a commercial (Terra) and a local (Ministral 3 8B) LLM. Decisions, achieved dose, problem recognition, and technical failures were recorded and also read from logs of 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of SAGE, a clinical LLM agent. Results: With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent had decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, respectively, yet escalated only 50% (95% confidence interval, 25-75%) and 25% (10-40%) of overlap contradictions, which required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met. In four SAGE runs, one goal failed at every attempt; the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping. Conclusions: Favorable aggregate scores concealed specific decision failures. Planning agents should be evaluated on their decisions as well as their dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.
papers.summary: Radiotherapy planning agents built on large language models (LLMs) decide whether to submit a plan or request review, yet they are mostly judged by dose metrics alone. `OpenGray` augments the `OpenKBP-Opt` head-and-neck dataset with tasks that have known correct decisions, including two contradictions where dose goals are provably incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal, and evaluates four systems ranging from a rule-based script to a full LLM agent on 30 patients using the commercial `Terra` model and the local `Ministral 3 8B`, plus logs from 39 runs of the clinical agent `SAGE`. **With `Terra`, decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1% concealed that the systems escalated only 50% and 25% of the overlap contradictions requiring arithmetic on the anatomy**, and 24% of submitted feasible plans missed a hard goal the stored plan had met. The authors argue planning agents should be evaluated on decisions as well as dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.

papers.title: Learning to Look Beyond Screens: Transferable Visual Observation from GUI Grounding
papers.abstract: Visual perception is evolving from passive recognition toward active, task-oriented observation. We investigate GUI grounding as a scalable source of spatial supervision for learning observation behaviors that transfer beyond interfaces. We introduce LBS (Look Beyond Screens), a vision-language model trained through supervised initialization on teacher-generated GUI grounding trajectories, followed by reinforcement learning for multi-turn crop-and-inspect decisions.
