Under fixed inference settings, LBS models based on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B consistently improve over their corresponding baselines. Gains beyond supervised fine-tuning transfer to PerceptionBench for both backbones and to HR-Bench and ChartQAPro for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, supporting observation strategies that generalize beyond GUI-specific imitation. Further analysis suggests complementary roles for the two stages: SFT establishes visual inspection primitives, while RL improves their downstream effectiveness. These findings support GUI grounding as a practical supervision paradigm for transferable active visual perception and broader multimodal reasoning. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/UI-Venus/tree/LBS and https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/LBS-27B, respectively.
papers.summary: Visual perception is shifting from passive recognition toward active, task-oriented observation, and the authors ask whether GUI grounding can serve as a scalable source of spatial supervision for observation behaviors that transfer beyond interfaces. `LBS` is a vision-language model trained first with supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated GUI grounding trajectories and then with reinforcement learning for multi-turn crop-and-inspect decisions. Under fixed inference settings, models built on `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` and `Qwen3.8-27B` consistently improve over their baselines, and **gains beyond supervised fine-tuning transfer to `PerceptionBench` for both backbones and to `HR-Bench` and `ChartQAPro` for the 35B model**. Analysis suggests the supervised stage establishes visual inspection primitives while reinforcement learning makes them more effective downstream.

papers.title: Hardware-Matched Spiking Neural Networks for Real-Time Purkinje Cell Spike Classification
papers.abstract: Distinguishing Purkinje cell (PC) simple spikes (SSs) from complex spikes (CSs) is key to studying cerebellar function. PC recordings commonly rely on wired headstages, whose tethers restrict natural movement in freely behaving animals. Untethered headstages remove this constraint, but cannot continuously transmit raw recordings within their power budgets, making on-headstage spike classification an attractive form of compression, provided it runs accurately in real time on constrained hardware. This work presents two compact spiking neural networks (SNNs) matched to their target hardware: ConvSNN, which maps to the Matrix Vector Processor (MVP) of an EFM32PG28 microcontroller, and StreamSNN, which processes one waveform value per timestep using learned time constants and fixed synaptic delays for a dedicated SKY130 circuit. Evaluated on cells unseen during training, ConvSNN achieves a CS F1 of 0.873 with 1,018 parameters and StreamSNN 0.837 with 527 parameters, both with eight-bit weights. On the microcontroller, MVP acceleration reduces ConvSNN latency by 62.3\% and extends estimated battery life to 33.73~hours on a 50~mAh battery. In SKY130, StreamSNN occupies 0.173~mm$^2$ and consumes 0.46~$\mu$J per event, with 0.2~ms of computation within an 8.3~ms end-to-end latency.
papers.summary: Separating cerebellar Purkinje cell simple spikes from complex spikes is central to studying cerebellar function, but wired headstages restrict animal movement and untethered ones lack the power budget to stream raw recordings, making real-time on-headstage classification an attractive form of compression. The authors design two compact spiking neural networks (SNNs) matched to their hardware: `ConvSNN`, mapped to the Matrix Vector Processor of an EFM32PG28 microcontroller, and `StreamSNN`, which consumes one waveform sample per timestep using learned time constants and fixed synaptic delays for a dedicated SKY130 circuit. On cells unseen during training, **`ConvSNN` reaches a complex-spike F1 of 0.873 with 1,018 eight-bit parameters and `StreamSNN` 0.837 with 527**. Hardware acceleration cuts `ConvSNN` latency by 62.3% and extends estimated battery life to 33.73 hours on a 50 mAh battery, while `StreamSNN` occupies 0.173 square millimeters and uses 0.46 microjoules per event.

papers.title: A First-Step Bias Restores Lost Diversity in Diffusion Model Distillation
papers.abstract: Distribution-matching distillation enables high-quality image generation in only a few denoising steps. However, distilled student models often map different initial noise samples to similar outputs under the same prompt. To locate where diversity is lost, we compare the teacher and student along the sampling trajectory. The largest measured reduction in the response to different initial noises occurs during the first, high-noise step. When we replace the first step with the teacher's corresponding trajectory and leave the final three student steps unchanged, most of the output diversity returns. This suggests that the first step is a key point for restoring diversity. Motivated by this finding, we introduce \emph{ReSeed}, a post-distillation method that adds a seed-response bias adapter only to the first student step and aligns its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity. All student weights and later denoising steps remain unchanged. We evaluate ReSeed on three text-to-image models (SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev) and one text-to-video model (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B). For a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model, \emph{ReSeed} requires only $0.00196\%$ additional trainable parameters relative to the base model and is trained on 8,000 prompt--noise pairs, while keeping the distilled student fully frozen and requiring no target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses. It improves DINO diversity by $48.3\%$ while maintaining competitive visual quality. These results show that substantial diversity can be recovered through a lightweight, data-efficient tuning of only the first denoising step, without finetuning the full student model.
papers.summary: Distribution-matching distillation lets diffusion models generate images in a few denoising steps, but the distilled students tend to collapse different initial noise samples into near-identical outputs for the same prompt. By comparing teacher and student along the sampling trajectory, the authors find that most diversity is lost in the first, high-noise step, and that swapping only that step for the teacher's restores most of it. `ReSeed` exploits this by attaching a tiny seed-response bias adapter to the first student step and aligning its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity, leaving all student weights and later steps frozen. On a distilled 4-step `FLUX.1-dev`, it adds only 0.00196% trainable parameters, trains on 8,000 prompt-noise pairs with no target images or adversarial losses, and **improves DINO diversity by 48.3%** while keeping visual quality competitive; results also hold on `SD3-Medium`, `SD3.5-Medium`, and `Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B`.

papers.title: Prospector: learning a compact graph traversal policy for scientific reasoning
papers.abstract: Scientific reasoning in specialized engineering fields depends on knowledge scattered across the literature, often proprietary and absent from frontier LLM training data. In such domains, frontier models tend to give generic answers. Knowledge graphs (KGs) can ground LLM reasoning. Because a graph is too large to provide in full, typical LLM+KG systems preselect a portion, deciding relevance before reasoning begins. Here we train a compact model, Prospector, to reason over a domain knowledge graph by traversing it step by step, seeking evidence in light of what it has already found. Prospector calls a small set of tools one at a time to progressively build its context, and answers with a chain of evidence that can be checked edge by edge against what its tools retrieved from the graph. On a knowledge graph built from the semiconductor-manufacturing literature, Prospector approaches the strongest off-the-shelf models given the same graph and tools, and it far exceeds off-the-shelf models answering closed-book or from a pre-selected portion of the graph. Although trained only on the semiconductor graph, Prospector transfers to unseen knowledge graphs from three other distinct fields: bio-inspired materials, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and materials properties. Served on a single GPU, Prospector answers faster and at a fraction of the cost of a hosted service, while keeping proprietary data on the owner's hardware. We find that the policy's latent state is indicative of its next move on both seen and unseen graphs, and modulating the latent state can steer the policy from one behavior mode to another. These results suggest a practical LLM + KG paradigm for scientific and engineering reasoning over private data, in which a compact model trained on a graph from published literature transfers its traversal to unseen graphs that stay with their owners.
papers.summary: Frontier language models give generic answers in specialized engineering fields whose knowledge is scattered across proprietary literature, and typical systems that pair a model with a knowledge graph (KG) preselect a subgraph before reasoning starts. `Prospector` is a compact model trained to traverse a domain knowledge graph step by step, calling a small set of tools one at a time to build its context and returning a chain of evidence that can be checked edge by edge against what the tools retrieved. On a graph built from semiconductor-manufacturing literature it approaches the strongest off-the-shelf models given the same graph and tools, and **far exceeds them when they answer closed-book or from a preselected portion of the graph**, while transferring without retraining to unseen graphs on bio-inspired materials, PFAS, and materials properties. Served on a single GPU it answers faster and cheaper than a hosted service while keeping proprietary data local, and its latent state predicts its next traversal move and can be modulated to steer it between behavior modes.

papers.title: SFE-O: An Ontology for Knowledge-Grounded AI in Supercritical CO$_2$ Biomass Extraction and Fractionation
papers.abstract: Supercritical CO$_2$ extraction (CO$_2$-SFE) offers a sustainable route for recovering high-value compounds from biomass while limiting the use of conventional organic solvents, but its design and interpretation require heterogeneous knowledge spanning biomass properties, operating conditions, mass transfer, and product fractionation, typically fragmented across technical reports, engineering models, external databases, and expert practice. This paper introduces SFE-O, a modular Web Ontology Language (OWL 2) ontology for supercritical CO$_2$ biomass extraction, structured around interconnected Biomass, Process, and Product dimensions and extended with explicit representations of process topology, parameter provenance, external and internal mass-transfer phenomena, and the Constant Extraction Rate (CER) / Falling Extraction Rate (FER) mechanisms. Computational dependencies among process quantities are represented explicitly, without embedding numerical solving in the ontology, so that input, measured, computed, externally retrieved, and fitted parameters remain traceable. SFE-O reuses established semantic resources (ChEBI, QUDT, OWL-Time, PROV-O) and is evaluated through a worked example that instantiates a real pilot-scale extraction batch, a reasoner-based consistency check, and a competency-question SPARQL query. The resulting knowledge model provides a machine-actionable foundation for querying, consistency checking, and mechanistic explanation of SFE processes, and establishes a knowledge layer that could support future ontology-grounded AI reasoning, a direction this paper motivates but does not evaluate.
papers.summary: Designing and interpreting supercritical CO2 extraction (CO2-SFE) of biomass requires knowledge about feedstock properties, operating conditions, mass transfer, and product fractionation that is fragmented across technical reports, engineering models, external databases, and expert practice. `SFE-O` is a modular Web Ontology Language (OWL 2) ontology organized around Biomass, Process, and Product dimensions, with explicit representations of process topology, parameter provenance, mass-transfer phenomena, and the Constant Extraction Rate (CER) and Falling Extraction Rate (FER) mechanisms, and it reuses `ChEBI`, `QUDT`, `OWL-Time`, and `PROV-O`. Computational dependencies among process quantities are modeled without embedding numerical solving, so input, measured, computed, retrieved, and fitted parameters stay traceable. Evaluation consists of **instantiating a real pilot-scale extraction batch, a reasoner-based consistency check, and a competency-question SPARQL query**; the authors motivate but do not evaluate ontology-grounded AI reasoning on top of it.

papers.title: MRI-to-CT Translation of Spinal Images via Anatomy-Guided Pseudo-Pairing and Adversarial Diffusion
papers.abstract:
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is routinely used to diagnose spinal disorders, but surgical planning often requires Computed Tomography (CT) for better visualization of vertebral bone anatomy. Synthesizing CT from MRI could avoid additional radiation exposure and streamline preoperative assessment.
  We propose a three-stage framework for spine MRI-to-CT synthesis. First, an anatomy-guided vertebral matching system identifies similar sagittal MRI and CT slices using spine segmentations and aligns them through rigid registration, creating pseudo-paired data from unpaired scans. Second, these pairs train an adversarial diffusion model for MRI-to-CT translation. Third, synthesized slices are assembled into 3D volumes and refined by a network that improves inter-slice continuity and structural coherence.
  The framework was trained on over 10,000 unpaired sagittal MRI and CT slices and evaluated on 1,911 slices from 83 MRI volumes spanning all spinal regions. Assessment combined distribution-based measures with vertebral segmentation metrics. Compared with diffusion alone, the proposed approach increased binary 3D vertebral Dice from 0.666 to 0.739. Volumetric post-processing reduced visible discontinuities between stacked slices and improved vertebral coherence in axial and coronal views.
  Combining anatomy-guided pseudo-pairing, adversarial diffusion and 3D refinement improves spine MRI-to-CT synthesis. Vertebral matching primarily enhanced anatomical alignment and fidelity, while volumetric refinement improved 3D consistency. These findings support further development of MRI-derived CT-like visualization for preoperative planning, particularly to preserve fine intensity details while maintaining volumetric coherence.
papers.summary: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is standard for diagnosing spinal disorders, but surgical planning often needs Computed Tomography (CT) to visualize vertebral bone, so synthesizing CT from MRI could spare patients extra radiation. The proposed three-stage pipeline first builds pseudo-paired training data from unpaired scans by matching sagittal MRI and CT slices via spine segmentations and rigid registration, then trains an adversarial diffusion model on those pairs, and finally stacks the synthesized slices into 3D volumes refined by a network that enforces inter-slice continuity. Trained on over 10,000 unpaired slices and evaluated on 1,911 slices from 83 MRI volumes across all spinal regions, the full framework **raises binary 3D vertebral Dice from 0.666 to 0.739** over diffusion alone, with the matching stage mainly improving anatomical fidelity and the volumetric refinement reducing visible discontinuities in axial and coronal views.

papers.title: What the Primary Lund Plane Omits: A Model-Stitching Diagnosis of a Jet-Tagger Representation Gap
papers.abstract: Lund-plane and Particle Transformer (ParT) jet taggers can differ in performance because one representation is weaker, or because a weaker downstream computation reads an adequate one. Standalone performance cannot separate these. Model stitching can: it links the frozen early layers of one network to the frozen late layers of another through a single trained linear map. As a positive control we use an incomplete Lund representation, the primary declustering branch, whose deficit is known independently. Stitched into ParT's downstream, it reaches a background rejection at least as much as its own downstream recovers, yet far below ParT's background rejection: the deficit is representational, not computational. A hypergraph reader over splitting triplets does no better, ruling out higher-order correlations as the cause. The gap is invisible in AUC, which stays within 1\% of its target value, and appears only in background rejection at low signal efficiency. It localizes to 0.6\% of background jets, at and above the top mass, with more constituents but fewer primary splittings than typical background. Rebuilding the representation on the full Cambridge/Aachen declustering tree repairs the deficit as predicted: standalone rejection rises, closing 72\% of the gap. Masking nodes at inference shows the repaired network still relies almost entirely on the primary branch; the secondary splittings make the representation learnable rather than supplying information it reads. Along the primary branch, the widest-angle splitting, near the top and $W$ opening angles, is worth nearly twice a random one. For quark/gluon tagging the primary branch is far less deficient, retaining 77.6\% of ParT's rejection (46.9\% for top), and the full tree closes only 33\% of the gap (72\% for top).
papers.summary: When two jet taggers such as a Lund-plane network and the Particle Transformer (`ParT`) differ in performance, standalone metrics cannot tell whether the input representation is weaker or the downstream computation reading it is. Model stitching, which joins the frozen early layers of one network to the frozen late layers of another through a single trained linear map, separates the two: using the primary declustering branch as a positive control, its deficit proves representational rather than computational, since even the `ParT` downstream cannot recover the gap and a hypergraph reader over splitting triplets does no better. The gap is invisible in AUC, which stays within 1% of target, and shows up only as background rejection at low signal efficiency, localized to 0.6% of background jets at and above the top mass. **Rebuilding the representation on the full Cambridge/Aachen declustering tree closes 72% of the gap for top tagging** (33% for quark/gluon, where the primary branch is far less deficient), and masking studies show the secondary splittings make the representation learnable rather than supplying information the network actually reads.

papers.title: Generative Replay for Equilibrium Propagation: Toward Edge-Friendly Continual Learning in Hopfield Networks
papers.abstract: Equilibrium Propagation (EqProp) offers a biologically grounded and hardware-aligned alternative to backpropagation for training Hopfield Networks. However, its behavior in continual learning settings remains largely unexplored. This work confronts catastrophic forgetting in EqProp-trained Hopfield Networks from the inside out, eliminating the need for external data buffers or architectural overhead that standard Experience Replay \textbf{(ER)} and Generative Replay \textbf{(Gen-Replay)} inevitably require. We introduce an Energy-Based Generative Replay strategy \textbf{(EB-Gen)} which exploits the intrinsic generative dynamics of Hopfield Networks, allowing a single model to act as both classifier and replay samples generator. Samples capturing past task knowledge are generated by relaxing a frozen copy of the network, enabling rehearsal solely through internally generated pseudo-data. We evaluate the proposed method in the Class-Incremental setting, using the split versions of the MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks and compare it with FineTune, Experience Replay, Generative Replay, Sleep-Like Replay Consolidation (SRC) and Joint training. Our results show that EB-Gen significantly improves stability while preserving plasticity, achieving a 75\% and 64\% average accuracy on Split MNIST and Split CIFAR10 respectively. These findings show that Equilibrium Propagation can be adapted to alleviate catastrophic forgetting without forgoing the traits which made it compelling in the first place.
papers.summary: Equilibrium Propagation (EqProp) is a biologically grounded, hardware-friendly alternative to backpropagation for training Hopfield Networks, but its behavior under continual learning, where catastrophic forgetting is the main obstacle, has barely been studied. The proposed Energy-Based Generative Replay (`EB-Gen`) avoids the external data buffers of Experience Replay (ER) and the separate generator of Generative Replay (Gen-Replay) by relaxing a frozen copy of the network itself to produce pseudo-samples of past tasks, so one model serves as both classifier and replay generator. In class-incremental experiments on `Split MNIST` and `Split CIFAR10` against FineTune, ER, Gen-Replay, Sleep-Like Replay Consolidation (SRC), and joint training, the method **reaches 75% and 64% average accuracy** respectively, substantially improving stability while preserving plasticity.

papers.title: Beyond Parameter Protection: Fisher-Shaped EWC for Replay-Free Continual Learning
papers.abstract: In replay-free continual learning, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) uses Fisher information matrix (FIM) to protect acquired knowledge by penalizing changes to historically important parameters. However, a local importance estimate at the retained solution does not in general characterize sensitivity after finite parameter displacement. This motivates controlling Fisher sensitivity over a neighborhood of potential future updates. We propose Fisher-Shaped EWC (FS-EWC), which extends the role of FIM from parameter protection to solution formation for future retention. During task learning, FS-EWC minimizes the worst-case empirical FIM trace within a prescribed neighborhood, explicitly favoring solutions that are less sensitive to bounded future displacement. At task completion, trajectory-based model merging constructs the retained solution from multiple optimization states rather than a single terminal iterate, after which FIM is estimated for subsequent consolidation. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that FS-EWC improves performance over EWC, while controlled studies indicate a more favorable stability--plasticity balance and greater tolerance to parameter drift. These results suggest that effective knowledge retention requires both forming solutions with future retention in mind and protecting acquired knowledge.
papers.summary: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) protects old knowledge in replay-free continual learning by using the Fisher information matrix (FIM) to penalize changes to important parameters, but a local importance estimate at the retained solution says little about sensitivity after the finite parameter shifts that future tasks cause. Fisher-Shaped EWC (`FS-EWC`) extends the FIM from protection to solution formation: during each task it minimizes the worst-case empirical FIM trace within a prescribed neighborhood, favoring solutions that tolerate bounded future displacement, and at task completion it builds the retained solution by merging multiple states along the optimization trajectory rather than taking the final iterate. Across several benchmarks the method **improves over standard EWC**, and controlled studies show a more favorable stability-plasticity balance and greater tolerance to parameter drift.

papers.title: GCSR-OCC: Geometry Calibration and Semantic Routing for Open-Vocabulary Occupancy Prediction
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction represents scene geometry and semantics in a unified voxel grid, enabling recognition beyond predefined categories. One approach reconstructs scenes with 3D Gaussians and converts them into voxel occupancy. However, Gaussian scale inflation and excessive overlap can distort voxel occupancy predictions, while semantic mixing can arise within Gaussians spanning multiple categories and during 3D--2D semantic feature alignment. We propose GCSR-OCC, which combines geometry calibration and multi-mode query-conditioned semantic routing for indoor occupancy prediction from a single RGB image. The Evidence-Conserving Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator (EC-G2O) uses kernel mass normalization, $p$-norm aggregation, and a learnable gain to suppress scale inflation and excessive local evidence accumulation while calibrating occupancy responses. Multi-mode Query-First Gaussian Semantic Routing (MM-QGSR) matches multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and aggregates query-specific evidence into voxels through a learnable text-conditioned router. Fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation further refine voxel-level predictions. Without 3D semantic annotations, GCSR-OCC achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary occupancy prediction on Occ-ScanNet, with 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU. It also reduces geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms. Our code will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction encodes scene geometry and semantics in a single voxel grid, and one approach reconstructs the scene with 3D Gaussians before converting them to voxels, but Gaussian scale inflation and overlap distort occupancy while Gaussians spanning several categories mix semantics. `GCSR-OCC` predicts indoor occupancy from a single RGB image using two components: an Evidence-Conserving Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator (EC-G2O) that applies kernel mass normalization, p-norm aggregation, and a learnable gain to calibrate occupancy responses, and Multi-mode Query-First Gaussian Semantic Routing (MM-QGSR) that matches multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and routes query-specific evidence into voxels through a learnable text-conditioned router. Without any 3D semantic annotations it reaches **state-of-the-art 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU** on `Occ-ScanNet` and cuts geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms.

papers.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
papers.abstract: Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.
papers.summary: Supervised training of agents for professional work needs large numbers of diverse, executable tasks, but tasks with missing or inconsistent information derail the teacher model that produces demonstrations and weaken the resulting supervision. `WorkFactory` starts from professional intents, builds an information support graph that records where each piece of information required for the intended outputs lives and how the pieces depend on each other, then runs probe executions to detect support failures and repair them while preserving the intended work. The pipeline yields 112,686 tasks across 612 occupations, and fine-tuning `Qwen` models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales on the collected teacher trajectories produces the `WorkPilot` family, all of which beat their base models on four professional-work benchmarks, with the 35B-A3B model **rising from 879 to 1565 Elo** on `GDPval-AA v2.1`. Scaling analyses show model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first rising then falling, and ablations attribute the gains to planning and repair reducing probe-diagnosed environment defects.

papers.title: LiveSearch: Questions as Executable Verifier Code for a Live Benchmark of Professional-Source Financial Search Agents
papers.abstract: In finance, the answer that matters is usually the current one: prices, rates, and disclosures hold only as of a given day, so retrieving up-to-date facts is a core capability of a financial agent. Yet most financial benchmarks overlook timeliness. They fix each answer at annotation time, so the gold goes stale as markets move and, once leaked into training data, rewards recall rather than search and analysis. We introduce LiveSearch, a live benchmark that stores each question as executable verifier code: a typed program of calls to a professional financial data service, followed by a declarative extractor. The question is frozen, while its gold answer is determined by executing the program against professional financial data at evaluation time, and a daily job re-executes it with no human or language model in the loop. A memorized answer is thus likely outdated, and a model must reach the current one through tools and analysis. Construction is equally automatic: a language model only verbalizes programs enumerated from real tool responses and never chooses an answer. Under general web search, six contemporary tool-calling models reach 70.9% to 76.7% answer accuracy. Over three consecutive days, 70% of served questions change their gold value, and even under tolerance-aware matching, a literally reused earlier snapshot fails on a majority of questions within a single day. Per-question tracking uncovers dynamic shifts in correctness masked by aggregate accuracy.
papers.summary: Financial questions about prices, rates, and disclosures have answers that hold only as of a given day, yet most financial benchmarks freeze gold answers at annotation time, so they go stale and, once leaked into training data, reward memorization over search. `LiveSearch` stores each question as executable verifier code, a typed program of calls to a professional financial data service plus a declarative extractor, so the question stays fixed while a daily job recomputes the gold answer from live data with no human or language model in the loop; construction is equally automatic, with a language model only verbalizing programs enumerated from real tool responses. Under general web search, six contemporary tool-calling models reach 70.9% to 76.7% answer accuracy, and **70% of served questions change their gold value over three consecutive days**, so a literally reused earlier snapshot fails on most questions within a single day even under tolerance-aware matching. Per-question tracking reveals shifts in correctness that aggregate accuracy hides.

papers.title: R\`enyi-Regularized Flow-Based Variational Inference for Bayesian Calibration
papers.abstract: Variational inference with normalizing flows provides a flexible posterior approximation for Bayesian model calibration, but struggles when the posterior has several modes separated by regions of low probability mass. We study this behavior in a two-parameter twin experiment and regularize the variational objective. Under Gaussian observation errors and a Gaussian prior, the corresponding minimization objective is the expected Tikhonov calibration objective minus the differential entropy of the approximating distribution. However, the expected Tikhonov term favors concentration near one of the modes, while entropy maximization does not guarantee multimodality. We introduce a regularization term based on R\'enyi divergence that encourages the approximate posterior to cover the prior support. In the connected bimodal case, a flow approximation represents both modes; in the case with well-separated modes, the flow and Gaussian mixture frequently miss one mode. The introduced regularization reduces the near-collapse fraction from 50% to 25%. While the regularization improves mode coverage in this experiment, it changes the Bayesian variational objective, introduces a trade-off in approximation accuracy, and does not provide a general solution to mode collapse.
papers.summary: Normalizing-flow variational inference offers flexible posterior approximations for Bayesian model calibration but tends to collapse onto one mode when the posterior has several modes separated by low-probability regions. In a two-parameter twin experiment with Gaussian observation errors and a Gaussian prior, the variational objective reduces to an expected Tikhonov calibration term, which favors concentrating on a single mode, minus the entropy of the approximation, which does not guarantee multimodality, so the authors add a Rényi-divergence regularizer that pushes the approximate posterior to cover the prior support. With well-separated modes both the flow and a Gaussian mixture frequently miss one of them, and the regularizer **reduces the near-collapse fraction from 50% to 25%**, though it alters the Bayesian objective, trades off approximation accuracy, and is not a general fix for mode collapse.

papers.title: MLE-World: Predicting Machine Learning Experiment Outcomes with a Learned World Model
papers.abstract: AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However, executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, together with a confidence score estimating the prediction's correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for these agents. We build five TTS policies, guided by MLE-World, that compare several candidates per step by their predicted outputs: Sequential revision, Best-of-N, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and a UCB style rule that also adds an exploration bonus from this confidence score. Since predictions can be wrong, we run a candidate for real only when its confidence score is low. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models. MLE-World guided TTS achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without a world model, with less real execution. Project webpage: https://mle-world.github.io/.
papers.summary: AI research agents that propose and refine programs for machine learning tasks are bottlenecked by having to train and evaluate a model for every candidate. `MLE-World` is a world model fine-tuned from `Qwen3.5-4B` that predicts a program's terminal output, including error traces, training logs, and validation scores, from its code and a data description without running it, and attaches a confidence score to each prediction. Because a prediction costs one inference call instead of a training run, it makes test-time scaling (TTS) affordable, and the authors build five TTS policies on top of it (sequential revision, best-of-N, pairwise judging, fusion, and a UCB-style rule with an exploration bonus from the confidence score), running a candidate for real only when confidence is low. On 17 `MLE-bench Lite` tasks the model **matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held-out programs versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models**, and world-model-guided TTS lifts observed mean performance by up to 22.1% over the agent alone while executing less code for real.

papers.title: Action-Value Calibration via Continuation Sharing for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on feedback from sequences of interactions, making credit assignment to individual actions difficult. Existing methods such as GiGPO compare actions at shared states to compute relative advantages, but estimate each action's value from a single sampled continuation. The resulting local credit remains sensitive to decisions made later in the trajectory. To address this problem, we propose ConCal (Continuation Calibration), a recursive continuation-value estimator that incorporates continuation evidence already present in a rollout batch. ConCal matches visits from the same task by their incoming state-action-state transitions, combines shared continuation evidence with each visit's own transition estimate, and propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates. This reduces dependence on individual sampled continuations and mitigates local credit distortions without additional rollouts. Held-out return diagnostics show lower error in within-group value differences and higher agreement with reference action orderings than estimates based on individual continuations. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ConCal improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 and 5.86 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yingjian-Chen/ConCal.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents must assign credit to individual actions from feedback on whole interaction sequences, and methods like `GiGPO` that compare actions at shared states estimate each action's value from a single sampled continuation, leaving local credit hostage to decisions made later in the trajectory. Continuation Calibration (`ConCal`) is a recursive estimator that reuses continuation evidence already present in a rollout batch: it matches visits from the same task by their incoming state-action-state transitions, blends shared continuation evidence with each visit's own estimate, and propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action values, all without extra rollouts. Held-out return diagnostics show lower error in within-group value differences and closer agreement with reference action orderings, and with `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` the method **improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 and 5.86 percentage points** on `ALFWorld` and `WebShop`.

papers.title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution
papers.abstract: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/BiPA.git.
papers.summary: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks by rewriting the natural-language procedure in its context and keeping edits that raise success on a small dev set, but success on such tasks is noisy, so a dev-set gain does not prove an edit helps and a success score says nothing about what it costs. `BiPA` replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to the seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read so extra input tokens can be traced to the behavior that caused them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks, and two models, **learned skills succeed only 0.1 points more often on average than their hand-written seeds**, their dev gains vanish on test (picking the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when nothing changed), and they consume about 16% more input tokens because the optimizers almost always add rules that make the agent re-check work or act one call at a time, each extra turn re-sending the whole conversation. Four design principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain beats what selection alone reports, charge it for the turns it adds rather than its length, let the editor delete and merge rules, and show it what earlier rules cost.

papers.title: Retrieve to Act: Motion Primitive Graph Retrieval for Robust VLA Execution
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies demonstrate remarkable semantic generalization, yet remain highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts during execution. While existing test-time methods attempt to suppress spurious visual cues, they fundamentally overlook the rich, uncorrupted kinematic priors embedded in the policy's own training experience. We introduce Retrieve to Act (R2A), a test-time scaling framework that formulates OOD robustness purely as a geometric motion primitive retrieval problem. R2A bypasses fragile visual features by structuring successful training demonstrations into an offline spatiotemporal motion primitive graph. During inference, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network dynamically localizes the robot's ongoing execution within this graph, retrieving structurally compatible future motion primitives. These retrieved geometric priors are then seamlessly harmonized with the frozen VLA's predicted actions via a learned, dimension-wise gating mechanism, adaptively rectifying erroneous spatial trajectories while preserving the policy's local reactivity. Extensive experiments across three state-of-the-art VLA architectures, GR00T N1.7, $\pi_{0.5}$, and StableVLA, demonstrate that R2A consistently and significantly enhances robustness against diverse contextual perturbations. R2A achieves absolute success rate improvements of up to +12% in simulation benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin2.0-Plus) and +40% in real-world deployments, without requiring any finetuning of the base policies. Project page: https://retrieve2act.github.io/r2a/
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies generalize well semantically but break under out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts at execution time, and existing test-time fixes try to suppress spurious visual cues while ignoring the clean kinematic priors in the policy's own training demonstrations. Retrieve to Act (`R2A`) recasts OOD robustness as geometric motion-primitive retrieval: successful demonstrations are organized offline into a spatiotemporal motion primitive graph, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network localizes the robot's current execution within that graph at inference to retrieve structurally compatible future primitives, and a learned dimension-wise gate blends these priors with the frozen VLA's predicted actions, correcting erroneous spatial trajectories while keeping local reactivity. Applied without fine-tuning to `GR00T N1.7`, `π0.5`, and `StableVLA`, it improves success rates by up to 12% on the `LIBERO-Plus` and `RoboTwin2.0-Plus` simulation benchmarks and **by up to 40% in real-world deployments** under diverse contextual perturbations.

papers.title: Spine: Compiling Subtask Trees into Structured Context for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
papers.abstract:
Long-horizon coding tasks contain nested subtasks. Typically, agents record interactions sequentially into a growing history, causing context inflation and performance degradation. Compressing or trimming the history without explicit subtask boundaries can discard information needed by unfinished subtasks. Conversely, recursive subagent delegation isolates completed subtasks through child agents by assigning every subtask boundary to delegation, which conflates subtask granularity with executing agent choice, adding execution and coordination overhead. We introduce Spine, an interface and runtime that align model context with subtask nesting and completion. An agent declares explicit subtask boundaries through work scopes, allowing the same agent to execute nested subtasks inline while reserving delegation for independent parallel tasks. The runtime organizes execution in SpineTree, a persistent tree recording subtask relations, local interactions, completion states, and returned results. Before each model call, it compiles the tree into model context just in time, retaining unfinished subtasks' interactions and replacing completed subtasks' details with their results, while preserving prefix-cache reuse.
  We integrate Spine into Codex to build SpineCodex. With GPT-5.6 Sol, compared with native Codex, SpineCodex improves SWE-Milestone Score by 11.8% while reducing total cost by 32.4%, improves the average ProgramBench test-pass rate by 17.3%, and improves Mean@5 on eight of the ten evaluated FrontierSWE tasks. On SWE-Milestone, it also achieves a comparable Score to Recursive Subagent at 73.7% lower total cost. We also integrate Spine into Pi through a reusable software package: with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Qwen 3.8 27B, it improves SWE-Milestone Score by 9.5-17.5% and the average ProgramBench test-pass rate by 4.3-8.7% compared with native Pi.
papers.summary: Long-horizon coding tasks decompose into nested subtasks, but agents usually append every interaction to one growing history, inflating context and degrading performance; trimming without subtask boundaries can drop information unfinished subtasks still need, while recursive subagent delegation isolates finished subtasks only by forcing every boundary into a child agent, adding coordination overhead. `Spine` is an interface and runtime in which the agent declares explicit subtask boundaries as work scopes, so the same agent can execute nested subtasks inline and reserve delegation for independent parallel work; the runtime records subtask relations, local interactions, completion states, and results in a persistent `SpineTree` and compiles it into model context just in time before each call, keeping unfinished subtasks' interactions, replacing completed ones with their results, and preserving prefix-cache reuse. Integrated into Codex as `SpineCodex` with `GPT-5.6 Sol`, it **improves the SWE-Milestone score by 11.8% while cutting total cost by 32.4%** versus native Codex, raises the average `ProgramBench` test-pass rate by 17.3%, improves Mean@5 on eight of ten `FrontierSWE` tasks, and matches Recursive Subagent's `SWE-Milestone` score at 73.7% lower cost. A reusable package integrating `Spine` into Pi with `Gemini 3.8 Flash` and `Qwen 3.8 27B` yields 9.5 to 17.5% `SWE-Milestone` gains and 4.3 to 8.7% `ProgramBench` gains over native Pi.

papers.title: GraphRAGProv: GraphRAG Meets How-Provenance
papers.abstract: GraphRAG systems often use knowledge graphs to retrieve relevant context for an LLM that produces the final answer. That makes answers more inscrutable and therefore less appealing for domains where transparency is paramount. We present GraphRAGProv, an architecture that executes SPARQL queries over source-grounded RDF graphs to compute answers and their how-provenance polynomials. These polynomials record which statement occurrences were used and how they were combined. Because each occurrence is linked to its source text, users can follow these links to check whether the extracted statements reflect the text and whether the query combines them to answer the question. Querying thereby becomes a way to inspect and evaluate the text-to-graph transformation. Our interactive demo examines 400 cases from two multi-hop QA benchmarks, revealing extraction and query errors even when the final answer is correct.
papers.summary: GraphRAG systems retrieve context from a knowledge graph and hand it to an LLM that writes the final answer, which makes answers hard to inspect in domains where transparency matters. `GraphRAGProv` instead executes SPARQL queries over source-grounded RDF graphs to compute both the answer and its how-provenance polynomial, a record of which statement occurrences were used and how they were combined, with each occurrence linked back to the source text so users can check whether extracted statements reflect the text and whether the query combines them correctly. Querying thereby doubles as a way to audit the text-to-graph transformation, and an interactive demo over **400 cases from two multi-hop QA benchmarks surfaces extraction and query errors even when the final answer is correct**.

papers.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.
papers.summary: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and action, raising the question of when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. The first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, with a sharp window, and on real graphs validated gating gains exactly on the relations meeting those conditions; the second gives a per-node exposure bound, extended to message passing, under which exposure per unit cost computed without any attack **picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases**, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or equal-cost analysis. Supporting tools provide exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for `R-GCN` and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph and mostly abstains when relations are few, and without cost information the safe choice is to abstain.

papers.title: Grounding LLM Agents in Business Processes: Process-Aware Knowledge Graphs for Reliable Multi-Step Service Invocation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that call enterprise APIs must select the correct endpoints, follow process order, use valid payload keys, and choose coded values from predefined lists. However, current retrieval-augmented service discovery treats endpoints independently and therefore misses process and schema constraints. We address this limitation by integrating Open Data Protocol (OData) metadata and Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) reference processes in a typed property graph. A hybrid retriever identifies candidate endpoints using dense embeddings and follows process edges to retrieve subsequent endpoints. We evaluate the method on 42 enterprise services with process-chain ground truth. For queries with low lexical overlap between the query and downstream entities, it improves Recall@3 by 5.7 points (n=74), with consistent gains across embedding models and cut-offs. It matches dense retrieval on other queries and provides no improvement on OpenAPI services without a process layer, indicating that the gains arise from process structure. We also evaluate an LLM agent on 81 multi-step queries. It completes 38.7% of tasks, compared with 10.3% for a chunk-based baseline. In an elicitation probe, providing valid code lists eliminates invented codes but leaves invalid keys in 46% of write runs. Full typed context reduces invalid calls to 3% (3 of 101 runs), with no invented codes. These results show that exposing process and schema constraints during retrieval improves the reliability of agent-driven API calls.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents calling enterprise APIs must pick the right endpoints, respect process order, use valid payload keys, and select coded values from predefined lists, but retrieval-augmented service discovery treats endpoints independently and misses these process and schema constraints. The approach integrates Open Data Protocol (OData) metadata and Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) reference processes into a typed property graph, and a hybrid retriever finds candidate endpoints via dense embeddings then follows process edges to pull in subsequent endpoints. On 42 enterprise services with process-chain ground truth, it improves Recall@3 by 5.7 points on queries with low lexical overlap, matches dense retrieval elsewhere, and yields no gain on OpenAPI services lacking a process layer, isolating the benefit to process structure. An LLM agent using it **completes 38.7% of 81 multi-step queries versus 10.3% for a chunk-based baseline**, and in an elicitation probe supplying valid code lists eliminates invented codes but leaves invalid keys in 46% of write runs, whereas full typed context cuts invalid calls to 3 of 101 runs.

papers.title: TCM-DiagCommit: A TCM-SD-Derived Benchmark for Evidence-Conditioned Syndrome Selection and Commitment
papers.abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome differentiation is usually evaluated as static final-label selection over complete clinical records. This setting hides three diagnostic behaviors: whether a model distinguishes semantic-neighbor syndrome labels from easy random distractors, whether it updates predictions as evidence fields are revealed, and whether it should commit under uncertainty. We introduce TCM-DiagCommit, a benchmark derived from the public TCM-SD/ZY-BERT resource while retaining its source syndrome labels; it converts 1,834 source cases into 23,842 task rows over 148 syndrome labels. The benchmark combines random, profile-neighbor, and full-vocabulary candidate ladders with staged t1/t2/t3 evidence. It also includes fixed-label tongue/pulse perturbations and insufficient-evidence variants. A benchmark-defined action contract scores commit, acquire, defer, and abstain. Across five zero-shot DirectLLM calibrations, random10 top-1 accuracy is 63.2% to 66.4%, but hard20 falls to 24.7% to 30.3% and full148 to 14.8% to 22.3%; on hard20, WT(all) wrong-terminal commits remain 62.2% to 74.3%. These results show that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for diagnostic benchmark evaluation: answer selection, evidence use, and benchmark commitment scoring should be measured separately.
papers.summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome differentiation is normally evaluated as picking a final label from complete clinical records, which hides whether a model can separate semantically neighboring syndromes from easy random distractors, whether it updates as evidence is revealed, and whether it should commit under uncertainty. `TCM-DiagCommit` converts 1,834 cases from the public `TCM-SD`/`ZY-BERT` resource into 23,842 task rows over 148 syndrome labels, combining random, profile-neighbor, and full-vocabulary candidate ladders with staged evidence, fixed-label tongue and pulse perturbations, insufficient-evidence variants, and an action contract that scores commit, acquire, defer, and abstain. Across five zero-shot direct-LLM calibrations, top-1 accuracy of 63.2% to 66.4% with ten random candidates **falls to 24.7% to 30.3% with twenty hard neighbors and to 14.8% to 22.3% over all 148 labels**, and on the hard set 62.2% to 74.3% of terminal commits are wrong, arguing that answer selection, evidence use, and commitment should be scored separately.

papers.title: Aligning Large Language Models for Safety in African Languages: A Case Study of Hausa
papers.abstract: Safety alignment research for large language models (LLMs) remains concentrated on high-resource languages, leaving open how existing alignment methods perform in low-resource, culturally distinct settings. We study this question for Hausa, a language spoken by more than 200 million people across West Africa. We introduce HausaSafeLM, one of the first Hausa safety preference dataset, built from 10,000 prompts derived from PKU-SafeRLHF: 3,000 human-corrected (gold) and 7,000 machine-translated (silver) examples spanning six harm macro-categories. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and SFT followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) under both data regimes, evaluating on 500 harmful and 200 benign Hausa prompts.We find that the untuned base model appears highly safe by refusal-rate metrics alone, but this reflects limited Hausa generation ability rather than genuine alignment: its refusals are almost uniformly low quality. SFT improves both refusal fluency and precision and benefits substantially from the larger, noisier silver-tier data, while DPO sharpens refusal precision but comes at a steep, largely data-invariant cost to linguistic quality. No single configuration jointly maximizes safety, helpfulness, and fluency. Our results suggest that current alignment techniques teach models when to refuse more readily than how to do so fluently in underrepresented languages, and that refusal-rate metrics alone are an unreliable signal of safety in low-resource settings.
papers.summary: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is studied almost entirely in high-resource languages, so this work asks how standard methods behave in Hausa, a West African language with more than 200 million speakers. The authors build `HausaSafeLM`, a preference dataset of 10,000 prompts derived from `PKU-SafeRLHF` with 3,000 human-corrected gold and 7,000 machine-translated silver examples, and compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) against SFT followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`. **The untuned base model looks safe by refusal rate alone, but its refusals are almost uniformly low quality, reflecting weak Hausa generation rather than real alignment.** SFT improves refusal fluency and precision and benefits from the larger noisy silver data, while DPO sharpens precision at a steep cost to linguistic quality, suggesting current techniques teach models when to refuse more readily than how to refuse fluently in underrepresented languages.

papers.title: Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation. Evaluation both guides subsequent search and determines the final scaffold, but evaluating every candidate on the full task set incurs substantial execution costs. We investigate how evaluation budgets can be allocated across these two roles. Our experiments show that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while additional targeted evaluation improves final selection. Replay analyses further show that shared informative items and a common scoring reference support comparisons among closely matched candidates. Motivated by these findings, we propose \method, an evaluation allocation framework that combines sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation. A short fully evaluated warm-up establishes a shared informative core and calibrates a response model whose item parameters remain fixed during search. After search, \method refits the model and applies paired successive halving, reusing accumulated observations and executing only missing evaluations. Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, \method achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution generates and evaluates candidate workflows iteratively, but scoring every candidate on the full task set is expensive, and evaluation serves two different roles: guiding the search and picking the final scaffold. Experiments show that sparse feedback is enough to sustain productive evolution while extra targeted evaluation mainly helps final selection, and replay analyses indicate that shared informative items and a common scoring reference are what make close candidates comparable. The proposed allocation framework runs a short fully evaluated warm-up to fix a shared item core and calibrate a response model, uses sparse feedback during search, then refits the model and applies paired successive halving that reuses accumulated observations. **Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks it beats full evaluation on mean performance in most settings while using roughly half as many evaluation cells.**

papers.title: RPSD: Retrieval-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from historical behavior. Recent LLM-based methods recast this task as generative recommendation and increasingly adopt reinforcement learning such as GRPO for post-training. However, these methods suffer from two limitations, namely credit-blind optimization, where a sequence-level reward is shared across all generated tokens, and collaborative-blind supervision, where each training signal is derived from a single user and ignores behavioral patterns shared across similar users. To address both issues, we propose Retrieval-Privileged on-policy Self-Distillation (RPSD). For credit-blind optimization, we introduce on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), in which a teacher with privileged knowledge re-evaluates the student's on-policy response, and the token-level confidence difference between the student and teacher reshapes the shared sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit. However, the privileged knowledge in vanilla OPSD is still derived from a single user, leaving collaborative-blind supervision unresolved. We therefore ground the teacher in collaborative behavioral evidence from similar users. Specifically, we use temporally aware optimal transport (OT) to compare interaction trajectories across users by jointly considering item similarity and temporal structure, and further apply diversity-aware selection to retain complementary trajectories as privileged evidence. In this way, on-policy self-distillation provides fine-grained token-level credit, while OT enriches the teacher with structured cross-user evidence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bring on-policy self-distillation to sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as its privileged signal. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RPSD achieves state-of-the-art performance.
papers.summary: LLM-based sequential recommenders that are post-trained with `GRPO` share one sequence-level reward across every generated token and derive each training signal from a single user, ignoring patterns shared across similar users. Retrieval-Privileged on-policy Self-Distillation (`RPSD`) has a teacher with privileged knowledge re-score the student's own on-policy response, and uses the token-level confidence gap between teacher and student to turn the shared advantage into token-specific credit. To ground the teacher in cross-user evidence, temporally aware optimal transport compares interaction trajectories across users by item similarity and temporal structure, with diversity-aware selection keeping complementary trajectories. **The authors report state-of-the-art results across multiple real-world datasets and describe this as the first use of on-policy self-distillation with cross-user behavior as the privileged signal in sequential recommendation.**

papers.title: A Lightweight Attention-Based CNN with Saliency-Map Interpretability for Skin Cancer Detection
papers.abstract: Skin cancer is among the most prevalent and life threatening forms of cancer worldwide. Early and accurate diagnosis significantly improves patient survival rates. However, manual dermoscopic assessment remains challenging due to visual similarity. This study proposes an Explainable AI-driven framework for automated binary classification of skin lesions using a lightweight attention-based convolutional neural network (CNN-Attention). The model integrates channel attention to focus on informative regions of dermoscopic images while maintaining low computational complexity. A publicly available dataset comprising 2,637 training and 660 test images was used, with balanced class weights. The proposed model achieved 87 percent accuracy with 1.95 million parameters and 7.45 MB of storage, matching the best baseline (MobileNet) while using approximately half as many parameters and half as much storage. ROC AUC and PR AUC scores reached 0.9475 and 0.9430, respectively. Additionally, saliency maps were incorporated as an explainability technique to visualize regions that influence model decisions. Comparative analysis with VGG16,VGG19,ResNet101,and MobileNet demonstrates the proposed models effectiveness in balancing classification results, computational efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.summary: Dermoscopic skin lesion assessment is difficult because benign and malignant lesions look alike, motivating an automated binary classifier that stays small enough for constrained deployment. The model is a lightweight convolutional neural network with channel attention (`CNN-Attention`) trained with balanced class weights on a public dataset of 2,637 training and 660 test images, with saliency maps added to show which regions drive predictions. **It reaches 87 percent accuracy with 1.95 million parameters and 7.45 MB of storage, matching `MobileNet` at about half the parameters and storage**, with ROC AUC of 0.9475 and PR AUC of 0.9430. Comparisons against `VGG16`, `VGG19`, `ResNet101`, and `MobileNet` frame the contribution as a balance of accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.

papers.title: ReForest: Interpretability Meets Reasoning in Isolation Forest
papers.abstract: Statistical anomaly detection methods like Isolation Forest are efficient but suffer from a critical semantic gap. They identify numerical rarities but fail to understand the contextual meaning of data, often missing subtle, context-dependent anomalies. Conversely, Large Language Models possess strong semantic reasoning capabilities but are prohibitively expensive and slow for large-scale deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose ReForest, a novel framework that synergizes the statistical efficiency of Isolation Forest with the reasoning power of LLMs. ReForest transforms the latent decision paths of Isolation Forest into natural-language explanations, enabling an LLM to refine anomaly detection through an uncertainty-aware dynamic ensemble. This approach allows the model to adaptively weigh statistical and semantic signals based on uncertainty-driven instance-level confidence. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets (Healthcare, Finance) demonstrate that ReForest significantly outperforms baselines, achieving an average 21% improvement in Recall and a 10% gain in F1-score. Our framework not only improves detection performance but also enhances model transparency by grounding semantic narratives in statistical evidence, providing interpretable rationales essential for high-stakes decision-making.
papers.summary: Statistical anomaly detectors like `Isolation Forest` are fast but flag numerical rarities without understanding context, while large language models can reason semantically but are too slow and expensive to run over large datasets. `ReForest` converts the decision paths of `Isolation Forest` into natural-language explanations so an LLM can refine the detections, and an uncertainty-aware dynamic ensemble weighs the statistical and semantic signals per instance according to confidence. **On four real-world healthcare and finance datasets the method improves Recall by an average of 21% and F1-score by 10% over baselines.** The authors also argue the natural-language rationales, grounded in statistical evidence, make the detector more transparent for high-stakes decisions.

papers.title: AnalogScout: Simulation-Efficient PVT-Aware Analog Sizing with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Analog device sizing must satisfy all specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners to ensure tape-out success, but simulating every candidate at all corners dominates the sizing time and slows design iteration. Conventional surrogate-based optimizers search the sizing space directly, while recent large language model (LLM) agents add circuit knowledge to designs but still delegate the sizes to global optimizers. Both learn the circuit response from repeated multi-corner SPICE simulations and optimize on top of it, which becomes expensive under a limited simulation budget. Providing an agent with reusable verified designs and sizing sub-blocks analytically could save most of this budget. We propose AnalogScout, a simulation-efficient PVT-aware sizing framework driven by an LLM agent. Combining elite-design reuse, analytic gm/Id local sizing and global refinement under full-corner verification, AnalogScout reduces power by 43.3% relative to the evolution strategy CMA-ES at an equal budget of 16k simulations on three SKY130 OTAs of increasing complexity, and reaches the final CMA-ES power after 7.0% of that budget. It also attains lower power than Bayesian optimization on all three OTAs and than two re-implemented LLM-driven flows on the two OTAs where they were tested.
papers.summary: Analog circuit sizing must meet every specification across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners, and simulating each candidate at all corners dominates design time for both surrogate-based optimizers and recent LLM agents that still hand sizing to a global optimizer. `AnalogScout` is an LLM-agent-driven framework that reuses verified elite designs, sizes sub-blocks analytically with the gm/Id method, and performs global refinement under full-corner verification to save simulation budget. **On three SKY130 operational transconductance amplifiers it reduces power by 43.3% relative to `CMA-ES` at an equal budget of 16k simulations and reaches the final `CMA-ES` power after 7.0% of that budget.** It also achieves lower power than Bayesian optimization on all three circuits and than two re-implemented LLM-driven flows on the two circuits where they were tested.

papers.title: WCC: A Learning-Based Framework for Deciding When to Apply Cooperative Coevolution in Large-Scale Optimization
papers.abstract: Cooperative Coevolution (CC) and Non-Decomposition Algorithms (NDAs) are two primary approaches for large-scale global optimization (LSGO). Although both have achieved success, they exhibit markedly different performance across problem types and each faces approach-specific limitations, leaving the question of "when to use CC" unresolved. We address this gap with WCC, a novel learning-based framework that dynamically decides when to deploy CC in LSGO. WCC employs a streamlined design for efficient adaptive learning. We formulate the decision as a Markov decision process, designing a targeted feature set, a robust reward, and a tailored network architecture to provide the agent with rich information about the problem state and optimization progress. Our auto-regressive policy enables WCC to perform fine-grained, dynamic switching between CC and NDAs while conditionally allocating the computational budget without expert specifications. WCC shows strong competitiveness and superior generalization across problems, optimization horizons, and baseline optimizers. It realizes a "train-once and reuse" paradigm under a low budget, significantly curbing LSGO cost. Additionally, in-depth analyses yield insights not captured by existing theory, offering practical guidance on when and how to effectively deploy CC.
papers.summary: Cooperative Coevolution (CC) and Non-Decomposition Algorithms (NDAs) are the two main approaches to large-scale global optimization (LSGO), but their relative performance varies sharply by problem type and there is no settled rule for when CC is worth using. `WCC` frames that decision as a Markov decision process with a targeted feature set, a robust reward, and a tailored network, and its auto-regressive policy switches dynamically between CC and NDAs during a run while allocating computational budget without expert input. **The learned policy generalizes across problems, optimization horizons, and baseline optimizers under a train-once-and-reuse paradigm at low cost.** The accompanying analyses offer practical guidance on when and how to deploy CC that the authors say existing theory does not capture.

papers.title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization. CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations. On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.
papers.summary: Low-bit weight quantization reduces the memory footprint of large language models, but existing vector quantization (VQ) methods gain accuracy by raising the codeword dimension, which complicates independent lookup and local codeword updates. Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization (`CoS-VQ`) keeps codewords low-dimensional and instead jointly optimizes the hard indices and a scale shared across positions, addressing the coupling in which the best scale depends on the whole codeword combination and changes candidate rankings so pointwise updates stall. It gathers candidates at several probe scales and builds a tangent separable upper bound on the residual-aware quadratic objective, reducing comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales and yielding finitely many representative intervals for joint index-and-scale updates. **On `Qwen3.8-27B` the method outperforms `QTIP` and `LLVQ` on language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks**, and ablations attribute more of the gain to joint updates than to scale-only refinement.

papers.title: Aligning Institutional Power and Operational Ability
papers.abstract: To be socially sustainable, Agentic AI systems require normative designs that align responsibilities with the ability to fulfil them. Identifying incongruences such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation is crucial in avoiding normative pitfalls. In this study, we discuss design dimensions suitable for describing multi-agent systems in light of this norm-ability alignment requirement. We propose a formal framework centred on process-oriented modelling and institutional power for the analysis of a given normatively relevant process, discuss strategies for repairing it, and elaborate on how the symmetrical relation between operational process and institutional state affects the lifecycle of normative positions.
papers.summary: Agentic AI systems need normative designs in which assigned responsibilities match the ability to fulfil them, and mismatches such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation are flagged as the pitfalls to avoid.
