The paper lays out design dimensions for describing multi-agent systems under this norm-ability alignment requirement and proposes a formal framework built on process-oriented modelling and institutional power for analysing a normatively relevant process. **The core claim is that the symmetrical relation between an operational process and its institutional state governs the lifecycle of normative positions**, which the authors use to discuss repair strategies for misaligned processes.

papers.title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.

Xinxin Fan (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
Shaoye Luo (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are usually judged on final-output correctness or safety, which hides how a failure unfolds during reasoning, so this work asks whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced ones can be described in the same internal coordinates. `CauTrace` is a white-box diagnostic that defines seven functional states covering support and constraint processing, measures how changes among those states propagate across subsequent Transformer blocks, and characterizes when commitment and verification occur relative to support along with how the dominant state sequence evolves over inference. **Across `Qwen` and `LLaMA`-family models, failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment**, though the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests produce the predicted directional changes for certain models and settings.

papers.title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model
papers.abstract: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.
papers.summary: Sampling several solutions to a problem often yields paraphrases of one dominant approach rather than genuinely different methods. Agent-Conditioned Routing (`ACR`) assigns each of several parallel trajectories a persistent, untrained mask over which shared and private experts it may use in a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts model, while leaving the learned token router intact, with no roles, fine-tuning, or model copies. **On a 126-question mathematics and physics benchmark, the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among correct solutions roughly doubles under `GLM 5.3` (37.3 versus 18.7) and rises 1.67 times under `GPT-5.6 Sol` (45.00 versus 27.00) relative to the best temperature setting at matched output budgets.** A blinded expert audit confirms more multi-method solutions but lower correctness, an informed sequential prompt elicits still more diversity, and the masks add about 160 KiB of state with latency and peak VRAM within 3% of batched temperature sampling.

papers.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoding at small batch sizes is bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory, so channel selectors read only the intermediate channels predicted to matter for a token, usually those above a threshold calibrated on offline data. The authors show that calibration buys nothing: a calibrated threshold does not fix the read budget because the number of passing channels varies per input, with `Prox` calibrated for 18% actually reading 12.9% on average, and a calibration-free top-k rule on the same scores matches or beats the threshold version in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets while avoiding the repetition-loop collapse thresholds cause on `Gemma 4`. They further introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights that screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers skipped ones with a low-rank map. **Across three post-trained MoE models this reader keeps 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with `Triton` kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized `vLLM` at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches.**

papers.title: JEPA-Inspired Latent Field Prediction for Sparse-Pilot MIMO-OFDM Channel Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Accurate acquisition of full channel state information (CSI) is essential for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) wireless systems, while dense pilot-based estimation incurs substantial overhead. Directly minimizing the prediction error over raw CSI coefficients is fragile in realistic propagation environments, since small-scale fading, mobility, local scattering, and small spatial perturbations can induce large phase-sensitive variations. Nevertheless, wireless channels contain strong spatial, temporal, and frequency-domain correlations that can be more predictably represented in a latent propagation-field domain. Motivated by this observation, we propose a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA)-inspired field world model, defined as a latent predictive model of the wireless propagation field, for sparse-pilot channel reconstruction. The model maps CSI observations into latent time-frequency tokens, predicts masked or future latent field states from historical multi-band context, and fuses the predicted latent prior with sparse noisy current pilots to reconstruct the full MIMO-OFDM channel. Ray-tracing experiments show that the proposed method improves normalized mean square error (NMSE) over pilot-only and direct reconstruction baselines, supporting latent field prediction as an effective prior for sparse-pilot channel acquisition.
papers.summary: Multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems need full channel state information (CSI), but dense pilots are costly and directly regressing raw CSI coefficients is fragile because fading, mobility, and small spatial perturbations cause large phase-sensitive swings. The proposed model, inspired by the joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), maps CSI observations into latent time-frequency tokens, predicts masked or future latent field states from historical multi-band context, and fuses that latent prior with sparse noisy current pilots to reconstruct the full channel. **In ray-tracing experiments the approach lowers normalized mean square error relative to pilot-only and direct reconstruction baselines**, supporting latent field prediction as a prior for sparse-pilot channel acquisition.

papers.title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
papers.summary: Robot policies are usually evaluated on binary task success, yet deployments also care about quality attributes such as speed and motion smoothness that should be adjustable at run time. Quality-Controllable Policy (`QCP`) conditions a policy on individual quality attributes and their combinations at inference, and an iterative hindsight relabeling loop collects rollouts under target quality labels, keeps the successful ones, relabels the accumulated trajectories by their measured quality, and fine-tunes again to push the controllable range beyond the original demonstrations. **On `Robomimic` and `RoboEval` the method improves both execution quality and success rate across iterations, producing rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations.** Real-world tests show speed control raising throughput in conveyor operations and transport-stability control improving success when carrying wine glasses.

papers.title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.
papers.summary: A large language model (LLM) agent can answer a factual question correctly without retrieving the knowledge graph (KG) triples that support it, because existing KG agents are trained on data that carries answers but not evidence and rewarded on answers alone. `FoG` combines evidence-grounded synthesis, which recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions so every question comes with its supporting triples by construction, a KG interaction agent that records the triples the graph returns, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR) that credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. **On three knowledge graph question answering benchmarks, 3B to 4B open-source agents trained this way outperform substantially larger baselines in both answer accuracy and evidence coverage**, and they transfer zero-shot to unseen knowledge graphs.

papers.title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
papers.abstract:
Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations.
  A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral.
  The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.
papers.summary: Agentic entity resolution systems iteratively retrieve evidence, revise identity hypotheses, and propose graph mutations, so a wrong hypothesis can steer later retrieval into apparent self-confirmation. The proposal draws on Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and the Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI) to separate evidence the agent may reason over from evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing commits: a domain-governed function maps reconstruction-failure distinctions to identity-preserving constraints, and a two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific eligible evidence supports every required proposition, conflicts are resolved, scope is respected, and state and policy versions remain valid. Evidence admitted as unverified never gains authorization eligibility, and insufficient support leads to deferral. **This is a conceptual architecture with no implementation or empirical validation**, and the authors note it does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval.

papers.title: Beyond the Readout: A Latent Numerical Frame Shared Across Modality and Operation
papers.abstract: When a multimodal model computes 17+35 from text or 91-39 from a rendered image, it produces the same answer, 52. Does it use one internal concept of number for both, or separate machinery for each path? Similarity metrics such as RSA or CKA cannot settle this question. They give the same score to identical and to rotated directions, and two representations can look alike only because both prepare the same output digits. We therefore use causal interventions. For four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction), we learn a small subspace of Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream in which swapping coordinates swaps the model's answer. The subspaces answer three questions. First, do the conditions write numbers along the same directions? They do not. Reusing a subspace from text in an image on the same operation recovers only 53.2% of its causal effect. A single rotation and rescaling maps one subspace onto the other and raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinates. Second, does this shared geometry only reflect the digit the model is about to print? To test this, we split each subspace into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions that it cannot see. The 13 hidden directions still carry the number, yet changing them barely alters the digit being written. Third, what are these hidden directions for? A model must emit a multi-digit answer one digit at a time, so it can compute the full result early and keep it in reserve. When two numbers share their first digit, swapping the number in the hidden directions leaves the digit being written intact and redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases. The model thus forms an abstract numerical concept upstream and unfolds it across time: multimodal representations share meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames.
papers.summary: When a multimodal model adds numbers from text or subtracts them from a rendered image, it is unclear whether one shared concept of number underlies both paths, and similarity metrics like RSA or CKA cannot tell because they are blind to rotations and to shared output-digit preparation. Using causal interventions on `Gemma4-12B-it`, the authors learn a small residual-stream subspace for each of four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction) in which swapping coordinates swaps the answer. **Reusing a text subspace on images recovers only 53.2% of the causal effect, but a single rotation and rescaling raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinate frames.** Splitting each subspace into 9 directions the output layer reads and 13 it cannot see shows the hidden directions still carry the number, and swapping them redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases when two numbers share a first digit, indicating the model computes the full result early and unfolds it digit by digit.

papers.title: Bayes-Adaptive MDPs for Rollout Allocation to Enhance GRPO Training
papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has demonstrated strong performance in LLM post-training. However, it allocates a uniform rollout budget to every training question, ignoring variations in question difficulty. As a result, highly difficult questions may receive too few rollouts to generate informative positive reward signals, limiting their contribution to training, while moderately difficult questions often receive more rollouts than necessary. In this work, we formulate the problem of difficulty-aware rollout budget allocation to maximize training utility under the same total rollout budget as standard GRPO. We propose AdaRoll-GRPO, which reformulates rollout allocation as a sequential decision-making problem and leverages a Bayes-adaptive Markov decision process (MDP) to learn an adaptive allocation policy. The learned policy is computed offline and applied during GRPO training without introducing additional online optimization overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures demonstrate that AdaRoll-GRPO consistently improves GRPO training performance under a fixed rollout budget, highlighting the effectiveness of adaptive rollout allocation for GRPO in LLM post-training.
papers.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) gives every training question the same number of rollouts, so very hard questions may never produce a positive reward while moderately hard ones get more samples than they need. `AdaRoll-GRPO` casts difficulty-aware rollout allocation as a sequential decision problem and solves it with a Bayes-adaptive Markov decision process, yielding an allocation policy that is computed offline and applied during training with no extra online optimization. **Under the same total rollout budget as standard `GRPO`, the method consistently improves training performance across multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures.**

papers.title: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features
papers.abstract: A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.
papers.summary: Real software features grow through successive extensions that build on earlier code, but most feature benchmarks test a single request against a fixed codebase. `FeatureArc` evaluates coding agents on multi-stage feature evolution, with a pipeline that mines tasks from repository histories and validates fail-to-pass tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass tests for existing behavior at every stage across four programming languages, and each agent works in one persistent session without external test feedback or rollback. **Across 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages, pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code.** Trajectory analysis finds inherited defects in 72.9% of failed later stages, with agents leaving an earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time in subsequent stages, and the pipeline is used at Tencent to guide development of the `Hunyuan` model family.

papers.title: Representing the Unseen: Rethinking Visual Imagination for Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.
papers.summary: Visual world models support spatial reasoning by imagining RGB views of unobserved states, yet RGB is the default mainly because it suits generation, not because it is the best input for downstream reasoning. `ImagiRep` is a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions across seven question types in Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration settings, providing oracle RGB plus six alternative representations such as depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry of the same unseen state. **Even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, different question types benefit from different representations, and estimated RGB alone can actively mislead while alternative representations retain complementary value.** Building on this, `GEARS` is a lightweight test-time strategy that adaptively selects the representation per question and outperforms existing spatial imagination methods.

papers.title: Test-Time Communication in Trading Agent Swarms
papers.abstract: Communication between agents has mostly been studied on tasks with a shared objective and fast, clear feedback. Trading has neither: each agent manages its own account, with decisions being scored by markets late and noisily. A trading swarm is thus a population of independent decision-makers rather than a team, for which convergence is a risk and not the goal. We ran 200 agents from four model families in groups of ten under five communication regimes, from isolation to message boards and shared notes, over seven US trading days (1 to 9 October 2026), logging everything each agent read before every decision. In two of the four families, communicating groups came to hold far more of the same stocks than the isolated group. A group's return was largely the return on what its members held in common. Seeing a post from a groupmate made an agent 7 percentage points more likely to reuse an eight-word phrase from it. Agents that started too close together to see each other's posts shared such a phrase in 14% of cases, the rate that common inputs produce. Seeing the post did not detectably change that morning's trades. Case studies traced the adoption of positions and decision rules over subsequent days, and communicating groups sold in step more often than isolated ones. Because isolated groups also converged on the same stocks, sometimes completely, assessments of herding need to measure excess convergence relative to a no-peer baseline.
papers.summary: Communication among LLM agents is usually studied on cooperative tasks with fast, clear feedback, but trading gives each agent its own account and scores decisions late and noisily, so a trading swarm is a population of independent decision-makers for which convergence is a risk rather than a goal. The authors ran 200 agents from four model families in groups of ten under five communication regimes, from isolation to message boards and shared notes, across seven US trading days, logging everything each agent read before every decision. **In two of the four model families, communicating groups held far more of the same stocks than the isolated group**, a group's return was largely the return on its common holdings, and seeing a groupmate's post made an agent 7 percentage points more likely to reuse an eight-word phrase from it without detectably changing that morning's trades. Because isolated groups also converged on the same stocks, sometimes completely, the authors argue that herding must be measured as excess convergence relative to a no-peer baseline.

papers.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
papers.abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.
papers.summary: Clinical research on electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions live outside the schema in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and conclusions. `M4Bench` provides 28 derivation tasks across 15 task families on `MIMIC-IV` and `eICU` to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce these derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results, with controls that decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated `Codex` campaign with `GPT 5.4 Mini` and `GPT 5.5`, skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, but **an operational specification alone accounts for nearly all of that gain, with skills adding only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero**; decoy skills score like no skill, and a `Claude Code` replication is directionally consistent. These gains reflect partial agreement with the reference rather than completed tasks, since only 25 of 280 with-skill runs pass every strict check and skills barely change which rows agents return.

papers.title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.
papers.summary: LLM agents that cancel bookings, issue refunds, or change accounts are typically governed by rules stated in the prompt, which the model follows only as reliably as it chooses. `Concordat` is a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol in the spirit of typestate and session types and enforces it at run time: on each turn the model is offered only the tools legal in the current state, out-of-protocol calls are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when defined, and a subclass that could bypass its parent's protocol is rejected, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. On the 50 airline tasks of `tau-bench` with simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation, the standard agent made changes without the required explicit confirmation in 13 of 50 tasks with `gpt-4.1` and 29 of 128 task-runs with `Claude Haiku 5.5`, while **the Concordat agent made no such violations with no significant difference in task success**, violations that tau-bench's own reward mostly failed to detect.

papers.title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
papers.summary: Long-endurance strike drones such as Shahed-type systems are too expensive to counter at scale with conventional air defense, quadcopter interceptors lack the flight time to reach high-altitude targets at long range, and fixed-wing interceptors that could are still flown manually. The authors train a neural network policy that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands, using reinforcement learning with `proximal policy optimization` in a custom Python environment, and compare it in simulation against two classical guidance controllers. The policy outperforms the classical controllers under most simulated conditions, and **it was validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets** after deployment on a physical fixed-wing platform.

papers.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
papers.summary: Fine-grained visual perception is a bottleneck in post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), since perceptual errors limit gains from reasoning-focused optimization and dense, subjective captions are hard to turn into verifiable rewards. `PerceptRL` uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into question-answer pairs with fixed labels and rule-based rewards, chaining correlated errors and combining unrelated ones into multiple-choice items, with a specialized route for high-error domains and a domain-agnostic route for the rest. A second stage, Perception Agentic RL, handles dense cases through multi-turn inspection with visual tools, using Coordinate Injection to fix spatial drift in cold-start trajectories and a grounding-aware process reward that supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, **the method reaches 71.6% average accuracy, 15.7 points above the base model with the same tools and 5.2 points above the strongest evaluated frontier VLM**.

papers.title: How Reliable Is Individualized Functional-Network Attribution in Resting-State fMRI Cognitive Prediction in ADNI?
papers.abstract: Individualized attribution estimates which functional networks drive a model prediction for a given subject and is often proposed as an interpretable resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) biomarker, but its test-retest reliability is rarely quantified. We evaluate per-subject network-ablation attribution for a frozen resting-state functional connectivity (FC) predictor (Schaefer-200 FC predicting MMSE/ADAS-Cog13) trained on N=875 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), using, and (iii) a subject-level permutation null. Split-half reliability is near-ceiling (Spearman p=0.948/0.950) but drops on scan-rescan (p=0.609/0.616). Under the mismatched-subject null, correlations remain substantial (p~0.46-0.47), indicating strong population-shared structure, yet matched pairs exceed this null (z~6.6-6.9, p<=10-4). Thus, in ADNI, individualized network attribution contains a modest but non-zero person-specific component atop a strong population-shared pattern. We recommend reporting scan-rescan reliability together with a permutation-null control, rather than within-session proxies alone, to avoid overstating individual specificity.
papers.summary: Individualized attribution estimates which functional brain networks drive a model's prediction for a given subject and is often proposed as an interpretable resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) biomarker, but its test-retest reliability is rarely quantified. The authors evaluate per-subject network-ablation attribution for a frozen functional connectivity predictor of `MMSE` and `ADAS-Cog13` scores trained on 875 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (`ADNI`), comparing split-half reliability, scan-rescan reliability, and a subject-level permutation null. Split-half reliability is near ceiling, but **scan-rescan reliability drops to a Spearman correlation of about 0.61**, and a mismatched-subject null still reaches roughly 0.46, indicating a strong population-shared pattern with only a modest person-specific component on top. They recommend reporting scan-rescan reliability together with a permutation-null control rather than within-session proxies alone.

papers.title: HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design
papers.abstract: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across e_coli_core, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.
papers.summary: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, where cell growth is tied to synthesis of a target compound through gene deletions, typically requires a separate constraint-based search over a large space of deletion combinations for each target. The authors present a reproducible protocol that learns continuous gene-deletion priority rankings from previously curated strain designs, builds candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates them through constraint-based metabolic analysis; its learning component, `HGPRGDel`, explicitly encodes gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes jointly support a reaction or alternative genes maintain it, alongside molecular and reaction-level information. Across `e_coli_core`, `iMM904`, and `iML1515`, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among evaluated learning configurations, and **its rankings recover an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from `MetNetComp` while examining fewer genes than the baseline methods**.

papers.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning large language models on instruction data can quietly erode their safety even when no training example looks harmful, so standard content filters struggle to catch the responsible data. `SimpleLoRIF` is a scalable gradient-embedding method that simplifies a low-rank attribution approach and restricts backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, making it possible to embed datasets of around a million examples and flag those whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. On emergent misalignment, gradients connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning with AUC up to 0.865, and removing the 20% of `Tulu 3` examples most aligned with unsafe responses yields `SafeTulu`, which **reduces `GCG` attack success rate by up to 22% across `Qwen`, `Llama`, and `Olmo`** while largely preserving or improving capability and outperforming LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering. Analysis of the removed data points to under-studied sources of safety degradation such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic, and a Hugging Face Space lets researchers build customized variants of the filtered dataset.

papers.title: From Interaction to Capability: Task Advancement as State and Supervision for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: GUI memory should preserve the results of past actions and learn reusable operations. This is difficult in long-horizon workflows, where agents must use information across applications and useful operations are interleaved with failed attempts. We introduce Task Advancement Memory (TAM), which defines task advancement as verified task progress, and supports ongoing task execution and learns reusable operations. During execution, Task Advancement State represents how verified task progress changes the remaining goals, allowing the agent to build on earlier achievements across applications. After each task, advancement supervision identifies and abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result. The learned operations preserve the relation between required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions. This retains locally successful operations from both successful and failed tasks. On MobileWorld GUI-only tasks, Advancement State alone raises success from 12.0% to 28.2%. Full TAM achieves a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest evaluated baseline and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%. On SPA-Bench, TAM achieves state-of-the-art task success in the single-app English Level 3 setting.
papers.summary: GUI agents working through long-horizon workflows need memory that preserves the results of past actions and extracts reusable operations, which is difficult when useful steps are interleaved with failed attempts and span multiple applications. Task Advancement Memory (`TAM`) defines task advancement as verified progress: during execution, a Task Advancement State tracks how verified progress changes the remaining goals so the agent can build on earlier achievements across apps, and after each task, advancement supervision abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result into operations that preserve required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions, retaining useful steps from failed tasks as well as successful ones. On `MobileWorld` GUI-only tasks, the advancement state alone lifts success from 12.0% to 28.2%, and **full TAM delivers a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest baseline while cutting lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%**; it also reaches state-of-the-art success on the single-app English Level 3 setting of `SPA-Bench`.

papers.title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule. Together, monotonicity and the critical payment ensure strategyproofness and individual rationality, while the neural rule provides flexibility and imitation improves training efficiency. Empirically, on a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot represent, the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound, compared with 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served, closing 65% and 80% of the remaining optimality gap, respectively. Moreover, imitation reaches 97.5% in only 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.
papers.summary: Online resource allocation must assign scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand while ensuring agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully, and existing strategyproof reinforcement learning relies on linear allocation rules that cannot represent interactions between resources. The authors propose a strategyproof deep RL mechanism built from a monotonic neural network in which a higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it, a generalised critical payment equal to the lowest accepted value with all other inputs fixed, and training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule, which together guarantee strategyproofness and individual rationality. On a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot capture, **the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound versus 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served**, and imitation training reaches 97.5% in 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.

papers.title: Orthogonal and Parametrized Multi-Attribute Steering of LLMs
papers.abstract: Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.
papers.summary: Activation steering modifies a large language model's behavior at inference time, but it has been unclear how to keep the signal consistently strong or give the steering strength a universally interpretable meaning. The authors identify the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescale the steering range accordingly, then introduce parameterized steering, which sets activations at a desired trait strength instead of pushing them in a direction. For multi-trait steering, they find that naively combining vectors causes interference, and **orthogonalizing the vectors decouples the traits so that several behaviors can be steered simultaneously without one inducing the others**.

papers.title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning
papers.abstract: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
papers.summary: A common assumption holds that sufficiently large learners trained on enough data make explicit domain knowledge optional. The authors define structure-encoded problems, whose input-output map is determined or sharply constrained by a known solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective, and introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. **For a Gaussian inverse problem they prove that the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk while a dense empirical learner in the correct linear class retains persistent expected excess risk**, and they add a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate these mechanisms, supporting the claim that validated structure should constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins and leave learning to the components structure does not specify.

papers.title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
papers.abstract: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.
papers.summary: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision-language models (VLMs) trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration, but bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips in its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes can be read from the recorded trace, the authors measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell: the slip is readable on the tool hand, which hand was late requires sensing on both arms, and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. **Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause.** A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one, and whether the answer reports it depends on how the question is worded.

papers.title: GroundControl: Satellite-Conditioned Multi-View Diffusion for Reconstruction-Free Novel View Synthesis
papers.abstract: Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. While they can produce high quality images, they tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the input views (scene extrapolation). We propose to address this challenge for outdoor scenes by using satellite images as an additional information source to condition the multi-view generative model. We introduce a new satellite-conditioned multi-view diffusion model that combines conditioning from a satellite image and street-level input images when generating novel-views. Our cross-attention based conditioning allows us to retain pretrained multi-view diffusion priors to generate seamless, realistic, novel views from a handful of source views, while also adhering to the scene layout as seen from satellite images. Our model does not use 3D scene reconstruction, and only relies on posed street and satellite views. Our experiments on outdoor datasets show that our model is better than both satellite-conditioned or street-view conditioned baselines on novel-view synthesis, especially on challenging cases where target views have very little overlap with source views. Project page: https://nianticspatial.github.io/groundcontrol
papers.summary: Multi-view and video diffusion models produce high-quality novel views from sparse image collections but tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the inputs. `GroundControl` conditions a pretrained multi-view diffusion model on a satellite image in addition to posed street-level views through cross-attention, retaining the pretrained multi-view priors while keeping generated views consistent with the scene layout seen from above, and it requires no 3D scene reconstruction. On outdoor datasets, **the model outperforms both satellite-conditioned and street-view-conditioned baselines, with the largest gains on target views that overlap very little with the source views**.

papers.title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to determine 'when' residual control should become active and correction geometry to determine 'where' in residual action space autonomous refinement should explore; task reward determines 'what' residual is ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC improves average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%. The human corrections define task-dependent 2-3 dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain 96.0-97.7% of squared correction magnitude. Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction itself to serve as the final action target.
papers.summary: Imitation policies that execute most of a manipulation trajectory reliably can still fail in localized regions that require last-mile precision, and updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. Adaptive Residual Correction (`ARC`) is a lightweight post-training module that learns a residual correction with reinforcement learning on top of a frozen policy, using pre-intervention states from sparse human corrections to decide when residual control should activate and the geometry of those corrections to decide where in residual action space to explore, while task reward decides what residual is finally executed. **Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC raises average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%**, and the human corrections define task-dependent two- to three-dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain about 96 to 98% of squared correction magnitude.

papers.title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
papers.abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.
papers.summary: Manipulation policies for articulated objects are evaluated mostly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded motion is one the object's kinematics admit. Constraint-Referenced Strategy (`CRS`) projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste, and needs only a joint model plus a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, with no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, binary success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none of them, whereas the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature; **a door-trained behavior-cloning policy that opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes commands about 40 times the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy in its successful passes, 1.27 versus 0.032 rad/s**. CRS verdicts stay unchanged under joint-axis errors up to 30 degrees, compared with roughly 8 degrees for absolute thresholds.

papers.title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
papers.abstract:
Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity.
  Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion.
  Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.
papers.summary: Selective prediction systems defer ambiguous cases to human experts and automate high-confidence decisions, but this safety mechanism assumes that uncertainty scores reflect genuine clinical ambiguity. Under the severe class imbalance typical of prognostic tasks, the authors argue, standard uncertainty measures instead become a proxy for class membership and systematically penalize minority-class patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts covering multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease, **their `CCR` correction combined with threshold-aware metrics maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories, while global metrics either collapsed minority sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients**; applying the correction with standard entropy fails because it breaks within-class monotonicity. They recommend threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation for any clinical pipeline deploying selective prediction under imbalance.

papers.title: Gym-Anything-RT: Scaling Real-Time Environments for Vision-Language Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents have made substantial progress in domains where they have a non-trivial amount of time to deliberate between actions, such as mathematics, software engineering, and performing tasks on desktop applications. It is less clear how such models fare in settings that demand real-time interaction, such as playing a video game or operating a physical device. In these settings, the environment state may evolve as the agent is reasoning, or even as the underlying model is performing a forward pass. To gain insight into the real-time interaction capabilities of vision-language agents, we introduce Gym-Anything-RT. Our key idea is to construct visual minigames that demand a portfolio of capabilities required for interactive real-time settings. Gym-Anything-RT uses an agentic pipeline to automatically generate such environments based on a taxonomy of six capabilities required for real-time interaction, including the ability to perceive the environment and act under an evolving environment state. A key feature of Gym-Anything-RT is that it allows for controlled comparison of real-time interaction capabilities: we can run the same minigame in real time, or pause or slow down the environment to relax the requirement for real-time actions. We use Gym-Anything-RT to construct 100 real-time minigames and evaluate AI agents on them. We find large capability gaps in real-time interaction. For example, GPT-6 Astra (xHigh) achieves a pass rate of only 9.0% on the real-time minigames, which rises to 75.0% when the environment is paused. We also identify intriguing behaviors by the most powerful frontier agents: for instance, when given the ability to write code, these agents write code that bypasses the need to perceive and act in real time. We publicly release Gym-Anything-RT and the generated minigames to spur further research on AI agents in real-time interactive settings.
papers.summary: AI agents have progressed in domains where they can deliberate between actions, such as mathematics, software engineering, and desktop applications, but it is unclear how they fare when the environment keeps evolving while the model reasons or even during a single forward pass. `Gym-Anything-RT` uses an agentic pipeline to automatically generate visual minigames from a taxonomy of six capabilities required for real-time interaction, and each minigame can be run in real time, paused, or slowed down to isolate the cost of acting under time pressure. Evaluating agents on 100 generated minigames reveals large gaps: **`GPT-6 Astra (xHigh)` passes only 9.0% of the minigames in real time but 75.0% when the environment is paused**. The strongest frontier agents, when given the ability to write code, produce programs that bypass the need to perceive and act in real time, and the benchmark and generated minigames are publicly released.

papers.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
papers.abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss.
