Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.
papers.summary: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants, yet AI agents are still mostly trained and benchmarked in isolation. `TeamGym` constructs team decision-making problems from real legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora and introduces a method to identify pivotal information, a minimal set of facts each necessary and jointly sufficient for the correct decision, which lets it control how that information is distributed and track whether agents identify and integrate it. Across 8 language models and 12 source corpora, **distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average compared with giving the same information to a single model**, and requiring participants to retrieve it from source material rather than receiving it directly costs a further 19.9 points. Training policies with reinforcement learning on team decision loss improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

papers.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We further develop a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Building on this analysis, we distill a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes along the target SID path, jointly optimizing this objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing GR baselines and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.
papers.summary: Generative recommendation (GR) autoregressively generates discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) for items, but randomly initialized SID token embeddings and models trained from scratch do not inherit the semantic relations among items, and collaborative relations are learned only implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. `REGER` incorporates inter-item relations explicitly across semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation: it pretrains the model through generative semantic retrieval, learning to generate the SIDs of semantic neighbors, and combines global attention with local attention aligned to SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. The authors also prove an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions over the SID prefix tree and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional terms, which motivates distilling a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens along the target SID path jointly with cross-entropy. **Experiments on real-world datasets show consistent improvements over existing GR baselines** and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.

papers.title: Timestral
papers.abstract: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.
papers.summary: A family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, at 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters, is trained with three ingredients. Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF) separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value acts as both a forecast target and context for later forecasts, while a covariate framework natively supports known-future covariates within the causal architecture and a two-stage pipeline pretrains only on a large synthetic corpus before post-training on mixed real and synthetic data with extended context. **The two largest models take the top two places on every metric of `GIFT-Eval`, `TIME`, and `fev-bench`.** Weights for all four models and inference code are released.

papers.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
papers.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.
papers.summary: World models are proposed as the component that lets agents reason over long temporal and spatial horizons, but current evaluations report task performance without testing whether the learned latent dynamics reflect the environment's structure. A faithful latent world model is defined through an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics, and latent rollout consistency (LRC) is proposed as a metric for action-conditioned latent prediction. **Across the state-of-the-art latent world models studied, none solves its task by faithfully modeling the environment's dynamics.**

papers.title: GAS-PFN: Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Zero-Shot Traffic Forecasting
papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting requires modeling complex temporal dynamics and the spatial dependencies imposed by road topology. Supervised graph-based models achieve strong performance, but are often trained for a particular dataset and sensor graph, making deployment to new or evolving networks costly. Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) offer a zero-shot alternative by learning in-context inference from synthetic task priors, which provide an explicit mechanism for encoding domain-specific assumptions. Existing forecasting PFNs, however, do not explicitly represent the graph-structured dependencies governing traffic dynamics. To combine graph-aware traffic modeling with zero-shot adaptation, we introduce the Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Network (GAS-PFN). GAS-PFN incorporates sampled road topology into its synthetic task prior through random-walk diffusion, teaching the model to learn graph-coupled dynamics during pretraining. Its co-designed inference architecture uses two mask-conditioned passes through a shared Transformer backbone to separately model sensor-specific temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal interactions among neighboring sensors before integrating their representations for prediction. This design enables GAS-PFN to use target-network structure and context without parameter updates. Across six benchmarks at the 90-minute horizon, GAS-PFN reduces MSE by 34.0% on average relative to TimePFN, its closest PFN-based predecessor. It also reduces MSE by 27.7% on average relative to four recent industry-developed general-purpose zero-shot forecasters. In this comparison, all models receive 90 minutes of contiguous recent history, and any additional context is drawn from each dataset's chronological training split. These results indicate that aligning PFN priors and inference architectures with graph structure improves in-context learning for zero-shot traffic forecasting.
papers.summary: Supervised graph-based traffic forecasters perform well but are tied to one dataset and sensor graph, so moving them to new or evolving road networks is costly. Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) learn in-context inference from synthetic task priors, and `GAS-PFN` makes that prior graph-aware by sampling road topology through random-walk diffusion, while its inference architecture runs two mask-conditioned passes through a shared Transformer backbone to model per-sensor temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal interactions among neighboring sensors before combining them, all without parameter updates on the target network. Across six benchmarks at the 90-minute horizon, **it reduces MSE by 34.0% on average relative to `TimePFN`**, its closest PFN-based predecessor, and by 27.7% relative to four recent industry-developed general-purpose zero-shot forecasters given the same 90 minutes of recent history.

papers.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
papers.abstract: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.
papers.summary: Existing image generation and editing benchmarks give little guidance on where compact on-device models fall short of server-side ones. `MoI-Bench` is grounded in mobile user needs, crossing 16 operations such as removal and replacement with eight visual target categories such as portraits and text to define 64 subtasks over 1150 samples, and the companion `MoI-Eval` scores instruction following, visual quality, and detail preservation with task-specific criteria aggregated into capability profiles along the operation, target, and criteria axes. Evaluating on-device and server-side models together with measured mobile deployment costs, a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability map shows that **current on-device models already generate and edit efficiently, so expanding task coverage deserves more attention than further deployment optimization**, with identity preservation and text rendering as the main quality gaps.

papers.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
papers.abstract: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.
papers.summary: When an audio-language model changes its answer after a local sound event is edited, the change could reflect sensitivity to the event's class, to the waveform rewrite itself, or both. The protocol compares same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event that share the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, with only the same-class replacement preserving the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, **different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements**, while same-class accuracy stays within 5.2 points of original accuracy and soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class reaches 73.7 to 81.9%.

papers.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning helps multimodal large language models (MLLMs) understand video, but text-only reasoning traces give no reliable way to revisit visual evidence, causing visual forgetting. Existing fixes either reference evidence by textual coordinates, which name locations rather than content, or reinsert cropped regions and frames at the cost of a much larger context. `VideoLVR` instead builds latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant moments and supervises it with a visual token prediction objective that casts visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, so text tokens and latent visual states share one token-prediction framework, and the same setup extends to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions optimized with final-answer rewards. **It improves video understanding across multiple benchmarks without substantially expanding the multimodal context**, with the largest gains on tasks that require fine-grained visual evidence.

papers.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
papers.abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.
papers.summary: When a discussion among LLM agents is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims most relevant to the decision criteria, and on hidden-profile tasks both look attractive because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. `CrossProfile` is a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates (480 tasks) with automatically verified answer keys in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed. Across `Qwen2.5-7B`, `Llama-3.1-8B`, and two `DeepSeek` models, relevance-based selection readmits on-topic decoys and loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration, while rarest-first is no better than random on average, and the decision model adds a social-proof failure by over-weighting facts attributed to many agents. **Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random, raises accuracy by 13 to 24 points**, and in natural discussions the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

papers.title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models
papers.abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.
papers.summary: Language models pretrained on web corpora spanning several years absorb both general and domain-specific knowledge, but how these kinds of knowledge are acquired as pretraining progresses is unclear. Using point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years, a temporal variability score (TVS) is defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across those models, with higher scores suggesting knowledge that is less consistently represented across years of web text. Evaluating six benchmarks with six models from multiple open-source families shows that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on, and **at the end of pretraining high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings**, by an average of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. The pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks and holds even when comparing items of similar difficulty.
papers.highlight_summary:
Language models pretrained on multi-year web crawls learn both stable general knowledge and knowledge whose prevalence shifts over time, but exact-match corpus counts cannot track what is learned when because the same fact is phrased in many ways. The authors instead score each benchmark item by how much its likelihood varies across models trained on different yearly web snapshots, and use that temporal variability as a wording-agnostic diagnostic of knowledge acquisition during pretraining.

- The temporal variability score `TVS` is the coefficient of variation of the per-token negative log-likelihood of each question plus gold answer across eight `PIT-4B` models trained on yearly `FineWeb` partitions from 2017 to 2024, with mean-normalization being essential because raw NLL standard deviation mostly selects harder items and reverses the result.
- The analysis covers 16,239 items from `ARC-Easy`, `ARC-Challenge`, `MMLU`, `HellaSwag`, `PIQA`, and `WinoGrande`, split into length-matched low, medium, and high `TVS` tertiles and tracked in chance-normalized accuracy across checkpoints of `Pythia` 1.4B and 6.9B, `TinyLlama` 1.1B, `SmolLM3` 3B, and `OLMo` 1B and 7B.
- Low- and high-`TVS` items start out indistinguishable (the low group leads in 13 of 24 early `Pythia` and `OLMo` checkpoints), but high-`TVS` items improve faster in the second half of training and finish ahead in **34 of 36** model–benchmark settings by an average of **+7.3 points**, from 1.7 on `WinoGrande` to 16.1 on `PIQA`.
- Much of that gap is difficulty rather than an independent `TVS` effect: conditioning on mean NLL roughly halves it to +3.7, it stays positive in all 18 `ARC` and `MMLU` settings (+6.9) but nearly vanishes on the commonsense benchmarks (+0.5), full conditioning leaves only +1.4, and answer-specific `TVS` predicts late gold-versus-distractor margin growth on `ARC` and `MMLU` at p below 10⁻⁶.
- Limitations include a single 4B point-in-time model size, one training run per setting so the confidence intervals reflect cross-setting variation rather than run-to-run noise, a late-slope advantage that is not significant across the four family averages (p = .13), contamination checks that cover only the `PIT-4B` corpus and not the evaluated models' own data, and a scope restricted to likelihood-ranked multiple-choice benchmarks.

papers.title: MuonGS: Pretraining LLMs with Relaxed Weight-Norm Control
papers.abstract:
Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints improve optimizer performance in language model pretraining, yet a unified understanding of why such control helps and how much is needed remains incomplete. We analyze norm control in Muon over the entire training trajectory using the \emph{accumulated effective learning rate}, $C_T=\sum_{t<T}\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$, where $\eta_t$ is the nominal learning rate and $\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$ is the effective learning rate relative to the weight norm. For bounded update directions, accumulation over any training interval bounds relative weight displacement. We show that vanilla Muon can accumulate only logarithmically, potentially limiting exploration and helping explain its slower empirical progress, whereas MuonW and MuonH guarantee at least linear accumulation under the stated conditions. Going beyond bounded-norm control, we show that sufficiently slow norm growth guarantees faster accumulation than the logarithmic worst case, opening up less restrictive optimizer designs.
  Based on this insight, we propose MuonGS, which uses Gram--Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of each Muon update without fixing the weight norm. With bounded update directions and a constant nominal learning rate, we prove that the weight norm grows at most proportionally to $\sqrt{t}$ after $t$ steps. Consequently, MuonGS guarantees $C_T=\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, with accumulation sustained even in later training. Further, for smooth scale-invariant objectives we establish its $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity guarantee. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models as well as a 135M active- and 1B total- parameter MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long training horizons. In particular, for the dense model it achieves an estimated token-equivalent speedup up to about $15\%$ at matched validation loss to MuonH.
papers.summary: Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints help the `Muon` optimizer in language model pretraining, but why such control helps and how much is needed has lacked a unified explanation. The analysis tracks the accumulated effective learning rate, the sum over steps of the nominal learning rate divided by the weight's Frobenius norm, which bounds relative weight displacement for bounded update directions, and shows that vanilla `Muon` accumulates only logarithmically while `MuonW` and `MuonH` guarantee at least linear accumulation, with sufficiently slow norm growth enough to beat the logarithmic worst case. `MuonGS` uses Gram-Schmidt projection to remove the radial component of each update without fixing the weight norm, which provably keeps norm growth at most proportional to the square root of the step count, sustains accumulation into late training, and gives an O(T^-1/2) stationarity guarantee for smooth scale-invariant objectives. In pretraining of 160M and 400M dense models and a 135M-active, 1B-total mixture-of-experts model, it reaches lower validation perplexity than `MuonH` at long horizons, with **an estimated token-equivalent speedup of up to about 15% at matched validation loss** for the dense model.

papers.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
papers.summary: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation, so the question is whether large language models (LLMs) dropped into a world with altered physics can notice behavior such as heavier objects falling more slowly and uncover the changed law through experiments without being told what to investigate. `LongChang` is an automated framework that generates simulated worlds in which one or more physical laws differ from ordinary physics, lets the evaluated LLM manipulate objects and build tools to pursue its own questions with no research task or hints, and uses separate LLM agents to generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and grade reports for correctness and experimental support, with exploration records driving scene evolution so the whole cycle runs without human intervention. **Among 12 LLMs, `GPT-6-Astra` reaches a discovery rate of 16.7% while the other 11 score 0%**, and the exploration records show anomalies left uninvestigated and only partial identification of the altered laws.

papers.title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry
papers.abstract: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the \texttt{diffrax} library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30\% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4--5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics--machine-learning modelling.
papers.summary: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are usually distributed in the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP) language, which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are built. `KPPax` compiles KPP mechanisms into differentiable, just-in-time compiled, vectorisable JAX code, evaluating rate laws with sparse operations in log space and integrating the stiff system with the implicit solvers and forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the `diffrax` library, so exact sensitivities come without hand-derived adjoint code. On the `POLLU` benchmark mechanism, a Fisher information matrix from the automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts before any fit which of 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable coefficients to within about 30% while revealing clusters of fast reactions where only ratios are constrained. A neural-network correction to an emission inventory, trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, **reduces biogenic correction error by a factor of 2.4 to 5** and recovers low-temperature emission information that the individual retrievals lose.

papers.title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
papers.abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = \Psi(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $\Psi$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.
papers.summary: Relations compose through the entity they share and the order of composition matters, so verifying a composed relation means closing a loop. Assuming each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently, the authors show that in the pure-gauge sector relations sharing no cycle cannot interact at all, that the only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy, the product of the three edge transforms around the loop known as a Wilson loop, and that the only equivariant edge update applies a conjugation-equivariant function of that holonomy to the edge, so edge attention through Wilson loops is the unique form the symmetry permits. Commuting-operator knowledge graph embeddings are the abelian sector of this form, `AlphaFold`'s triangle update and the `Edge Transformer` share its shape without its constraints, and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. Instantiated as holonomy attention on general relational graphs with no training, **it infers unobserved S4 relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083**, flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 versus a 0.76 cap for commuting scores, and separates clusters without labels.

papers.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation generalize only as far as their action-labeled demonstrations cover, while human videos offer far broader experience but no explicit action grounding. `ThinkWorld` represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens capturing the intermediate dynamics from the current world state to a future one, which serves as a common action representation across embodiments. The CoD is first initialized from action-labeled demonstrations, then the framework predicts the future each CoD would induce and reinforces those whose predictions better match the observed outcome, so videos without action annotations supervise the same reasoning space through their observed state transitions. **Experiments in simulation and on real robots show effective human-to-robot transfer** and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

papers.title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.
papers.summary: Radiance fields and splatting have advanced novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction, but their memory and compute demands limit use in resource-constrained settings. `Hexels` are planar hexagonal surface elements carrying a first-order spatial color field, so locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance can be covered by fewer, larger primitives whose hexagonal support is area- and boundary-efficient while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, **they improve PSNR over memory-matched `2DGS` by 4.53 to 7.38 dB** while using less training VRAM, and per primitive they beat `2DGS` by up to 4.74 dB at 2.31 times the frame rate. For surface reconstruction they reduce error by 28.9% versus memory-matched `2DGS` on 15 `DTU` scans, achieve the highest mean F1 among compared methods on six `Tanks and Temples` scenes (34.38% versus 31.72%), and also improve 2D image representation over `Image-GS`.
